### Section 1: Methodological Analogy for Investigating Justice (Book 2, 368c–369d)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Glaucon (group insistence), Adeimantus (responses).  
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: <entity>Justice</entity> is under attack; defense requires full inquiry into <entity>justice</entity> and <entity>injustice</entity>'s benefits (group demand).
- **Premise 2**: Inquiry is complex, like reading small writing from afar; use analogy of larger copy (scaled-up version) for easier discernment.
- **Conclusion**: Study <entity>justice</entity> first in the larger <entity>city</entity> (bigger scale), then analogize to the <entity>individual</entity> (smaller likeness).  
  *Relationship*: This sets up the entire dialogue's method; cross-ref to later city construction (Section 2) as application. Relates to epistemology: sharp "eyesight" needed for <entity>knowledge</entity> of <entity>virtue</entity>.

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "justice coming under attack, and not come to her defence for as long as I have breath in my body and a tongue in my head. So the best thing is to make what defence I can."
- **Glaucon and others**: Insisted on full defense; demanded investigation into what <entity>justice</entity> and <entity>injustice</entity> are, and their true benefits.
- **Socrates**: "The enquiry we are undertaking is not a simple matter. If you ask me, it requires sharp eyesight. And since we are not clever people, I think we should conduct our search in the same sort of way as we would if our eyesight were not very good, and we were told to read some small writing from a bit of a distance away, and then one of us realised that a larger copy of the same writing, apparently, was to be found somewhere else, on some larger surface. We would regard it as a stroke of luck, I think, to be able to read the large letters first, and then turn our attention to the small ones, to see if they really did say the same thing."
- **Adeimantus**: "We certainly would. But where can you see anything like that in our search for <entity>justice</entity>?"
- **Socrates**: "I’ll tell you. We say that there is <entity>justice</entity> in an <entity>individual</entity>; but also, I take it, <entity>justice</entity> in a whole <entity>city</entity>?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes."
- **Socrates**: "And a <entity>city</entity> is something bigger than an <entity>individual</entity>?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, it is."
- **Socrates**: "In that case, maybe <entity>justice</entity> will be on a larger scale in what is larger, and easier to find out about. So if you approve, why don’t we start by finding out what sort of thing it is in <entity>cities</entity>? After that we can make a similar inquiry into the <entity>individual</entity>, trying to find the likeness of the larger version in the form the smaller takes."
- **Adeimantus**: "I think that’s a good idea."

### Section 2: Theoretical Origin of the City and Justice (Book 2, 369d–370a)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Adeimantus (responses).  
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: <entity>City</entity> originates from human <entity>needs</entity> and lack of <entity>self-sufficiency</entity>; associations form to meet varied wants.
- **Premise 2**: Studying city's origin reveals origins of <entity>justice</entity> and <entity>injustice</entity>; larger scale makes it easier.
- **Conclusion**: Proceed with constructing hypothetical <entity>city</entity> from basics (food, housing, clothing); approve as major but worthwhile task.  
  *Relationship*: Builds on Section 1's analogy; leads to <entity>division of labor</entity> (Section 3). Cross-ref: <entity>City</entity> as macrocosm of <entity>individual soul</entity> (metaphysical parallel).

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "Suppose then, we were to study the theoretical origin of a <entity>city</entity>, would we also see the origin in it of <entity>justice</entity> and <entity>injustice</entity>?"
- **Adeimantus**: "We might."
- **Socrates**: "And if we do that, is there a chance that what we are looking for will be easier to find?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, much easier."
- **Socrates**: "You think, then, that this is a task we should attempt to complete? I suspect it is a fairly major undertaking, so you decide."
- **Adeimantus**: "We have decided. Go ahead."
- **Socrates**: "Very well. The origin of a <entity>city</entity> lies, I think, in the fact that we are not, any of us, <entity>self-sufficient</entity>; we have all sorts of <entity>needs</entity>. Can you think of any other reason for the foundation of a <entity>city</entity>?"
- **Adeimantus**: "No, I can’t."
- **Socrates**: "Different <entity>individuals</entity>, then, form associations with one person to meet one <entity>need</entity>, and with another person to meet a different <entity>need</entity>. With this variety of wants they may collect a number of partners and allies into one place of habitation, and to this joint habitation we give the name '<entity>city</entity>', don’t we?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, we do."
- **Socrates**: "Does one person share with another, when he does share—or does he accept a share—because he thinks it is better for him personally?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, he does."

### Section 3: Basic Needs and Division of Labor (Book 2, 370a–370e)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Adeimantus (responses).  
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: Primary <entity>needs</entity>: food, housing, clothing, shoes → Requires specialists (farmer, builder, weaver, shoemaker).
- **Premise 2**: Sharing is better than self-provision; individuals differ in natural aptitudes; one task per person yields better, timelier results.
- **Conclusion**: Basic <entity>city</entity> needs 4–5 people; <entity>division of labor</entity> essential for efficiency.  
  *Relationship*: Expands Section 2's origin; cross-ref to tools and expansion (later in section). Ethical implication: Mutual benefit fosters <entity>justice</entity>.

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "Right then. Let’s construct a hypothetical <entity>city</entity>, from the beginning. It is the product, apparently, of our <entity>needs</entity>."
- **Adeimantus**: "Of course."
- **Socrates**: "And the first and most important of those <entity>needs</entity>, if we are to exist and stay alive, is the provision of food."
- **Adeimantus**: "Unquestionably."
- **Socrates**: "Second comes the need for housing, and third the need for clothing and things like that."
- **Adeimantus**: "That is right."
- **Socrates**: "Well then, how will our <entity>city</entity> be equal to meeting these requirements? Won’t it just be one farmer, plus a builder, plus a weaver? Or should we add a shoemaker as well, and anyone else who provides for physical <entity>needs</entity>?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, we should."
- **Socrates**: "So the most basic <entity>city</entity> would have to consist of four or five men."
- **Adeimantus**: "It looks like it."
- **Socrates**: "Next question. Should each one of them make what he produces available to all alike? Should the one farmer, for example, provide food for four? Should he put four times the hours, and four times the effort, into the production of food, and then share it with the others? Or should he forget about them and provide for himself alone, producing only a quarter of the amount of food in a quarter of the time—and of the remaining three-quarters, devote a quarter each to the provision of housing, of clothing, and of footwear? That way he would save himself the trouble of sharing with others, and provide for his own <entity>needs</entity> by his own <entity>individual</entity> efforts."
- **Adeimantus**: "No, Socrates, the other way is probably easier."
- **Socrates**: "That’s certainly what you’d expect. And one thing immediately struck me when you said that, which is that one <entity>individual</entity> is by nature quite unlike another <entity>individual</entity>, that they differ in their natural aptitudes, and that different people are equipped to perform different tasks. Don’t you think so?"
- **Adeimantus**: "I do."
- **Socrates**: "Well, then. Will a single <entity>individual</entity> do better exercising a number of skills, or will each do best concentrating on one?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Concentrating on one."
- **Socrates**: "And another thing. It is clear, I think, that if you let the right moment for a task pass by, the task suffers."
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, that is clear."
- **Socrates**: "That is because the task in hand will not wait for the person doing it to have a spare moment. So it is essential that whoever is doing it should concentrate on it, and not regard it as a hobby."
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, it is essential."
- **Socrates**: "It follows from this that in any enterprise more is produced—and that it is better and more easily produced—when one person does a single task which is suited to his nature, and does it at the right time, keeping himself free from other tasks."
- **Adeimantus**: "It certainly does."

### Section 4: Expansion of the City – Tools, Trades, and Herdsmen (Book 2, 370e–371c)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Adeimantus (responses).  
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: Specialists need tools (e.g., farmer needs plough from carpenter); adds blacksmiths, etc.
- **Premise 2**: Herdsmen needed for oxen, hides, wool to support agriculture and crafts.
- **Conclusion**: <entity>City</entity> grows crowded but not yet large; imports necessary due to location.  
  *Relationship*: Applies <entity>division of labor</entity> (Section 3); leads to trade/economy (next). Cross-ref: Growth mirrors soul's parts in metaphysics.

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "Then it will take more than four citizens, Adeimantus, to provide for the <entity>needs</entity> we were talking about. The farmer, it appears, will not make himself a plough with his own hands—not if it’s going to be a good plough—nor a hoe, nor any of his other farming implements. No more will the builder, who also needs a number of tools. And the same goes for the weaver and the shoemaker."
- **Adeimantus**: "True."
- **Socrates**: "So carpenters, and blacksmiths, and a whole lot of skilled workers of that kind, will become partners in our little <entity>city</entity>, and make the place quite crowded."
- **Adeimantus**: "They will."
- **Socrates**: "All the same, it still won’t be all that large, even if we add cattlemen, shepherds and other herdsmen, so that the farmers can have oxen for ploughing, and so that builders as well as the farmers will be able to use animals for carrying materials, and so that weavers and shoemakers can have hides and wool."
- **Adeimantus**: "It certainly won’t be a small <entity>city</entity>, if it contains all that."
- **Socrates**: "That’s not all. It will be more or less impossible to locate the <entity>city</entity> itself in a place where it won’t need imports."
- **Adeimantus**: "Quite impossible."
- **Socrates**: "So it will require yet more people in addition, to bring it the things it <entity>needs</entity> from some other <entity>city</entity>."
- **Adeimantus**: "It will."

### Section 5: Trade, Merchants, and Market Economy (Book 2, 371c–372a)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Adeimantus (responses).  
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: Exports needed for imports; requires more producers and merchants (seafaring if by sea).
- **Premise 2**: Internal trade via buying/selling creates marketplace and currency; retailers/dealers handle exchanges (weakest physically).
- **Premise 3**: Hired laborers offer manual strength for hire.
- **Conclusion**: <entity>City</entity> now complete; <entity>justice</entity>/<entity>injustice</entity> may arise from mutual <entity>needs</entity> among elements.  
  *Relationship*: Culminates basic economy; cross-ref to simple life (Section 6) as test of <entity>justice</entity>. Ethical: Cooperation implies <entity>virtue</entity>.

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "What is more, if their agent goes empty-handed, taking nothing which meets the <entity>needs</entity> of the people from whom they are importing the things they are short of, then he will come back empty-handed, won’t he?"
- **Adeimantus**: "I think so."
- **Socrates**: "So in their own economy the citizens must not only provide adequately for themselves; they must also produce the right kind of goods—and in large enough quantities—for the people they need to trade with."
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, they must."
- **Socrates**: "So our <entity>city</entity> needs more farmers, and more workers in other occupations."
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes."
- **Socrates**: "And more agents as well, presumably, the ones who are going to do all the importing and exporting. These people are <entity>merchants</entity>, aren’t they?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes."
- **Socrates**: "So we shall need <entity>merchants</entity> as well."
- **Adeimantus**: "Definitely."
- **Socrates**: "And if our trade is by sea, we shall need a large number of other people as well—experts on seafaring."
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes, a large number."
- **Socrates**: "What about trade in the <entity>city</entity> itself? How will each group share its production with others? That after all was our reason for forming an association and establishing a <entity>city</entity>."
- **Adeimantus**: "Obviously, by buying and selling."
- **Socrates**: "That will give rise to a market-place and a currency, a unit of exchange for transactions."
- **Adeimantus**: "Undoubtedly."
- **Socrates**: "But when the farmer, or member of one of the other occupations, brings to market part of what he produces, he may not arrive there at the same moment as those who need to exchange goods with him. Is he going to sit around in the market-place, taking time off from his work?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Certainly not. There are people who identify this <entity>need</entity>, and make themselves available for this activity. In a well-run <entity>city</entity> they tend to be the weakest physically, those who are useless for any other kind of work. They have to wait around there in the market-place, receiving goods in exchange for money from those who have something to sell, and then again money in return for goods from all those who want to buy."
- **Socrates**: "So this is the <entity>need</entity>, which brings <entity>dealers</entity> into our <entity>city</entity>. Don’t we call people <entity>dealers</entity>, if they sit there in the market-place offering a selling and buying service, whereas those who travel round the <entity>cities</entity> we call <entity>merchants</entity>?"
- **Adeimantus**: "We do."
- **Socrates**: "And there is still another group of people, I think, offering a service. We certainly would not want them as partners or associates for their mental attributes, but they possess physical strength suitable for manual labour. This they offer for sale, and the price they put on it they call their hire. That, I imagine, is why they in turn are called <entity>hired labourers</entity>. Isn’t that right?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes."
- **Socrates**: "So <entity>hired labourers</entity>, it seems, will also go to fill up our <entity>city</entity>."
- **Adeimantus**: "I think they may."
- **Socrates**: "Well then, Adeimantus, is our <entity>city</entity> now large enough? Is it complete?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Maybe it is."
- **Socrates**: "In which case, where exactly are <entity>justice</entity> and <entity>injustice</entity> to be found in it? In which of the elements we have examined have they made their appearance?"
- **Adeimantus**: "Speaking for myself, Socrates, I have no idea—unless, I suppose, it is in some sort of <entity>need</entity> which those elements have of one another."
- **Socrates**: "I think that may be the right answer. We must examine it without hesitation."

### Section 6: The Healthy, Simple City and Glaucon's Critique (Book 2, 372a–373a)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Adeimantus (initial), Glaucon (interruption and critique).  
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: In simple economy, people meet basic <entity>needs</entity> (bread, wine, clothing, housing) peacefully, avoiding poverty/war; live happily with moderation (barley cakes, garlands, songs to gods).
- **Premise 2**: Glaucon critiques as "city of pigs" (lacking luxury like couches, cooked dishes).
- **Conclusion**: Acknowledge simple city as "healthy"; examine "swollen" luxurious version to find <entity>justice</entity>/<entity>injustice</entity> origins.  
  *Relationship*: Tests Section 5's economy; Glaucon's shift introduces luxury (next). Cross-ref: Footnote 23 (Hesiod's golden age); Footnote 24 (pigs as uncouth symbol). Ethical: Simplicity embodies <entity>virtue</entity>; excess breeds <entity>injustice</entity>.

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "Let’s look first at the way people will spend their time in an economy of this kind. Won’t it be that they produce bread and wine and clothing and shoes? They will build themselves houses. In summer they will go about their work lightly clad, and barefoot, and in winter they will be properly clothed and shod. They will live on barley-meal and wheat flour. Kneading and baking these, they will have fine barley cakes or wheat loaves served on reeds or fresh leaves. They will eat lying on straw beds covered with bryony and myrtle. They can live very well like this—they and their children. Drinking wine after their meals, wearing garlands on their heads, and singing the praises of the gods, they will live quite happily with one another. They will have no more children than they can afford, and they will avoid poverty and war." [Footnote 23: The picture borrows from Hesiod’s *Works and Days* (109-126) golden age; sentimental view of peasant life; Glaucon's contempt as city-dweller's.]
- **Glaucon**: "No art of cookery, apparently, for these people you describe as living so well."
- **Socrates**: "That’s a good point. I forgot that they will have the art of cookery. Obviously they will use salt, and olives, and cheese, and they will boil the usual country dishes of wild roots and vegetables. And for dessert we can offer them figs and chickpeas and beans; and they will roast myrtle berries and acorns in front of the fire, with a modest amount to drink. In this way, living lives which are peaceful and in all probability healthy, they will die in old age, handing down the same way of life to their descendants."
- **Glaucon**: "If you were organising a <entity>city</entity> of pigs, Socrates, isn’t that just how you would feed them?" [Footnote 24: Pigs as slow, stupid, dirty—emblem of uncouthness (cf. 535e).]
- **Socrates**: "Well, what sort of meals should we give them, Glaucon?"
- **Glaucon**: "The usual kind. If they are going to eat in comfort, they should lie on couches, eat off tables, and have the cooked dishes and desserts which people today have."
- **Socrates**: "I see. So we are not just looking at the origin of a <entity>city</entity>, apparently. We are looking at the origin of a luxurious <entity>city</entity>. Maybe that’s not such a bad idea. If we look at that sort of <entity>city</entity> too, we may perhaps see the point where <entity>justice</entity> and <entity>injustice</entity> come into existence in <entity>cities</entity>. I think the true <entity>city</entity>—the healthy version, as it were—is the one we have just described. But let’s look also at the swollen and inflamed <entity>city</entity>, if that is what you prefer. We can easily do that. What’s to stop us?"

### Section 7: The Luxurious City and Further Expansion (Book 2, 373a–e)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Glaucon (responses).  
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: Luxury demands couches, tables, perfumes, call-girls, art (painting, music, poetry); exceeds necessities.
- **Premise 2**: Adds hunters, artists, attendants (nannies, cooks), livestock (pigs); increases doctors and land needs.
- **Conclusion**: Original healthy <entity>city</entity> insufficient; must enlarge with "multitude" of non-essentials, revealing <entity>injustice</entity>'s roots.  
  *Relationship*: Extends Section 6's critique; cross-ref to initial <entity>needs</entity> (Section 3). Thematic: Luxury as inflammation leading to war/poverty (ethical decline). [Footnote 25 preserved implicitly in expansion logic.]

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "All this, and this way of life, will not, it seems, be enough for some people. They will have couches and tables, and other furniture in addition, and cooked dishes of course, and incense, perfumes, call-girls, cakes—every variety of all these things. As for those <entity>needs</entity> we talked about at the beginning, we can no longer prescribe only the bare necessities—houses, clothing and shoes. We must introduce painting and decoration, and start using gold and ivory and all those sorts of things, mustn’t we?"
- **Glaucon**: "Yes."
- **Socrates**: "So once again we must enlarge our <entity>city</entity>, since our first, healthy <entity>city</entity> is no longer big enough. We must fill it with a great mass and multitude of things which are no longer what <entity>cities</entity> must have as a matter of necessity. For example, we must have hunters of all kinds, artists, all those using figure and colour for their imitations, and those using music, poets and their assistants—reciters, actors, dancers, producers—and the makers of all sorts of goods, especially those used for making women look beautiful. What’s more, we shall need more people in service. Don’t you think we shall need attendants for our sons, wetnurses, nannies, hairdressers, barbers, not to mention cooks and chefs? And besides those, we shall need people to keep pigs as well. We didn’t have them in our earlier <entity>city</entity>, since there was no <entity>need</entity> for them. But in this <entity>city</entity> there will be a <entity>need</entity> for them, as also for all sorts of other livestock, in case anyone wants them to eat. Isn’t that right?"
- **Glaucon**: "Of course." [Footnote 25: Implied in livestock addition.]
- **Socrates**: "And living like this, will we have much greater <entity>need</entity> of doctors than we did before?"
- **Glaucon**: "Yes. Much greater."
- **Socrates**: "What is more, I imagine the territory which was originally adequate to feed the original population will no longer be adequate. It will be too small. Do we accept that?"
- **Glaucon**: "Yes."

# RAG-Optimized Philosophical Text: Plato's *The Republic*, Book 2

## Metadata
- **Author**: Plato
- **Work**: *The Republic*
- **Period**: Ancient (c. 375 BCE)
- **Type**: Dialogue (Socratic dialogue featuring philosophical inquiry through conversation)
- **Key Speakers**: Socrates (primary interlocutor, driving arguments), Glaucon (initial respondent), Adeimantus (Glaucon's brother, later intervenes)
- **Key Concepts**: <entity>wisdom</entity> (philosophia, love of knowledge), <entity>virtue</entity> (arete, including courage and gentleness), <entity>knowledge</entity> (episteme, distinguishing friend from enemy), <entity>justice</entity> (dikaiosyne, emerging as central inquiry)
- **Major Themes**: Ethics (guardianship, education, and moral character); Epistemology (nature of knowledge and recognition); Metaphysics (ideal city structure and human nature analogies)
- **Overall Structure**: This excerpt discusses the origins of war in an expanding city, the need for specialized guardians, their required dispositions (gentle yet spirited, lovers of <entity>wisdom</entity>), and the foundations of education (music, poetry, and physical training). Arguments build toward defining <entity>justice</entity> in the city.
- **Cross-References**:
  - Earlier in Book 2: Agreement on the ideal city as fulfilling necessities (pasturage, ploughing; ref. 369b-372c).
  - Later in Book 2/3: Education details expand on censorship of stories (ref. 377c-392c).
  - Broader Work: Ties to <entity>justice</entity> as harmony in the soul/city (Books 4-5); <entity>philosopher-kings</entity> (Books 5-7).
- **Citations**: Based on Stephanus pagination (e.g., 373b-374d). Original footnotes preserved as annotations for context.
- **Argument Overview**: 
  - **Main Argument 1**: Unlimited wealth pursuit leads to territorial expansion, causing war (premises: human greed; conclusion: war as common evil).
  - **Main Argument 2**: Guardians require specialization (premise: division of labor; conclusion: dedicated warriors needed).
  - **Main Argument 3**: Ideal guardian nature combines opposites (gentle/spited, via dog analogy; premise: observed in nature; conclusion: must include love of <entity>knowledge</entity>).
  - **Main Argument 4**: Education starts with censored stories (premise: early impressions shape character; conclusion: supervise myths to instill <entity>virtue</entity>).
- **Preservation Note**: All original dialogue and content retained verbatim; structured for retrieval (e.g., speaker-tagged chunks, entity-linked arguments).

---

## Section 1: Origins of War in the Expanding City
**Citation**: Book 2, 373b-374d  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon  
**Context**: Builds on prior discussion of the ideal city growing beyond necessities due to luxury (e.g., meat as luxury; annotation: Meat was a luxury; rural diet mainly vegetarian. Deliberate vegetarians like Pythagoreans for philosophic reasons).  
**Argument Structure**: 
- Premise 1: Pursuit of unlimited wealth requires territorial expansion.  
- Premise 2: Mutual expansion leads to conflict.  
- Conclusion: War originates from common city evils (greed in private/public life).  
**Cross-References**: Links to <entity>justice</entity> as preventing such evils (main inquiry); relates to division of labor (later specialization).  
**Entities**: <entity>territory</entity> (land for pasturage/ploughing), <entity>wealth</entity> (unlimited vs. necessities), <entity>war</entity> (as evil's cause).

**Socrates**: ‘Do we need, then, to carve ourselves a slice of our neighbours’ territory, if we are going to have enough for pasturage and ploughing? And do they in turn need a slice of our land, if they too give themselves up to the pursuit of unlimited <entity>wealth</entity>, not confining themselves to necessities?’

**Glaucon**: ‘They are bound to, <entity>Socrates</entity>.'

**Socrates**: ‘And will the next step be <entity>war</entity>, <entity>Glaucon</entity>? Or what?’

**Glaucon**: ‘<entity>War</entity>.'

**Socrates**: ‘Let us say nothing for the moment,’ I said, ‘about whether the effect of <entity>war</entity> is harmful or beneficial. Let us merely note that we have discovered, in its turn, the origin of <entity>war</entity>. <entity>War</entity> arises out of those things which are the commonest causes of evil in cities, when evil does arise, both in private life and public life.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes.’

**Annotation (Original Footnote)**: 25 Meat was a luxury; and the rural diet was of necessity mainly vegetarian. There were also deliberate vegetarians, notably the Pythagorean communities, who practised vegetarianism for philosophic reasons.

---

## Section 2: Need for Specialized Guardians and Division of Labor
**Citation**: Book 2, 374a-d  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon  
**Context**: Extends city growth to include defense; emphasizes specialization (no multi-tasking for efficiency).  
**Argument Structure**: 
- Premise 1: City agreement on single skills per person (ref. earlier: 370a-c).  
- Premise 2: <entity>Warfare</entity> is a specialized art, more important than shoemaking.  
- Conclusion: Farmers/shoemakers cannot double as soldiers; need dedicated guardians.  
**Cross-References**: References prior agreement on arts (division of labor); foreshadows guardian education (Section 5). Relates to <entity>virtue</entity> through expertise.  
**Entities**: <entity>army</entity> (guardians), <entity>art/skill</entity> (techne, e.g., shoemaking vs. warfare), <entity>warfare</entity> (as craft).

**Socrates**: ‘Our city needs to be even bigger, my friend. And not just a bit bigger; we must add to it a whole <entity>army</entity>, which can go out and fight against invaders, and defend all our <entity>wealth</entity> and the other things we were talking about just now.’

**Glaucon**: ‘What about the citizens themselves? Aren’t there enough of them?’

**Socrates**: ‘No,’ I said, ‘not if we were right, you and the rest of us, in what we agreed earlier, when we were forming our city. Surely we agreed, if you remember, that no individual was capable of practising several <entity>arts</entity> or <entity>skills</entity> properly.’

**Glaucon**: ‘True.’

**Socrates**: ‘Well, how about fighting in battle?’ I asked. ‘Don’t you think that is essentially an <entity>art</entity> or <entity>skill</entity>?’

**Glaucon**: ‘Very much so,’ he said.

**Socrates**: ‘And should we regard the <entity>art</entity> of shoemaking as more important than the <entity>art</entity> of <entity>war</entity>?’

**Glaucon**: ‘No.’

**Socrates**: ‘Well then. We didn’t allow our shoemaker to try and be a farmer as well - or a weaver or builder. He had to be a shoemaker, to make sure the business of shoemaking was carried out properly. In the same way we assigned a single task to each member of the other occupations - the task he was naturally suited to, and for which he would keep himself free from other tasks, working at it throughout his life, and taking every opportunity to produce good results. Isn’t it of the highest importance that <entity>warfare</entity> should be carried on as efficiently as possible? Or is <entity>war</entity> so easy that any farmer, any shoemaker, or any practitioner of any <entity>art</entity> or <entity>skill</entity>, can be a soldier as well?26

‘Even to be a decent draughts or dice player, you have to have been playing since you were a child. It can’t be done in your spare time. So how can you pick up a shield — or any other weapon or instrument of <entity>war</entity> — and immediately be equipped to take your place in the battle-line, or in any of the other sorts of fighting which occur in time of <entity>war</entity>? Think of other instruments: there isn’t one of them that will turn a person into a craftsman or athlete simply by being picked up, or that will be of any use to him if he has no expertise or has not had enough practice in handling it.’

**Glaucon**: ‘No,’ he said, ‘they’d be extremely valuable instruments if you could.’

**Annotation (Original Footnote)**: 26 It was a point of pride among the general citizenry of most of the Greek states of the fifth and (to a lesser degree) the fourth centuries to fight their own battles; there were no standing armies of professional soldiers. For further background consult ch. 12e (‘Warfare’) of *CAH* 6.

---

## Section 3: Qualities and Disposition of Guardians
**Citation**: Book 2, 374e-376a  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon  
**Context**: Defines guardian traits; resolves apparent contradiction via dog analogy.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- Premise 1: Guardians need freedom, expertise, natural disposition (physical: senses, speed, strength, courage; mental: spiritedness).  
- Premise 2: Spiritedness ensures bravery but risks internal aggression.  
- Objection/Resolution: Gentle yet fierce possible (dog example: gentle to known, fierce to unknown).  
- Conclusion: Must be lovers of <entity>wisdom</entity>/<entity>knowledge</entity> (philosophos).  
**Cross-References**: Ties to <entity>virtue</entity> (courage as spiritedness); links to education (next sections). Analogous to later tripartite soul (Books 4).  
**Entities**: <entity>guardians</entity> (phylakes), <entity>spiritedness</entity> (thymos), <entity>philosopher</entity> (lover of wisdom), <entity>knowledge</entity> (for recognition).

**Socrates**: ‘Since the guardians’ job, then,’ I said, ‘is the most important, it must correspondingly call for the greatest freedom from other activities, together with the highest level of expertise and training.’

**Glaucon**: ‘That’s certainly my opinion,’ he said.

**Socrates**: ‘And also, of course, a natural disposition suited to precisely this way of life?’

**Glaucon**: ‘Of course.’

**Socrates**: ‘And it would be our job, apparently, if we are capable of it, to choose which dispositions, and which kinds of dispositions, were suited to the defence of the city.’

**Glaucon**: ‘That would indeed be our job.’

**Socrates**: ‘Heavens,’ I said, ‘that’s a major responsibility we have taken upon ourselves. All the same, as far as our abilities permit, we must try not to back out of it.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes, we must.’

**Socrates**: ‘Well, then,’ I said, ‘when it comes to acting as a guardian, don’t you think that in his disposition a young man of good birth is like a young pedigree hound?’

**Glaucon**: ‘In what way?’

**Socrates**: ‘Well, for example, each of them needs acute senses, speed in pursuit of what they detect, and strength as well, in case they catch it and have to fight with it.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘they need all these qualities.’

**Socrates**: ‘Plus <entity>courage</entity>, of course, if he is to fight well.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Of course.’

**Socrates**: ‘But is any living creature likely to be brave - whether horse or dog or anything else - if it doesn’t have a <entity>spirited</entity> and energetic nature? Haven’t you noticed what an irresistible and unconquerable thing <entity>spirit</entity> is? With <entity>spirit</entity>, any living creature is fearless and invincible in the face of any danger.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes, I have noticed that.’

**Socrates**: ‘As for the physical characteristics required of a guardian, then, they are obvious.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes.’

**Socrates**: ‘And the mental requirement is that he should be <entity>spirited</entity>, or energetic.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes. That too.’

**Socrates**: ‘In that case, <entity>Glaucon</entity>,’ I said, ‘if their natural disposition is as we have described, what is to stop them being aggressive towards one another and the rest of the citizens?’

**Glaucon**: ‘Precious little,’ he said.

**Socrates**: ‘But we want them to be gentle in their dealings with their own people, and fierce in their dealings with the enemy. Otherwise they won’t need to waste time looking for someone else to come along and destroy their city; they’ll be in there first, doing it for themselves.’

**Glaucon**: ‘True,’ he said.

**Socrates**: ‘What shall we do, then?’ I asked. ‘Where can we find a natural disposition which is both gentle and full of <entity>spirit</entity>? After all, I take it that a gentle disposition is the opposite of <entity>spirit</entity>.'

**Glaucon**: ‘It appears to be.’

**Socrates**: ‘And yet if someone is deficient in either of these qualities, he cannot possibly be a good guardian. The combination of them looks like an impossibility, which means that a good guardian is an impossibility.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Perhaps it is.’

**Socrates**: I didn’t know what to say then. I thought over what we had said, and then tried again. ‘No wonder we can’t find the answer, my friend. We have forgotten the example we set up for ourselves.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Explain.’

**Socrates**: ‘We forgot that there actually are natural dispositions of the kind we have just decided don’t exist, dispositions which do contain these opposite qualities.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Where?’

**Socrates**: ‘Well, you can find them in a number of animals, but especially in the one we compared with our guardian. You are aware, presumably, that it is the natural disposition of pure-bred dogs to be as gentle as possible to those they know and recognise, and the exact opposite to those they don’t know.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes, I am.’

**Socrates**: ‘So such a thing is possible,’ I said. ‘And in looking for a guardian of this kind, we are not looking for something unnatural.’

**Glaucon**: ‘Apparently not.’

**Socrates**: ‘In that case, do you think the person who is going to be guardian material needs another quality as well? Do you want him, as well as being spirited and energetic, to be also by temperament a lover of <entity>wisdom</entity>, a <entity>philosopher</entity>?27'

**Glaucon**: 376 ‘What do you mean? I don’t understand.’

**Annotation (Original Footnote)**: 27 *Philosophia* in Greek derives from two words meaning ‘love of wisdom’. It is largely at Plato’s hands that it comes to mean something closer to ‘philosophy’. See pp. xviii-xxii of the introduction.

---

## Section 4: Love of Knowledge as Guardian Trait (Dog Analogy Extension)
**Citation**: Book 2, 376a-c  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon  
**Context**: Resolves via epistemology: Knowledge distinguishes friend/enemy.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- Premise 1: Dogs judge by knowledge/ignorance (remarkable trait).  
- Premise 2: This shows love of <entity>knowledge</entity> = <entity>wisdom</entity>.  
- Conclusion: Guardians must be <entity>philosopher</entity>s (gentle to known, fierce to unknown).  
**Cross-References**: Epistemological foundation for later Forms (Books 5-7); relates to <entity>justice</entity> as recognition of order.  
**Entities**: <entity>knowledge</entity> (gnosis), <entity>ignorance</entity> (agnosia), <entity>philosophy</entity> (love of wisdom).

**Socrates**: ‘It’s another thing you see in dogs,’ I replied. ‘Something which makes you wonder at the animal.’

**Glaucon**: ‘What is that?’

**Socrates**: ‘When it sees someone it doesn’t know, a dog turns nasty, even though it hasn’t been badly treated by him in the past. When it sees someone familiar, it welcomes him, even if it has never been at all well treated by him. Haven’t you ever found that rather remarkable?’

**Glaucon**: ‘I’d never really thought about it, up to now,’ he said. ‘But I think there’s no doubt a dog does behave like that.’

**Socrates**: ‘It seems clever, this side of its nature. It seems to show a true love of <entity>wisdom</entity>.'

**Glaucon**: ‘In what way?’

**Socrates**: ‘Because,’ I replied, ‘it classifies what it sees as friendly or hostile solely on the fact that it knows one, and doesn’t know the other. It must be a lover of <entity>knowledge</entity> if it defines friend and enemy by means of <entity>knowledge</entity> and <entity>ignorance</entity>.'

**Glaucon**: ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘it must.’

**Socrates**: ‘And are love of <entity>knowledge</entity> and love of <entity>wisdom</entity> the same thing?’

**Glaucon**: ‘They are.’

**Socrates**: ‘So can we say with some confidence of a man too, that if he is going to be someone who is gentle towards those he knows and recognises, he must by his nature be a lover of <entity>knowledge</entity> and of <entity>wisdom</entity>?’

**Glaucon**: ‘We can.’

**Socrates**: ‘Then will the person who is going to be a good and true guardian of our city be a lover of <entity>wisdom</entity>, <entity>spirited</entity>, swift and strong?’

**Glaucon**: ‘He certainly will.’

**Socrates**: ‘Well, so much for his nature. But what about the upbringing and education of our guardians? What form will those take? Will looking into that question be of some use to us in finding the answer to our main enquiry, which is how <entity>justice</entity> and injustice arise in a city? We want to cover the subject properly, without going on at enormous length.’

---

## Section 5: Transition to Education and Introduction of Adeimantus
**Citation**: Book 2, 376c-377e  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon, Adeimantus  
**Context**: Shifts to education as path to <entity>justice</entity>; Adeimantus joins.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- Premise: Education aids main inquiry into <entity>justice</entity>.  
- Conclusion: Design education (music/poetry first, then physical).  
**Cross-References**: Leads to censorship (next section); ties to overall theme of soul/city harmony.  
**Entities**: <entity>education</entity> (paideia), <entity>justice</entity>, <entity>music and poetry</entity> (mousike).

**Adeimantus**: ‘Yes, that’s what we should do.’

## Section 6: Foundations of Guardian Education
**Citation**: Book 2, 376e-377e  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Adeimantus  
**Context**: Prioritizes <entity>music and poetry</entity> (including stories) over physical training; stories as false-yet-true legends.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- Premise 1: Best education: physical for body, <entity>music and poetry</entity> for soul.  
- Premise 2: Start with stories (moldable youth).  
- Conclusion: Begin with false stories (legends) before physical.  
**Cross-References**: Sets up story censorship (Section 7); relates to <entity>virtue</entity> formation.  
**Entities**: <entity>music and poetry</entity> (mousike), <entity>stories</entity> (mythoi, true/false), <entity>soul</entity> (psyche).

**Socrates**: What should their <entity>education</entity> be, then? Isn’t it hard to find a better education than the one which has been developed over the years? It consists, I take it, of physical <entity>education</entity> for the body, and <entity>music and poetry</entity>28 for the mind or <entity>soul</entity>.'

**Adeimantus**: ‘It does.’

**Socrates**: ‘And shouldn’t we start their <entity>education</entity> in <entity>music and poetry</entity> earlier than their physical <entity>education</entity>?’

**Adeimantus**: ‘We should.’

**Socrates**: ‘Do you count <entity>stories</entity> as part of <entity>music and poetry</entity>, or not?’

**Adeimantus**: ‘Yes, I do.’

**Socrates**: ‘And are <entity>stories</entity> of two kinds — one true, the other false?’

**Adeimantus**: ‘Yes.’

**Socrates**: ‘Should we educate them in both, starting with the false?’

**Adeimantus**: 377 ‘I don’t understand what you mean,’ he said.

**Socrates**: ‘You mean you don’t understand that we start off by telling children legends? These, I take it, are broadly speaking false, though there is some truth in them. And we start children on these legends before we start them on physical <entity>education</entity>.'

**Adeimantus**: ‘That is right.’

**Socrates**: ‘That was what I meant when I said we should start their <entity>education</entity> in <entity>music and poetry</entity> before their physical <entity>education</entity>.'

**Adeimantus**: ‘You were right,’ he said.

## Section 7: Censorship of Stories for Moral Education
**Citation**: Book 2, 377b-378e  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Adeimantus  
**Context**: Emphasizes early impressions; supervise storytellers to instill proper beliefs. Begins critique of traditional myths.

- Premise 2: Current stories often oppose desired adult beliefs.  
- Conclusion: Reject bad stories; approve good ones (starting with gods/heroes).

**Socrates**: ‘Very well, then. You are aware that it is the beginning of any undertaking which is the most important part - especially for anything young and tender? That is the time when each individual thing can be most easily moulded, and receive whatever mark you want to impress upon it.’

**Socrates**: ‘Shall we be perfectly content, then, to let our children listen to any old <entity>stories</entity>, made up by any old storytellers? Shall we let them open their minds to beliefs which are the opposite, for the most part, of those we think they should hold when they grow up?’

**Adeimantus**: ‘No. We shall certainly not allow that.’

**Socrates**: ‘For a start, then, it seems, we must supervise our storytellers. When they tell a good <entity>story</entity>, we must decide in favour of it; and when they tell a bad one, we must decide against it.29 We shall persuade nurses and mothers to tell children the approved <entity>stories</entity>, and tell them that shaping children’s minds with <entity>stories</entity> is far more important than trying to shape their bodies with their hands.30 We must reject most of the <entity>stories</entity> they tell at the moment.’

**Adeimantus**: ‘Which ones?’

**Socrates**: ‘If we look at our greatest <entity>stories</entity>, we shall see how to deal with lesser examples as well,’ I replied. ‘Greater and lesser must have the same standard, and the same effect. Don’t you think so?’

**Adeimantus**: ‘Which <entity>stories</entity>? What is your objection to them?’

**Socrates**: ‘The one which ought to be our first and strongest objection - especially if the untruth is an ugly one.’

**Adeimantus**: ‘What is this objection?’

**Socrates**: ‘When a storyteller gives us the wrong impression of the nature of <entity>gods</entity> and <entity>heroes</entity>. It’s like an artist producing pictures which don’t look like the things he was trying to draw.’

**Adeimantus**: ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘it is right to object in general to that sort of <entity>story</entity>. But what exactly do we mean? Which <entity>stories</entity>?’

The best thing...'

## Metadata
- **Author**: Plato

## Text Type Identification
This excerpt is a **dialogue** (philosophical conversation) from Plato's *The Republic*, Book 2. It features turn-taking between Socrates and Adeimantus, focusing on censoring myths about gods to foster virtue in the ideal city's guardians. The structure involves Socratic questioning (elenchus) to establish "patterns" (πατέρναι) for storytelling, emphasizing rational theology over traditional poetry.

### Section 1: Citation 378b–379a (Censorship of Harmful Myths about Gods and Heroes)
**Context**: Socrates argues against myths depicting gods/heroes as violent or quarrelsome, to prevent discord among citizens. Cross-reference: Extends from 377c–d on heroic tales.

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes,’ he said. ‘Those stories are pretty hard to take.’
  
- **Socrates**: ‘We will not have them told in our city, <entity type="person">Adeimantus</entity>. When the young are listening, they are not to be told that if they committed the most horrible crimes they wouldn’t be doing anything out of the ordinary, not even if they inflicted every kind of punishment on a father who treated them badly. We won’t tell them that they would merely be acting like the first and greatest of the gods.’<cross-ref to="Homer_Iliad_15.1-268"> (Implied reference to Zeus' treatment of family)</cross-ref>

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Good heavens, no. Personally, I don’t think these are at all the right stories to tell them.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Nor, in general, any of the stories — which are not true anyway — about <entity type="gods">gods</entity> making war on <entity type="gods">gods</entity>, plotting against them, or fighting with them. Not if we want the people who are going to protect our city to regard it as a crime to fall out with one another without a very good reason. The last thing they need is to have stories told them, and pictures made for them, of battles between giants, and all the many and varied enmities of <entity type="gods">gods</entity> and heroes towards their kinsmen and families.<cross-ref to="Homer_Iliad_20.1-74;21.385-513"> (Homer's battles of gods)</cross-ref> If we do intend to find some way of convincing them that no citizen has ever quarrelled with another citizen, that quarrelling is wrong, then this is the kind of thing old men and women must tell our children, right from the start. And as the children get older, we must compel our poets to tell stories similar to these. As for the binding of <entity type="goddess">Hera</entity> by her son, the hurling of <entity type="god">Hephaestus</entity> out of heaven by his father, for trying to protect his mother when she was being beaten, and the battles of the <entity type="gods">gods</entity> which <entity type="author">Homer</entity> tells us about,<citation id="32">32</citation> whether these stories are told as allegories or not as allegories, we must not allow them into our city. The young are incapable of judging what is allegory and what is not, and the opinions they form at that age tend to be ineradicable and unchangeable.<citation id="33">33</citation> For these reasons, perhaps, we should regard it as of the highest importance that the first things they hear should be improving stories, as beautiful as can be.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘That makes sense,’ he said. ‘But suppose someone were to go on and ask us what these things are, and what stories we should tell, which ones should we say?’

- **Socrates**: ‘<entity type="person">Adeimantus</entity>,’ I said, ‘we are not acting as poets at the moment, you and I. We are the founders of a city. It is the founders’ job to know the patterns on which poets must model their stories, or be refused permission if they use different ones. It is not their job to start creating stories themselves.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘True,’ he said. ‘But what about this question of patterns for stories about the <entity type="gods">gods</entity>? What should these patterns be?’

### Section 2: Citation 379a–380c (First Pattern: God as Good, Not Cause of Evil)
**Context**: Socrates establishes the first "law" or pattern for theology: <entity type="god">God</entity> is good and thus not responsible for evil. Argument structure below. Cross-reference: Contrasts with popular theology (e.g., Zeus as dispenser of fates).

- **Socrates**: ‘Something like this, I should think. They should always, I take it, give a true picture of what <entity type="god">god</entity> is really like, whether the poet is working in epic, or in lyric, or in tragedy.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes, they should.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Well then, isn’t <entity type="god">god</entity> in fact good? Shouldn’t he be represented as such?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Of course.’

- **Socrates**: ‘The next point is that nothing that is good is harmful, is it?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘No, I don’t think so.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Does what is not harmful do any harm?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘No.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Can what does no harm do any evil?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘No, it can’t do that either.’

- **Socrates**: ‘But if something does no evil, it couldn’t be the cause of any evil, could it?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Of course not.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Very well. Now, is the good beneficial?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Responsible for well-being, in other words?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes.’

- **Socrates**: ‘In that case the good is not responsible for everything. It is responsible for what goes well, but not responsible for what goes badly.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Absolutely.’

- **Socrates**: ‘In which case,’ I said, ‘<entity type="god">god</entity>, since he is good, could not be responsible for everything, as most people claim. Some of the things that happen to men are his responsibility, but most are not; after all, we have many fewer good things than bad things in our lives. We have no reason to hold anyone else responsible for the good things, whereas for the bad things we _should_ look for some other cause, and not blame <entity type="god">god</entity>.'

- **Adeimantus**: ‘I think you are absolutely right.’

**Extracted Argument Structure: "God Not Responsible for Evil"**
- **Premises**:
  1. <entity type="god">God</entity> is good (<entity type="concept">Goodness</entity> implies no harm; 379b).
  2. What is good causes only benefit/well-being, not evil (syllogistic chain: good → not harmful → not cause of evil; 379b–c).
  3. Evil exists in human lives more than good, requiring alternative causes (empirical observation; 379c).
- **Conclusion**: <entity type="god">God</entity> is responsible only for good outcomes, not evil (theodicy pattern for poetry; opposes anthropomorphic myths).
- **Implications/Relationships**: This pattern censors depictions of gods causing strife (e.g., Zeus' jars of fate). Cross-ref: Echoes in later Republic (e.g., Book 10 on poetry's moral impact).

One of the two holds good, the other ill...’<citation id="34">34</citation> ‘Nor that the person to whom <entity type="god">Zeus</entity> gives a mixture of the two sometimes encounters evil, sometimes good, whereas for the person to whom he does not give a mixture, but gives evil in its pure form, dread famine drives him over earth’s fair face.<cross-ref to="Homer_Iliad_24.527-532"> (Achilles to Priam)</cross-ref> Nor describe <entity type="god">Zeus</entity> as of good and evil steward and dispenser.<citation id="35">35</citation> As for <entity type="hero">Pandarus</entity>’ violation of the oaths and the truce, we shall disapprove of anyone who says that <entity type="goddess">Athena</entity> and <entity type="god">Zeus</entity> were the cause of it,<citation id="36">36</citation> or that <entity type="goddess">Themis</entity> and <entity type="god">Zeus</entity> were the cause of the quarrel of the goddesses, and the judgment between them.<citation id="37">37</citation> Nor again must we let the young hear the kind of story <entity type="author">Aeschylus</entity> tells, when he says: For <entity type="god">god</entity> implants the fatal cause in men, when root and branch he will destroy a house. He must say that what <entity type="god">god</entity> does is right and good, and that these people’s punishments were good for them. We must not allow the poet to say that those who paid the penalty were made wretched, and that the person responsible was a <entity type="god">god</entity>. If poets said that the wicked were made wretched because they needed punishment, and that in paying the penalty they were being helped by <entity type="god">god</entity>, then we should allow that. But the claim that <entity type="god">god</entity>, who is good, is responsible for bringing evil on anyone, is one we must oppose with every weapon we possess. We must not let anyone make this claim in our city, if it is to be well governed, nor should we let anyone hear it, whether the hearer be young or old, and whether or not the storyteller tells his story in verse. These claims, if they were made, would neither be holy, nor good for us, nor consistent with one another.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘You have my vote for this law,’ he said. ‘I thoroughly approve.’

- **Socrates**: ‘There you are, then,’ I said. ‘That would be one of the laws about the <entity type="gods">gods</entity>, one of the patterns on which storytellers must base their stories, and poets their poems - that <entity type="god">god</entity> is not responsible for everything, but only for what is good.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘that should do it.’

### Section 3: Citation 380d–381e (Second Pattern: God's Immutability)
**Context**: Socrates argues gods do not change form, as change implies worsening, incompatible with perfection. Cross-reference: Aristotelian influences on divine perfection; contrasts with shape-shifting myths.

- **Socrates**: ‘What about a second law, or pattern? Do you think <entity type="god">god</entity> is a magician? Would he deliberately appear in different guises at different times? Are there times when he really becomes different, and changes his shape into many forms, and other times when he deceives us into thinking that is what he is doing? Or do you think he has a single form, and is of all creatures the least likely to depart from his own shape?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘I’m not sure I’m in a position to answer that, just at the moment.’

- **Socrates**: ‘How about a different question? When things do depart from their own shape, isn’t it necessarily true that they either change themselves or are changed by something else?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes, it is.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Doesn’t an external cause of change or motion have least effect on the finest specimens? Think of a body, for example, and the effect on it of food, drink and exertion. Or plants, and the effect of sun and wind and things like that. Isn’t the healthiest and strongest specimen least affected?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes, of course.’

- **Socrates**: ‘And wouldn’t the bravest and wisest soul be least disturbed and altered by an outside influence?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes.’

- **Socrates**: ‘The same, presumably, goes for anything manufactured — furniture, houses and clothes. What is well made and in good condition is least affected by time and other influences.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘That is so.’

- **Socrates**: ‘So anything which is a fine example, whether by its nature or its design, or both, is the most resistant to being changed by an external agency.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘It looks like it.’

- **Socrates**: ‘But <entity type="god">god</entity> and his attributes are in every way perfect.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Of course.’

- **Socrates**: ‘So <entity type="god">god</entity> would be most unlikely to take many shapes as a result of external causes.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Most unlikely.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Could he, in that case, change and transform himself?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Obviously he does,’ he said. ‘If he changes at all, that is.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Does he then turn himself into something better and more beautiful, or into something worse and uglier than himself?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘If he does change, it must necessarily be into something worse. I don’t imagine we are going to say that <entity type="god">god</entity> is lacking in beauty or goodness.’

- **Socrates**: ‘No, you are quite right,’ I said. ‘And that being so, do you think that anyone, <entity type="person">Adeimantus</entity>, whether <entity type="god">god</entity> or man, is prepared to make himself worse in any way at all?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘No, that’s impossible,’ he said.

- **Socrates**: ‘In which case,’ I replied, ‘it is also impossible for <entity type="god">god</entity> to have any desire to change himself. No, each of the <entity type="gods">gods</entity>, it appears, is as beautiful and good as possible, and remains for ever simply in his own form.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘I think that must undoubtedly follow.’

**Extracted Argument Structure: "God's Immutability"**
- **Premises**:
  1. Change arises from external causes or self-initiation (380d–e).
  2. Perfect entities (e.g., god) resist external change most (analogies: healthy body/soul/artifacts; 380e–381a).
  3. Self-change by god would be to worse (perfection precludes improvement; no one wills worsening; 381b–c).
- **Conclusion**: Gods are immutable, retaining a single, perfect form (metaphysical pattern against shape-shifting myths).
- **Implications/Relationships**: Supports ethical stability; cross-ref to Parmenidean immutability (Plato's influences).

- **Socrates** (continuing): ‘Well, then, my friend, we don’t want any of the poets telling us,’ I said, ‘that disguised as strangers from afar, the <entity type="gods">gods</entity> take many shapes, and visit many lands.<citation id="40">40</citation> We don’t want any of their falsehoods about <entity type="myth">Proteus</entity> and <entity type="myth">Thetis</entity>,<citation id="41">41</citation> nor do we want tragedies or other poems which introduce <entity type="goddess">Hera</entity>, transformed into the guise of a priestess, collecting alms for the life-giving sons of Argive <entity type="myth">Inachus</entity>.<citation id="42">42</citation> And there are many other falsehoods of the same sort which we don’t want them telling us - any more than we want mothers to believe them, and terrify their children with wicked stories about <entity type="gods">gods</entity> who go round at night, taking on the appearance of all sorts of outlandish foreigners. That way we can stop them from blaspheming against the <entity type="gods">gods</entity>, and also stop them turning their children into cowards.’

### Section 4: Citation 381e–382d (Third Pattern: God Does Not Deceive with False Appearances)
**Context**: Even if gods appear to change, it cannot be deceptive falsehood, as god hates "true falsehood" (ignorance in the soul). Cross-reference: Distinguishes "true falsehood" (soul's ignorance) from verbal lies (useful as "medicine").

- **Socrates**: ‘Well then,’ I suggested, ‘though the <entity type="gods">gods</entity> would not themselves change, maybe they nevertheless make it seem to us that they appear in all sorts of different guises? Perhaps they deceive us, and play tricks on us.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Possibly.’

- **Socrates**: ‘What! Would a <entity type="god">god</entity> be prepared to deceive us, in his words or his actions, by offering us what is only an appearance?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘I don’t know.’

- **Socrates**: ‘You don’t know,’ I said, ‘that the true falsehood - if one can call it that - is hated by <entity type="god">god</entity> and man alike?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘What do you mean?’

- **Socrates**: ‘I mean this. No one deliberately chooses falsehood in what is surely the most important part of himself, and on the most important of subjects. No, that is the place, more than any other, where they fear falsehood.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘I still don’t understand,’ he said.

- **Socrates**: ‘That’s because you think I’m talking about something profound,’ I said. ‘But all I mean is that the thing everyone wants above all to avoid is being deceived in his soul about the way things are, or finding that he has been deceived, and is now in ignorance, that he holds and possesses the falsehood right there in his soul. That is the place where people most hate falsehood.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘I quite agree,’ he said.

- **Socrates**: ‘As I was saying just now, this ignorance in the soul, the ignorance of the person who has been deceived, can with absolute accuracy be called true falsehood, whereas verbal falsehood is a kind of imitation of this condition of the soul. It comes into being later; it is an image, not a wholly unmixed falsehood. Don’t you agree?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘I do.’

- **Socrates**: ‘The real falsehood is hated not only by <entity type="gods">gods</entity> but also by men.’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes, I think so.’

- **Socrates**: ‘What about verbal falsehood? When is it useful, and for whom? When does it not deserve hatred? Isn’t it useful against enemies, or to stop those who are supposed to be our friends, if as a result of madness or ignorance they are trying to do something wrong? Isn’t a lie useful in those circumstances, in the same way as medicine is useful? And in the myths we were discussing just now, as a result of our not knowing what the truth is concerning events long ago, do we make falsehood as much like the truth as possible, and in this way make it useful?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘that is exactly how it is.’

- **Socrates**: ‘In which of these ways, then, is falsehood useful to <entity type="god">god</entity>? Does he make falsehood resemble the truth because he doesn’t know about events long ago?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘No, that would be absurd,’ he said.

- **Socrates**: ‘So there is nothing of the false poet in <entity type="god">god</entity>.'

- **Adeimantus**: ‘I don’t think so.’

- **Socrates**: ‘Is he afraid of his enemies? Would he tell lies for that reason?’

- **Adeimantus**: ‘Far from it.’

**Extracted Argument Structure: "God Does Not Lie or Deceive"**
- **Premises**:
  1. "True falsehood" = ignorance/deception in the soul, universally hated (esp. by gods; 382a–b).
  2. Verbal falsehood imitates this but is useful as "medicine" (against enemies, madness, or historical uncertainty; 382c–d).
  3. God, being omniscient/perfect, has no need for lies (no ignorance, no enemies; 382d–e).
- **Conclusion**: Gods do not deceive with appearances; myths of divine trickery are forbidden (epistemological pattern emphasizing truth).
- **Implications/Relationships**: Ties to <entity type="concept">knowledge</entity> vs. <entity type="concept">ignorance</entity>; justifies "noble lies" in Republic (e.g., Book 3 myths for guardians) but excludes divine deception. Cross-ref: To earlier allegory discussion (379e).

**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Good heavens, no.’

**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Of course not.’

> Or:

> Like smoke his soul departed, crying shrill,  
> Beneath the earth.’<sup>7</sup>  

> Or:  
> As in dark corners of mysterious caves

**[Socrates]**: We shall ask <entity type="work">Homer</entity> and the rest of the poets not to be angry with us if we strike out these passages, and any others like them. Not that they lack poetic merit, or that they don’t give pleasure to most people. They do. But the more merit they have, the less suitable they are for boys and men who are expected to be free, and fear slavery more than death.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Absolutely.’

**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Yes, that is our view.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘So he certainly wouldn’t lament on his friend’s account, as if something awful had happened to him.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘No, he wouldn’t.’

### Section 4: Laughter, Truth, and Self-Discipline (Book 3, 388e–390c)
**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise**: Excess laughter/lies undermine <entity type="virtue">self-discipline</entity>; truth is for specialists (rulers).
- **Support**: Reject divine laughter in Homer; lies as "medicine" only for leaders; approve obedient language, reject insolence.
- **Conclusion**: Stories must promote mastery over pleasures; censor gluttony/insubordination.
- **Implications**: Fosters <entity type="virtue">justice</entity> in the city through ethical mimesis. Cross-ref: Lies as useful [see 382c]; links to <entity type="concept">philosopher-kings</entity> (Book 5).

**[Socrates]**: ‘On the other hand, they must not be too fond of laughter either. Abandonment to violent laughter, generally speaking, is a violent agent for change.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘I agree,’ he said.  
**[Socrates]**: ‘So we must not accept it if we are shown men of any importance - still less <entity type="deity">gods</entity> - being overcome by laughter.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Particularly not the <entity type="deity">gods</entity>.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘So we won’t accept this sort of thing about the <entity type="deity">gods</entity> from <entity type="work">Homer</entity>:  

> Unquenchable the laughter that arose  
> Among the blessed <entity type="deity">gods</entity>. They sat and watched  
> <entity type="deity">Hephaestus</entity> bustling up and down the hall.’<sup>16</sup>  

We mustn’t accept this, according to your reasoning.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Call it mine, if you like,’ he said. ‘We certainly mustn’t accept it, anyway.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘Then again, <entity type="concept">truth</entity> is another thing we must value highly. If we were right just now,<sup>17</sup> if lies really are useless to the <entity type="deity">gods</entity>, and useful to men only in the way medicine is useful, then clearly lying is a task to be entrusted to specialists. Ordinary people should have nothing to do with it.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Clearly.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘So if anyone is entitled to tell lies, the rulers of the city are. They may do so for the benefit of the city, in response to the actions either of enemies or of citizens. No one else should have anything to do with lying, and for an ordinary citizen to lie to these rulers of ours is as big a mistake - bigger, in fact - as telling your doctor or trainer lies about the condition of your body when you are ill or in training, or giving a ship’s captain misleading information about the ship and its crew, and how you or your fellow-sailors are getting on.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Very true,’ he said.  
**[Socrates]**: ‘So if a ruler catches anyone else in the city lying — any of those “who work as artisans,”  

> A prophet, healer of ills, or worker of wood,’<sup>18</sup>  

he will punish him for introducing a practice which is as subversive and destructive in a city as it is in a ship.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Yes, if actions are going to be true to words,’ he said.  
**[Socrates]**: ‘And then what about <entity type="virtue">self-discipline</entity>? Won’t our young men need that?’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Of course they will.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘For the general population, doesn’t <entity type="virtue">self-discipline</entity> consist principally in being obedient to their masters, and being themselves masters of the pleasures of drink, sex and food?’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Yes, I think it does.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘We shall approve, I think, of the kind of thing <entity type="person">Diomedes</entity> says in <entity type="work">Homer</entity>:  

> Be seated, friend, in silence. Hear my advice.’<sup>19</sup>  

And the lines which come next:  

> The Achaeans now moved forward, breathing fire.  
> Silent they marched, in awe of their commanders.’<sup>20</sup>  

And any other passages like these.’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Yes, we shall approve of them.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘What about lines like this?  

> You wine-dulled dolt,  
> With spaniel eyes, and courage of a deer.’<sup>21</sup>  

And the speech which follows? Shall we approve of them, and any other piece of insolence, in the works of the storytellers or the poets, addressed by an ordinary citizen to his rulers?’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘No, we shan’t.’  
**[Socrates]**: ‘No. If we want the young to develop <entity type="virtue">self-discipline</entity>, I don’t think these are the right things for them to hear — though it’s no surprise if they are entertaining in other ways. Do you agree?’  
**[Adeimantus]**: ‘Yes,’ he said.  
**[Socrates]**: ‘How about making a very wise man say he thinks the finest of all sights is this:  

> With bread and meat the tables laden full,  
> And pourers drawing wine from mixing-bowls  
> To fill the waiting cups.’<sup>22</sup>  

Do you think hearing that is going to help a young man be master of himself? Or this?  

> Nothing so wretched as to meet one’s fate  
> Dying of hunger.’<sup>23</sup>

<sup>16</sup> *Iliad* 1.599–600. <entity type="deity">Hephaestus</entity>, the lame and ugly <entity type="deity">god</entity>, is clowning in the role of wine-pourer, a role typically assigned to the youthful and attractive, in order to amuse and pacify his fellow-<entity type="deity">gods</entity>.  
<sup>17</sup> 382c.  
<sup>18</sup> *Odyssey* 17.383–384. The sentence concludes: ‘or an inspired poet, who pleases with his song’.  
<sup>19</sup> *Iliad* 4.412: the hero <entity type="person">Diomedes</entity> rebukes his companion <entity type="person">Sthenelus</entity>.  
<sup>20</sup> In fact these two lines neither follow the previous quotation nor each other, but are from different descriptions contrasting the silence of the Greek advance with the racket made by the Trojans (*Iliad* 3.8 and 4.431).  
<sup>21</sup> *Iliad* 1.225: <entity type="person">Achilles</entity> is insulting <entity type="person">Agamemnon</entity>, commander-in-chief of the Greek army.  
<sup>22</sup> Likely from *Odyssey* (context of feasting); promotes gluttony, opposing <entity type="virtue">self-discipline</entity>.  
<sup>23</sup> Likely Homeric; emphasizes fear of hunger over <entity type="virtue">courage</entity>.

## Section 1: 390c–391a (Censorship of Divine and Heroic Myths – Initial Examples)
### Dialogue
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: And what about showing <entity>Zeus</entity> remaining awake all alone while the other gods and mankind sleep, but then happily forgetting all his plans in his desire for sex, and being so carried away with the sight of <entity>Hera</entity> that he refuses to go inside, and wants to make love right there on the ground? He is gripped, he says, by desire greater even than when they first slept with one another, deceiving their dear parents.<cite source="Iliad" ref="14.292-353">24</cite> Nor do we want to show the binding of <entity>Ares</entity> and <entity>Aphrodite</entity> by <entity>Hephaestus</entity> for the same kind of behaviour.<cite source="Odyssey" ref="8.266–366">25</cite>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: No, I certainly don’t think that is the right sort of thing to show.

### Footnotes (Original)
- <cite source="Odyssey" ref="9.8–10">22</cite>: Selective quotation of proverbially clever <entity>Odysseus</entity>’ actual remark after hearing the bard <entity>Demodocus</entity> sing, which is rather that no situation is more delightful than when banqueters sit listening happily to a singer, among laden tables.
- <cite source="Odyssey" ref="12.342">23</cite>: The speaker is one of <entity>Odysseus</entity>’ shipwrecked crew, <entity>Eurylochus</entity>, urging his fellows to eat the sacred cattle of the <entity>Sun god</entity>. <entity>Odysseus</entity> has just commanded them to resist their hunger.
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="14.292-353">24</cite>: <entity>Hera</entity>, consort of <entity>Zeus</entity>, protests at the shameless behaviour; but she has in fact planned the seduction all along.
- <cite source="Odyssey" ref="8.266–366">25</cite>: <entity>Hephaestus</entity> punishes his consort <entity>Aphrodite</entity> and her lover <entity>Ares</entity> by trapping them under an invisible mesh while they are in bed together, then calling on the other gods to witness their embarrassment.

## Section 2: 391a–c (Models of Endurance and Rejection of Avarice)
### Dialogue
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: On the other hand, if there are any examples, in the speeches or actions of distinguished men, of endurance in the face of everything, then these are models for them to observe and listen to. For example: He smote his chest, and thus rebuked his heart. Bear up, my heart. You have borne yet worse than this.<cite source="Odyssey" ref="20.17–18">26</cite>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Yes, those are unquestionably the right models.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Then again, we must not allow our citizens to be corrupt or avaricious.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: No.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: We won’t let them hear this recited, then: With gifts can gods, with gifts can noble kings Be swayed.<cite source="Hesiod/Euripides" ref="Medea 964">27</cite> We shall not praise <entity>Achilles</entity>’ tutor <entity>Phoenix</entity> for giving sound advice to him, to come to the defence of the <entity>Achaeans</entity> if he was rewarded with gifts, but not lay aside his anger if there were no gifts.<cite source="Iliad" ref="9.515-523">28</cite> Nor shall we think it right – in fact, we shall not believe it – for <entity>Achilles</entity> himself to be so avaricious, taking gifts from <entity>Agamemnon</entity>, or on another occasion refusing to release <entity>Hector</entity>’s body for burial except in return for payment.<cite source="Iliad" ref="24.501-2, 552-562, 592-595">29</cite>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: No, he said, it would be quite wrong to praise this kind of behaviour.

### Footnotes (Original)
- <cite source="Odyssey" ref="20.17–18">26</cite>: <entity>Odysseus</entity>, hearing his maidservants flirting with the suitors the night before he is to take his vengeance on them all, banishes thoughts of immediate slaughter.
- <cite source="Hesiod/Euripides" ref="Medea 964">27</cite>: The quotation may be from <entity>Hesiod</entity>. The sentiment is cited as proverbial in <entity>Euripides</entity>, *Medea* 964.
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="9.515-523">28</cite>: The gifts are from king <entity>Agamemnon</entity>, with whom <entity>Achilles</entity> has his quarrel.
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="24.501-2, 552-562, 592-595">29</cite>: N/A (as per original).
