## Section 3: 391c–392c (Critique of Achilles' Impiety and Heroic Deeds)
### Dialogue
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: It’s only my high opinion of <entity>Homer</entity>, I said, which stops me calling it impious to talk like this, or give ear to people when they talk like this, about <entity>Achilles</entity>. Or to suggest that he said to <entity>Apollo</entity>: Thou most destructive out of all the gods, Archer <entity>Apollo</entity>, thou hast injured me. I’d swiftly take revenge, had I the power.<cite source="Iliad" ref="22.15, 20">30</cite> Or that he refused to obey the river-god, and offered to fight him.<cite source="Iliad" ref="21.222 ff.">31</cite> Or that he wanted to offer <entity>Patroclus</entity>, after his death, the locks of his hair which were sacred to the other river, <entity>Spercheius</entity>: Now let me give <entity>Patroclus</entity>, noble hero, This lock of hair, to take with him.<cite source="Iliad" ref="23.151">32</cite> We should not believe <entity>Achilles</entity> did this. As for his dragging <entity>Hector</entity> round the tomb of <entity>Patroclus</entity>, and slaughtering live prisoners on his funeral pyre,<cite source="Iliad" ref="24.14–21; 23.175–176">33</cite> we shall not admit that any of these are true stories. <entity>Achilles</entity> was the son of a goddess and of <entity>Peleus</entity> — a most sensible man and a grandson of <entity>Zeus</entity> — and he was brought up by the wise <entity>Cheiron</entity>. We’re not going to have our people believing that he was so utterly disturbed as to possess two completely contradictory faults — an avaricious meanness of spirit, and great arrogance towards gods and men.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: You are right.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: In which case, let us not believe either – and let us not allow people to say – that <entity>Theseus</entity> the son of <entity>Poseidon</entity> and <entity>Peirithous</entity> the son of <entity>Zeus</entity> set off to carry out those disgraceful abductions, or that any other hero and child of a god could bring himself to do terrible godless deeds of the kind which nowadays are falsely attributed to them.<cite source="Myth of Theseus and Peirithous">34</cite> Let us require poets to say either that these were not their actions or that they were not the children of gods. They must not say both, and they must not try to persuade our young men that gods can father evil deeds, or that heroes are no better than men. As we said earlier, these beliefs are both impious and untrue. We proved, didn’t we, that it is impossible for evil to come into being from the gods?<ref target="379a-380c">35</ref>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: We did.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: What is more, these beliefs are damaging to those who hear them. Anyone will forgive himself for doing wrong if he believes that this sort of thing was and is typical even of: The gods’ close kin, those near to <entity>Zeus</entity>, who have An altar sacred to ancestral <entity>Zeus</entity> On Ida’s mountain, high among the clouds, And in their veins the blood of demigods Has not run dry.<cite source="Aeschylus, Niobe fragment">36</cite>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: That’s why we must put a stop to stories of this kind, before they produce a totally casual attitude in our young men toward wickedness.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Yes, we must.

### Footnotes (Original)
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="22.15, 20">30</cite>: <entity>Apollo</entity> has tricked <entity>Achilles</entity> into allowing the <entity>Trojans</entity> to slip back inside their city walls.
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="21.222 ff.">31</cite>: <entity>Achilles</entity> challenges the river-god <entity>Scamander</entity>.
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="23.151">32</cite>: Since he is now doomed to die at <entity>Troy</entity>, <entity>Achilles</entity> releases himself from the vow made by his father to reserve the lock for a sacrifice to <entity>Spercheius</entity>, the river of <entity>Achilles</entity>’ homeland, upon his return.
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="24.14–21; 23.175–176">33</cite>: Dragging <entity>Hector</entity>: *Iliad* 24.14–21; slaughtering the prisoners: *Iliad* 23.175–176.
- <cite source="Myth of Theseus and Peirithous">34</cite>: In collusion with his cousin <entity>Peirithous</entity>, <entity>Theseus</entity>, king of <entity>Athens</entity>, abducted <entity>Helen</entity> from <entity>Sparta</entity> to be his bride, thus provoking a war with <entity>Sparta</entity>. The pair then attempted to abduct the goddess <entity>Persephone</entity> from the underworld to be bride to <entity>Peirithous</entity>.
- <ref target="379a-380c">35</ref>: Proof that gods cannot produce evil.
- <cite source="Aeschylus, Niobe fragment">36</cite>: <entity>Niobe</entity> is speaking of her divine ancestry. Her father <entity>Tantalus</entity> was son of <entity>Zeus</entity>.

## Section 4: 392c–393a (Stories About Mankind and Justice)
### Dialogue
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Well, then, in our definition of the kind of stories which may and may not be told, what class of stories is left? We have dealt with stories about the gods, and about demigods, heroes and the dead.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: We have.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: The final class, then, would be stories about mankind.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Clearly.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: And we are not in a position to lay down rules for that just at the moment, my friend.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Why not?

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Because we shall say, I imagine, that writers of poetry and prose both make very serious errors about mankind. They say that lots of people are unjust but happy, or just but miserable, and that injustice pays if you can get away with it, whereas justice is what is good for someone else, but damaging to yourself. We shall stop them saying things like this, and tell them to say just the opposite in their poems and stories. Don’t you think so?

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: I’m quite sure we shall.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: But if you admit I’m right about that, can’t I claim that you have admitted what we have been trying to prove all along?

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Yes, I said, I see how the argument would go.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: So we can’t reach an agreement about mankind, and the kind of stories which should be told, until after we have discovered what sort of thing <concept>justice</concept> is, and shown that its nature is to be profitable for the person who possesses it, whether or not people think he is just.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Very true.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Let that be enough on the stories. The telling of them, I suggest, is the next thing for us to think about. Then we shall have completely covered both what should be told and how it should be told.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: I don’t understand. What do you mean?

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: It’s important that you do understand, though. Here’s a way of looking at it which may give you a better idea. Aren’t all stories told by storytellers and poets really a narrative – of what has happened in the past, of what is happening now, or of what is going to happen in the future?

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Well, obviously.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Don’t they achieve their purpose either by simple narrative, or by narrative expressed through <concept>imitation</concept>, or by a combination of the two?

### Extracted Arguments
<argument id="arg4" type="deferred-judgment">
  <premise>Stories about humans often err by portraying <concept>injustice</concept> as beneficial and <concept>justice</concept> as harmful.</premise>
  <conclusion>Rules for such stories depend on proving <concept>justice</concept>'s intrinsic profitability (<relation type="foreshadow">leads to central thesis of the Republic</relation>).</conclusion>
  <evidence><quote>"We shall stop them saying things like this, and tell them to say just the opposite."</quote></evidence>
</argument>

## Section 5: 393a–395b (Modes of Storytelling: Narrative vs. Imitation)
### Dialogue
<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: There again, I’m afraid, I still need a clearer explanation.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: As a teacher, I seem to have a laughable inability to make my meaning clear. I’d better do what people who are no good at speaking do – avoid generalisations, take a particular example, and try to use that to show you what I mean. You know the beginning of the <entity>Iliad</entity>, where the poet says that <entity>Chryses</entity> asks <entity>Agamemnon</entity> to let his daughter go, and <entity>Agamemnon</entity> loses his temper, and then <entity>Chryses</entity>, when his request is turned down, utters a prayer to <entity>Apollo</entity>?

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Yes. I do.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: In that case, you must be aware that down as far as the lines He implored the <entity>Achaean</entity> lords, but most of all Atreus’ two sons, the marshals of the host,<cite source="Iliad" ref="1.15–16">37</cite> the poet speaks in person. He does not attempt to direct our imagination towards anyone else, or suggest that someone other than himself is speaking. But in the lines which follow he talks as if he himself is <entity>Chryses</entity>, and does everything he can to make us imagine it is not <entity>Homer</entity> speaking, but the priest. He talks like an old man. The whole of the rest of his narrative is constructed along more or less the same lines – not only events at <entity>Troy</entity>, but also events in <entity>Ithaca</entity>, and the whole of the <entity>Odyssey</entity>.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Exactly.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: But it’s all narrative – both the individual speeches he delivers and the bits he says in between the speeches?

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Yes, of course.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: And when he makes a speech in the character of someone else, can we say that he always makes his own style as close as possible to that of the person he tells us is speaking?

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: No question of it.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: But making yourself resemble someone else – either in the way you speak or in the way you look – isn’t that <concept>imitating</concept> the person you make yourself resemble?

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Of course it is.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: In passages like this, apparently, <entity>Homer</entity> and the rest of the poets use <concept>imitation</concept> to construct their narrative.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Yes.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: If there were no passages where the poet concealed his own person, then his whole work, his whole narrative, would have been created without using <concept>imitation</concept>. To save you telling me again that you don’t understand how this can be, I will explain. Imagine <entity>Homer</entity> told us that <entity>Chryses</entity> came, bringing his daughter’s ransom, as a suppliant to the <entity>Achaeans</entity>, and in particular to their kings, but then went on to tell the story not in the person of <entity>Chryses</entity>, but still as <entity>Homer</entity>. You realise that would be simple narrative, not <concept>imitation</concept>. The story would go something like this. I’m no poet, so I won’t tell it in verse: “The priest came and prayed that the gods might grant to the <entity>Achaeans</entity> that they should capture <entity>Troy</entity>, and return home safely, but he asked them to release his daughter in return for the ransom, and out of reverence for the god. When he had finished, the rest of the <entity>Achaeans</entity> showed him respect, and would have agreed to his request, but <entity>Agamemnon</entity> lost his temper, telling him to depart immediately, and not come back again; otherwise his priest’s staff and the god’s garlands would be no protection to him. The priest’s daughter would be an old woman living in <entity>Argos</entity> with him before there was any question of releasing her. He told the priest to go away and stop bothering him, if he wanted to get home safely. The old man was alarmed by <entity>Agamemnon</entity>’s threats, and went away in silence. But after he had left the camp he addressed many prayers to <entity>Apollo</entity>, calling on the cult-names of the god, reminding him of past favours, and asking his help in return if he had ever, in the building of temples or the sacrifice of victims, given the god a gift which had been a source of pleasure to him. In return for these favours, he prayed that <entity>Apollo</entity>’s arrows might make the <entity>Achaeans</entity> pay for his tears.” That, my friend, is the simple narrative, without <concept>imitation</concept>.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: I see.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: In that case, you can also see that you get just the opposite if you omit what the poet says between the speeches, and leave the dialogue.

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: Yes, I can see that too. That’s the kind of thing you get in tragedy.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Exactly. Now I think I can make clear to you what I couldn’t make clear before, that one type of poetry and storytelling is purely imitative – this is tragedy and comedy, as you say. In another type, the poet tells his own story. I imagine you’d find this mainly in dithyramb. The third type, using both <concept>imitation</concept> and narrative, can be found in epic poetry, and in many other places as well. Are you following me?

### Footnotes (Original)
- <cite source="Iliad" ref="1.15–16">37</cite>: The passage <entity>Socrates</entity> is discussing runs from line 8 to line 42. <entity>Chryses</entity>, a priest of <entity>Apollo</entity>, comes to ransom his daughter. She has been captured in a raid by the <entity>Greeks</entity> (<entity>Achaeans</entity>) and is in the possession of the supreme commander <entity>Agamemnon</entity>, son of <entity>Atreus</entity>.
- <note>38</note>: Tragedy and comedy were in <entity>Socrates</entity>’ and <entity>Plato</entity>’s day the pre-eminent forms of literature. The dithyramb was a type of choral lyric, originally connected with the cult.

### Extracted Arguments
<argument id="arg5" type="poetic-modes">
  <premise>Poetry uses three modes: pure narrative (dithyramb), pure <concept>imitation</concept> (tragedy/comedy), or mixed (epic like <entity>Iliad</entity>/<entity>Odyssey</entity>).</premise>
  <conclusion><concept>Imitation</concept> risks moral corruption by encouraging false resemblances; simple narrative is preferable for education (<relation type="extension">builds on censorship of content</relation>).</conclusion>

### Section 2: Instruments for the Ideal City (400a–400b)  
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.400a–b.  
**Argument Structure**:  
- **Premise 1**: Complex instruments enable multiple modes, which imitate vice (e.g., excess, madness).  
- **Premise 2**: Simple instruments (e.g., **lyre**, **cithara**) promote harmony and virtue.  
- **Conclusion**: Restrict instruments to foster **self-discipline** (**sophrosyne**) and **courage** in guardians.  
**Philosophical Entities**: **Triangular harps** (Lydian, foreign excess); **Reed instruments** (**aulos**, wild tone); **Panpipe** (rustic, for herdsmen).  

**Speaker: Socrates**

**Speaker: Glaucon**

**Speaker: Socrates**  
What about the makers and players of reed instruments? Will you allow them into your city? Isn’t playing a reed instrument more “many-stringed” than anything else? And aren’t the instruments which can play many modes in fact just imitations of the reed-pipe?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes, obviously they are.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
That leaves you the lyre and the cithara. They’ll be right for the city. In the countryside, by contrast, there could be some sort of panpipe for our herdsmen.  

**Citation Note 48**: Harps were of Lydian origin and retained associations of foreignness.  
**Citation Note 49**: The reed-pipe (**aulos**) was nothing like a flute (the traditional translation of the word) but more like an oboe or clarinet. It had a strong and uncompromising tone, and was the favoured instrument of the wilder sorts of religious ritual. Many notes could be produced from manipulation of a single hole, whereas each string of a lyre produced only a single note. The lyre and the cithara were the fundamental stringed instruments. Their principal service was that of duplicating the sung melody. The reed-pipe, by contrast, lent itself to solos. (Cross-ref: **Aulos** linked to **Phrygian mode**'s ecstatic excess; contrasts with **lyre**'s harmonious imitation of virtue.)  

**Book Marker**: _Glaucon, Socrates_ _The Republic_  

### Section 3: Preference for Apollo over Marsyas; Purging Luxury (400c–400d)  
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.400c–d.  
**Argument Structure**:  
- **Premise**: Mythic preference for **Apollo** (god of order, lyre) over **Marsyas** (satyr, aulos) symbolizes choosing disciplined art.  
- **Conclusion**: Purging complex music removes luxury, aligning city with virtue.  
**Philosophical Entities**: **Apollo** (harmony, beauty); **Marsyas** (wildness, flaying myth as purging vice).  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Well, that’s certainly the way our reasoning points.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
There’s nothing very radical in our preferring Apollo and Apollo’s instruments to Marsyas and his instruments.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Good heavens, no. I’m sure there isn’t.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Ye dogs! Without meaning to, we have purged the city we said was too luxurious.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
That was sensible of us.  

**Citation Note 50**: It is characteristic of Socrates to swear ‘by the dog’—a euphemistic oath, comparable to our substitution of ‘gosh!’ for ‘God!’ (Cross-ref: Socratic irony in ethical purging.)  

### Section 4: Rhythms and Their Imitation of Virtuous Life (400d–401a)  
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.400d–401a.  
**Argument Structure**:  
- **Premise 1**: Rhythms must imitate **self-disciplined** and **courageous** life, not complexity.  
- **Premise 2**: Speech (language) precedes rhythm/melody; art conforms to virtuous character.  
- **Conclusion**: Refer to expert (**Damon**) for specifics; prioritize grace from good soul.  
**Philosophical Entities**: **Rhythm** (**rhythmos**); **Metre** (e.g., dactyl, iambic); **Damon** (musical theorist).  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Come on, then. Let’s purge the rest of it. Our next concern after mode will be rhythm. We should not pursue complexity, nor do we want all kinds of metres. We should see what are the rhythms of a self-disciplined and courageous life, and after looking at those, make the metre and melody conform to the speech of someone like that. We won’t make speech conform to rhythm and melody. Which these rhythms are is for you to say, as it was with the modes.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
I really don’t know what to say about that. In my experience, there are three types of rhythm from which metres are woven together, just as when it comes to tones, there are four elements from which all the modes are derived. But I have no idea which types imitate which lives.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
That’s something we can ask Damon about. He can tell us which metres are appropriate to meanness of spirit, arrogance, madness and other faults of character, and which rhythms should be left for those whose character is the opposite. I seem to remember, though I can’t be sure, hearing him use terms like “composite enoplion”; then there were “dactyls,” and “heroic metre,” which he arranged, somehow or other, so that upbeat and downbeat were made equal as it turns into short or long at the end. Then there was the “iambic,” I seem to remember, and another he called “trochaic,” with their long and short syllables. For some of them, I think he condemned or approved the pulse of the metrical feet as much as the rhythms themselves. Or possibly it was the two together, I can’t be sure. All these questions, as I say, can be referred to Damon. It would take us a long time to decide them. Or do you think we should try?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
God forbid.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
But that gracefulness and want of grace can follow on from what is rhythmical and unrhythmical, that is something you can decide.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Of course.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
But then if rhythm and mode follow language, as we said just now, and not the other way round, what is rhythmical must follow and imitate fine language, while what is not rhythmical follows the opposite. The same with harmony and discord.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes, rhythm and mode certainly should follow language.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
What about manner of speaking, and what is actually said? Don’t they follow from the nature of the speaker’s soul?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Of course.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
And the other things follow from manner of speaking?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
In that case, all these things—the right way of speaking, the right attunement, grace and rhythm—follow from a good nature. I don’t mean the good nature which is the polite name we give to stupidity, but the true intelligence which consists in a character which is rightly and properly constituted.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Exactly.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
So if the young are to perform their proper function, aren’t these the qualities they should be everywhere aiming at?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
They are.  

**Book Marker**: _Book 3 3gge~40ib_ _Socrates, Glaucon_  

**Citation Note 51**: Greek metre was based on length of syllable rather than stress-accent. One long syllable was the equal of two short. The three types of rhythm fundamental to poetic metre correspond to different proportions between the divisions (upbeat and downbeat) of the metrical foot: 2:2 or equal as in dactyl (ww), spondee (”), and anapaest (w w ”); 2:1 or double as in iamb (w ~) and trochee (” w); 3:2 as in cretic (” w ). The enoplion (or ‘martial’) was a rhythm used for processional and marching songs; heroic metre is the dactylic hexameter of Homeric epic, in which dactyl and spondee can be substituted for each other. (Cross-ref: Rhythms imitate **courage** in martial contexts; links to **Damon**'s expertise.)  

**Citation Note 52**: *Eu-etheia*, ‘good nature’, more usually meant ‘simplicity’ in the disparaging sense. (Entity: Distinguishes true **virtue** from naive simplicity.)  

### Section 5: Application to Crafts and Environment (401a–402a)  
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.401a–402a.  
**Argument Structure**:  
- **Premise 1**: Grace/rhythm in art reflects soul's nature; bad art corrupts like poor pasture.  
- **Premise 2**: Craftsmen must imitate **fine nature** (**kalon**); guardians raised in beautiful environment.  
- **Conclusion**: Musical education penetrates soul deeply, fostering perception of beauty/defect.  
**Philosophical Entities**: **Gracefulness** (**charis**); **Fine** (**kalon**); **Self-disciplined nature** (**sophron**).  
**Cross-Ref**: Analogy to "healthy breeze" from ideal forms (metaphysical link to Book 6–7).  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Painting is full of these qualities, I imagine, as is any skill of the same sort. So are weaving, embroidery, building—the manufacture of any household object, in fact—even the condition of our bodies and of all things that grow. All these contain gracefulness and want of grace. Want of grace or rhythm, and wrong attunement, are close relatives of wrong speech and a wrong nature, while their opposites are close relatives and imitations of the opposite, the self-disciplined and good nature.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Precisely.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Is it only the poets we have to keep an eye on, then, compelling them to put the likeness of the good nature into their poems, or else go and write poems somewhere else? Don’t we have to keep an eye on the other craftsmen as well, and stop them putting what has the wrong nature, what is undisciplined, slavish or wanting in grace, into their representations of living things, or into buildings, or into any manufactured object? Anyone who finds this impossible is not to be allowed to be a craftsman in our city. That way our guardians will not be brought up among images of what is bad, like animals put out to graze on bad pasture. We don’t want them browsing and feeding each day—taking in a little here and a little there and without realising it accumulating a single large evil in their souls. No, we must seek out the craftsmen with a gift for tracking down the nature of what is fine, what has grace, so that our young can live in a healthy environment, drawing improvement from every side, whenever things which are beautifully fashioned expose their eyes or ears to some wholesome breeze from healthy regions and lead them imperceptibly, from earliest childhood, into affinity, friendship and harmony with beauty of speech and thought.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes, that would be by far the best way for them to be brought up.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Aren’t there two reasons, Glaucon, why musical and poetic education is so important? Firstly because rhythm and mode penetrate more deeply into the inner soul than anything else does; they have the most powerful effect on it, since they bring gracefulness with them. They make a person graceful, if he is rightly brought up, and the opposite, if he is not. And secondly because anyone with the right kind of education in this area will have the clearest perception of things which are unsatisfactory—things which are badly made or naturally defective. Being quite rightly disgusted by them, he will praise what is beautiful and fine. Delighting in it, and receiving it into his soul, he will feed on it and so become noble and good. What is ugly he will rightly condemn and hate, even before he is old enough for rational thought. And when rationality does make its appearance, won’t the person who has been brought up in this way recognise it because of its familiarity, and be particularly delighted with it?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes. If you ask me, that certainly is the point of a musical and poetic education.  

### Section 6: Analogy to Literacy and Recognition of Virtues (402a–402d)  
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.402a–d.  
**Argument Structure**:  
- **Premise**: Musical education like learning letters: Recognize virtues (e.g., **self-discipline**, **courage**) recurring in all contexts.  
- **Conclusion**: Essential for guardians' expertise in imitating **justice** and opposites.  
**Philosophical Entities**: **Letters** (analogy for virtues); **Self-discipline** (**sophrosyne**); **Courage** (**andreia**); **Liberality** (**eleutheriotes**).  
**Cross-Ref**: Mirrors divided line analogy (Book 6, 509d–511e) for perceiving forms.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
It’s just like learning to read. We could do it as soon as we realised that there are only a few letters, and that they keep recurring in all the words which contain them. We never dismissed them as unworthy of our attention, either in short words or in long, but were keen to recognise them everywhere, in the belief that we would not be able to read until we could do this.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
True.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Well, then. We shan’t recognise copies of the letters—supposing reflections of them were to appear in water, or in a mirror—until we can recognise the letters themselves. Don’t both involve the same skill and expertise?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Of course they do.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
And isn’t it, as I say, exactly the same with musical and poetic education? There’s not the remotest chance of becoming properly educated—either for ourselves or for the people we say we must educate to be our guardians—until we recognise the sort of thing self-discipline is. Likewise courage, liberality and generosity of spirit, which keep recurring all over the place, plus all the qualities which are closely related to them, and their opposites. We must see the presence both of them and of their likenesses in all the things they are present in, and we must learn never to dismiss them, be the context trivial or important, but to regard them as part of the same skill and expertise.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes, it is absolutely essential that we learn this.  

**Book Marker**: _Socrates, Glaucon_ _The Republic_  

### Section 7: Beauty in Soul and Body; Love and Self-Discipline (402d–403b)  
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.402d–403b.  
**Argument Structure**:  
- **Premise 1**: Harmonious soul-body is fairest; well-educated love such beauty.  
- **Premise 2**: Excess pleasure (e.g., sexual) opposes **self-discipline**; right love is controlled.  
- **Conclusion**: Law against consummation in pederasty to preserve virtue.  
**Philosophical Entities**: **Good character** (**eugeneia**); **Harmony** (**harmonia**); **Sexual pleasure** (opposed to **sophrosyne**).  
**Cross-Ref**: Links to **philosophical eros** in *Symposium* (eros for beautiful souls).  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
So if someone is lucky enough to possess a soul containing a good character, and a physical form which matches and harmonises with that character, which is modelled on the same pattern, wouldn’t that be the fairest of sights for anyone with eyes to see it?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Very much so.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
But what is fairest is most desirable.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Naturally.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
So the well educated man will fall in love with people as much like this as possible. But he will not fall in love with someone whose soul and body are out of tune.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Not if the defect is in the soul. If it is in the body, he might put up with it, and be prepared to love him.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Ah, yes, of course. Am I right in thinking you are—or were—the lover of a boy like this? Anyway, be that as it may, I think you’re right. Now, the next question. Does too much pleasure have anything to do with self-discipline?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
How could it? Too much pleasure makes you as irrational as pain does.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Does it have anything to do with any other good quality?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
No.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
How about arrogance and indiscipline? Does it have anything to do with those?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes, everything.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Can you think of any pleasure greater or keener than sexual pleasure?  

**Book Marker**: _Glaucon_, _Socrates_ _The Republic_  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
No. Nor a more insane pleasure, either.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Whereas the right sort of love is by its nature the self-controlled and harmonious love of what is self-disciplined and beautiful?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Precisely.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
So we must not offer the right sort of lover what is insane, or what is related to lack of discipline?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
No, we mustn’t.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
In which case we mustn’t offer him sexual pleasure, must we? Neither lover nor boy must have anything to do with it, if they are loving and being loved in the right way.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Good heavens, no, Socrates. We certainly mustn’t offer them that.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
You will pass a law to that effect, presumably, in this city you are founding. A lover can kiss his boy friend, spend time with him and touch him, as he would a son—for beauty’s sake, and if the boy says “yes.” Apart from that, his relationship with the boy he is interested in should never allow anyone to imagine he has gone any further than that. Otherwise he will be condemned as uneducated, and blind to beauty.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes, I shall pass a law to that effect.  

### Section 8: Conclusion of Musical Education and Transition to Physical Training (403b–c)  
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.403b–c.  
**Argument Structure**:  
- **Premise**: Musical education ends in love of beauty; complements physical education for soul-body harmony.  
- **Conclusion**: Good soul improves body; avoid excesses like drunkenness.  
**Philosophical Entities**: **Physical education** (**gymnastike**); **Drunkenness** (vice opposing guardianship).  
**Cross-Ref**: Transitions to gymnastic training (next section); soul primacy echoes *Phaedo* (body as soul's instrument).  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Well, then, do you think our discussion of musical and poetic education has come to an end? It has certainly ended where it ought to end. Music and poetry ought, I take it, to end in love of beauty.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
I agree.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
And after musical and poetic education, our young men must be given a physical education.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Naturally.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Here, too, from their earliest childhood and throughout their lives, they must be brought up very carefully. The situation is something like this, I believe, but see what you think. It’s my opinion that if the body is in good shape, it does not by its own excellence make the soul good. On the other hand, a good soul can by its own excellence make a body as good as it is capable of being. What is your opinion?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
I agree with you.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Let’s assume we have made adequate provision for the mind. If we were now to entrust it with making detailed prescriptions for the body, contenting ourselves for brevity’s sake with providing general guidelines, would we be going about things in the right way?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
We would.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
Well, drunkenness was one thing we said they should avoid. A guard is the last person who can be allowed to get drunk, and not know where on earth he is.  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes. It’s absurd for a guardian to need a guardian.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
What about their food? After all, these men are competing for us, aren’t they, in the most important of all competitions?  

**Speaker: Glaucon**  
Yes.  

**Speaker: Socrates**  
In that case, would the diet of present-day athletes be the right thing...  

**Book Marker**: _Socrates_, _Glaucon_  

## Overall Argument Summary for Retrieval
- **Central Thesis**: Musical and poetic education, through restricted modes/rhythms and imitation, cultivates virtues in the soul, essential for guardians' justice in the ideal city. It precedes and informs physical training, ensuring harmony between soul and body.
- **Key Relationships**: Virtues (**sophrosyne**, **andreia**) are foundational to **justice**; art/crafts as mimesis must reflect them (epistemological training via recognition); excess (pleasure, complexity) corrupts, linking ethics to metaphysics of forms.
- **Retrieval Tags**: Plato Republic Book 3, musical education, virtues imitation, Socratic dialogue, guardian training, soul harmony.

## Structured Dialogue and Arguments

### Section 404a–c: Critique of Athletic Diets and Proposal for Simple Regimen
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic* 3.404a–c  
**Summary**: **Socrates** criticizes overly restrictive athletic diets for producing lethargy and vulnerability, advocating a balanced, simple regimen for **guardian-warriors** to ensure alertness and resilience. This mirrors the simplicity in **musical education** (<cross-ref: harmony of body and soul for **virtue**>).

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "404 for them?"
- **Glaucon**: "It might well be."
- **Socrates**: "It’s a pretty soporific diet, and unreliable from a health point of view. Haven’t you noticed that these athletes spend most of their lives asleep, and that if they depart even slightly from their prescribed regime, they contract serious and acute diseases?"
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, I have noticed that."
- **Socrates**: "We need something a bit less crude as a regimen for our warrior-athletes. It’s vital that they should be alert, like hounds, as keen of sight and hearing as possible, and capable, when they are on active service, of tolerating a variety of drink and food, extremes of heat, storms, without any adverse effect on their health."
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, I think I agree."
- **Socrates**: "Well, then, won’t the best **physical education** be sister, in a way, to the **musical and poetic education** we have just outlined?"
- **Glaucon**: "How do you mean?"
- **Socrates**: "It will be **physical education**, I take it, of a simple and judicious type—especially since it is intended for those who are soldiers."
- **Glaucon**: "Simple and judicious in what way?"
- **Socrates**: "This is the sort of thing you could learn from **Homer**, actually. In the heroes’ feasts when they are on campaign, you remember, he does not feast them on fish—despite the fact that they are on the **Hellespont**, right by the sea—nor on stewed meat, but only on roast, which is what soldiers would find easiest to cope with. Wherever you are, more or less, it is easier just to use fire than to carry pots and pans around with you."
- **Glaucon**: "It certainly is."
- **Socrates**: "As for seasonings, **Homer** never, as far as I remember, says anything about them. All athletes know, don’t they, that if you want your body to be in good shape you must avoid anything like that?"
- **Glaucon**: "They are right about this, and they do well to avoid that kind of thing."

**Extracted Argument Structure** (On Simple Diet for **Guardians**):
- **Premise 1**: Athletic diets cause sleepiness and disease vulnerability (e.g., athletes "spend most of their lives asleep").
- **Premise 2**: **Guardians** require alertness and resilience for **active service** (e.g., tolerating "variety of drink and food, extremes of heat").
- **Premise 3**: **Homer**'s depiction of heroes' simple feasts (roast meat, no fish/seasonings) suits soldiers' needs (<cross-ref: *Iliad* for ethical exemplars>).
- **Conclusion**: **Physical education** must be "simple and judicious," paralleling **musical education** to foster **self-discipline** and **health** in the soul-body harmony.

**Entities**:
- **Philosophical Figures**: **Socrates**, **Glaucon**, **Homer**
- **Concepts**: **Physical Education**, **Musical and Poetic Education**, **Health**, **Self-Discipline**, **Active Service**
- **Places**: **Hellespont**

**Annotations** (from original footnotes): None in this section.

### Section 404c–d: Rejection of Luxurious Foods and Parallels to Music
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic* 3.404c–d (p. 95)  
**Summary**: **Socrates** rejects elaborate cuisines (**Syracusan**, **Sicilian**, **Corinthian**, **Attic**) as breeding disease, analogous to complex music breeding indiscipline (<cross-ref: Book 3 on music's role in **virtue**>).

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "Then if you think this is right, my friend, **Syracusan** cuisine and the **Sicilian a la carte** are apparently not things you approve of." [53]
- **Glaucon**: "No, I don’t think I do approve of them."
- **Socrates**: "Then you disapprove also of **Corinthian** girl friends for men who are going to be in good shape physically." [54]
- **Glaucon**: "Definitely."
- **Socrates**: "How about the delights, so-called, of **Attic** pastries?"
- **Glaucon**: "I have no choice but to condemn those too."
- **Socrates**: "I suspect that if we likened these foods, and this whole regimen, to the music and song that uses every mode and all the rhythms, that would be an accurate comparison."
- **Glaucon**: "Indeed it would."
- **Socrates**: "There, variety and luxury bred indiscipline. Here it breeds disease. And as simplicity in music and poetry gave souls **self-discipline**, so simplicity in **physical training** gives bodies **health**, doesn’t it?"
- **Glaucon**: "That is absolutely right."

**Extracted Argument Structure** (Luxury as Impediment to **Virtue**):
- **Premise 1**: Luxurious foods (e.g., **Syracusan** cuisine) parallel complex music, breeding "indiscipline" and "disease."
- **Premise 2**: Simplicity in **music/poetry** instills **self-discipline** in the soul.
- **Conclusion**: Simplicity in **physical training** ensures **health** in the body, essential for **guardians**' **civic function** (<cross-ref: ethical education in ideal state>).

**Entities**:
- **Philosophical Concepts**: **Self-Discipline**, **Health**, **Indiscipline**, **Physical Training**
- **Places/Cultures**: **Syracuse**, **Sicily**, **Corinth**, **Attica**

**Annotations**:
- [53] **Sicily** in general, and the court of **Dionysius** at **Syracuse** in particular, were noted for elaborate cuisine.
- [54] **Corinth** was a noted supplier of *hetairai*—female dining companions, professionals something like the Japanese geisha, except that sex was taken for granted as part of the service.

### Section 404d–405c: Consequences of Poor Education (Lawcourts and Clinics)
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic* 3.404d–405c  
**Summary**: Poor education leads to proliferation of lawcourts and doctors, a "disgrace" indicating lack of internal **justice** and **health** (<cross-ref: **justice** as internal harmony in Book 4>).

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "As lawlessness and disease multiply in a city, don’t lawcourts and clinics start opening up all over the place? And when even free men, in large numbers, start taking them seriously, don’t these disciplines become extremely self-important?"
- **Glaucon**: "How can they fail to?"
- **Socrates**: "You won’t be able to find any clearer evidence of bad, inferior education in a city, will you, than the need for skilled doctors and judges. And not just among ordinary manual workers, but even among those with pretensions to a free and enlightened upbringing? Don’t you think it’s a disgrace, and a sure sign of poor education, to be forced to rely on an extraneous **justice**—that of masters or judges—for want of a sense of **justice** of one’s own?" [55]
- **Glaucon**: "The greatest disgrace possible."
- **Socrates**: "And yet, is it really any more disgraceful, would you say, than the person who in addition to spending the greater part of his life in the lawcourts as defendant or plaintiff, is also convinced, such is his ignorance of what is good, that his cleverness at committing crimes, and his subsequent ability to use every evasion and loophole to escape conviction and avoid paying the penalty, is actually a matter for self-congratulation? And all for the sake of what is trivial and of no importance, because he does not realise how much finer and better it is to see to it that his life does not depend on finding a juror who is half-asleep."
- **Glaucon**: "You’re right. That is worse than the previous example."

**Extracted Argument Structure** (Poor Education as Disgrace):
- **Premise 1**: Multiplication of lawcourts/clinics signals "lawlessness and disease" from inferior education.
- **Premise 2**: Reliance on external **judges** or doctors shows lack of internal **justice** and **health**—a "disgrace" even for "free men."
- **Premise 3**: Litigiousness from ignorance of "what is good" is worse, as it celebrates evasion over true **virtue**.
- **Conclusion**: True education fosters self-reliant **justice** and **health**, reducing need for external aids (<cross-ref: **knowledge** of good in epistemology>).

**Entities**:
- **Concepts**: **Justice**, **Lawcourts**, **Clinics**, **Education**, **Disgrace**
- **Figures**: None new.

**Annotations**:
- [55] **Athenian** lawcourts were in fact staffed by amateurs—jurymen chosen by lot from a pool of citizen volunteers, and a judge who was no more than a presiding magistrate, also chosen by lot, and held office only for a year. Hence the word translated as ‘judges’ at 405a also means ‘jurors’.

### Section 405c–406a: Critique of Modern Medicine and Herodicus
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic* 3.405c–406a (pp. 96–97)  
**Summary**: **Socrates** contrasts ancient medicine (**Asclepius**' sons) with modern, protracted treatments (e.g., **Herodicus**), which prolong invalidity and disrupt **civic function**.

**Dialogue**:
- **Socrates**: "And don’t you think it’s a disgrace, to need medical attention, not as a result of injuries or the onset of some seasonal illness, but because our inactivity, and a routine such as we have described, have filled us up with gas and ooze, like a marsh, and compelled those clever doctors of the school of **Asclepius** to invent names like “wind” and “flux” for our diseases?"
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, they really do have some extraordinary new names for diseases."
- **Socrates**: "It wasn’t so, I believe, in **Asclepius**’ time. I am thinking of his sons, at **Troy**. When **Eurypylus** is wounded, and is given **Pramnian** wine with a lot of barley sprinkled over it and cheese grated on to it—which does indeed seem likely to cause a fever—they do not criticise the woman who gives him the drink, nor do they find fault with **Patroclus**, who is responsible for the treatment."
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, it certainly is a surprising drink to give someone in that condition."
- **Socrates**: "Until you remember that it was not until the time of **Herodicus**, or so they say, that the school of **Asclepius** took up the modern medicine which is a slave to the disease. **Herodicus** was an athletics coach who became an invalid. With a combination of physical regimen and medicine, he started off by making his own life a misery, and then graduated to making other people’s lives a misery as well—lots of them."
- **Glaucon**: "How did he do that?"
- **Socrates**: "By making his own death such a long-drawn-out business. He devoted himself to his terminal illness—without ever really managing to cure himself—and spent his whole life completely wrapped up in the business of being a patient. He had a wretched time if he departed in any way from his normal routine, but using his knowledge to give himself a hard death, he did reach old age."
- **Glaucon**: "A fine reward for his skill."
- **Socrates**: "No more than he deserved, for not realising that **Asclepius**’ failure to explain this branch of medicine to his sons was not the result of ignorance or lack of experience. It was because he knew that in any well-run society each citizen has his own appointed **function** to perform in the state, and that no one can afford to spend his whole life being ill and being an invalid. We recognise this when it’s the man in the street, but then rather absurdly fail to recognise it in the case of those who are rich and supposedly fortunate."

**Extracted Argument Structure** (Medicine and **Civic Function**):
- **Premise 1**: Modern medicine (**Herodicus**) prolongs illness, creating "misery" and invalidity.
- **Premise 2**: Ancient medicine (**Asclepius**' sons at **Troy**) treated acute wounds simply (e.g., **Eurypylus**' posset), assuming prior **health**.
- **Conclusion**: Medicine should serve **civic function**; chronic treatment disrupts the state's division of labor (<cross-ref: **justice** as each performing their role>).

**Entities**:
- **Figures**: **Asclepius**, **Herodicus**, **Eurypylus**, **Patroclus**
- **Concepts**: **Civic Function**, **Medicine**, **Health**
- **Places**: **Troy**
- **Myths**: **Iliad** references

**Annotations**:
- [56] Felt caps for the head, typically worn by long-term invalids—not a treatment, but something like staying on the couch all day in one’s dressing-gown.

### Section 406d–407a: Carpenter vs. Rich Man on Illness
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.406d–407a (p. 97–98)  
**Summary**: **Socrates** argues laborers accept short treatments to resume **function**, unlike the rich who indulge invalidity, impeding **virtue** (citing **Phocylides**).

**Dialogue**:
- **Glaucon**: "What do you mean?"
- **Socrates**: "When a carpenter falls ill, he has no objection to taking some medicine from the doctor to purge the disease, or to getting rid of it by means of an emetic, or cauterisation, or surgery. But if he is prescribed a long course of treatment, and has to wear special caps, with all that involves, he’ll soon tell you he can’t afford to be ill, and that life is not worth living if he has to spend all his time thinking about his illness, and neglecting his business. Then he’ll bid a doctor of this kind good day, and resume his normal routine. If he regains his health, he can get on with his life, and do his work. If he is too weak physically, he will die, and so escape his troubles."
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, I think that’s the right kind of attitude towards **medicine** for someone like that."
- **Socrates**: "Because he had a certain **function** to perform, and his life was worth nothing to him if he couldn’t perform it?"
- **Glaucon**: "Clearly."
- **Socrates**: "Whereas the rich man, in our view, has no prescribed **function** of the kind which makes life not worth living if he is forced to give it up."
- **Glaucon**: "Not if we’re to believe what people say."
- **Socrates**: "You’re obviously not aware of **Phocylides**’ saying, that once you have the means of subsistence you should start to practise **goodness**."
- **Glaucon**: "I am aware of it, but I don’t think people should wait that long."
- **Socrates**: "Well, we won’t argue with him about that. However, here’s a question we can settle for ourselves. Is practising **goodness** something the rich man should devote himself to, and is life not worth living for a rich man who can’t devote himself to it? Or is being an invalid a handicap to carpentry, or any other art or skill, because it stops people concentrating on them, and yet not an impediment to following **Phocylides**’ advice?"

**Extracted Argument Structure** (Invalidity vs. **Virtue**):
- **Premise 1**: Laborers (e.g., carpenter) prioritize **function** over prolonged illness.
- **Premise 2**: Rich lack such **function**, indulging illness despite **Phocylides**' call to "practise goodness."
- **Conclusion**: Invalidity impedes **virtue** and **knowledge** more than crafts; true life requires fulfilling **civic role** (<cross-ref: **ethics** of the good life>).

**Entities**:
- **Figures**: **Phocylides**
- **Concepts**: **Function**, **Goodness**, **Virtue**, **Medicine**

### Section 407b–408a: Invalidity as Impediment to **Virtue** and Learning
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.407b–408a (p. 98)  
**Summary**: Excessive bodily concern hinders household management, military service, and especially **philosophy** and **virtue** (<cross-ref: soul's priority in metaphysics>).

**Dialogue**:
- **Glaucon**: "It certainly is an impediment. In fact, this exaggerated concern for the body, going beyond normal **physical exercise**, is just about the greatest impediment of all. It creates difficulties when you are running a household, or on military service, or even in some sedentary job holding public office."
- **Socrates**: "Worst of all, it is a problem when it comes to any form of learning, thought or self-development. Concern for the body is for ever imagining headaches or dizziness, and saying they are caused by **philosophy**, so that wherever it appears, it is in every way an impediment to the practice and study of **virtue**. It makes people spend their whole time thinking they are ill."
- **Glaucon**: "That wouldn’t surprise me."
- **Socrates**: "Are we going to say, then, that this too is something **Asclepius** was aware of? There are some people whose constitution and regimen give them good **physical health**, but who have contracted some identifiable illness. It was for their benefit, and for people in their situation, that he taught the art of **medicine**, using drugs and surgery to rid them of their diseases, but then prescribing their normal daily routine, to avoid disruption to civic life, whereas he did not try to prescribe for those whose bodies are internally riddled with disease. He didn’t try to draw off a little bit here, pour in a little bit there, and in this way give men long and unpleasant lives, and enable them to produce children, in all probability, no different from themselves. He thought it wrong to treat those who were unable to take their place in the daily round, on the grounds that they were worth nothing either to themselves or to the city."
- **Glaucon**: "A bit of a statesman, your **Asclepius**."
- **Socrates**: "He obviously was. And as for his children—with a father like that—you can see both that they distinguished themselves at **Troy** on the field of battle, and that they employed **medicine** in the way I have described. Do you remember how they treated **Menelaus** for the wound he received from **Pandarus**? They sucked the blood, And to the wound applied their soothing herbs. [57] They did not try to tell him what he should eat or drink afterwards, any more than they tried to tell **Eurypylus**. They thought that for men who had been in good **health** and living a sober life before they were wounded, their drugs were a sufficient cure. They could even drink a posset of barley and cheese immediately afterwards. But if someone was naturally unhealthy, and leading a dissolute life, they regarded his life as of no value either to himself or to anyone else. They did not believe their art was intended for people like this, and they refused to treat them, even if they were richer than **Midas**."

**Extracted Argument Structure** (Bodily Concern Impedes **Virtue**):
- **Premise 1**: Exaggerated bodily focus disrupts practical roles (household, military, office).
- **Premise 2**: It worst impedes "learning, thought or self-development," blaming **philosophy** for ills.
- **Premise 3**: **Asclepius** treated only those able to resume **civic life**, rejecting chronic cases as valueless to state/self.
- **Conclusion**: **Medicine** serves **virtue** and society; invalidity produces unworthy offspring and disrupts **justice** (<cross-ref: eugenics in guardian breeding, Book 5>).

**Entities**:
- **Concepts**: **Philosophy**, **Virtue**, **Physical Exercise**, **Physical Health**, **Medicine**, **Civic Life**
- **Figures**: **Asclepius**, **Menelaus**, **Pandarus**, **Midas**
- **Places**: **Troy**

**Annotations**:
- [57] *Iliad* 4.218.

### Section 408a–c: Myth of **Asclepius** and Pindar's Critique
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.408a–c (p. 99)  
**Summary**: **Socrates** reconciles myths: **Asclepius** was no mercenary (as **Pindar**/tragedians claim), but a statesman prioritizing societal **good** (<cross-ref: gods as non-mercenary in Book 2>).

**Dialogue**:
- **Glaucon**: "Very enlightened, the way you describe them, these sons of **Asclepius**."
- **Socrates**: "So they should be. All the same, **Pindar** and the tragedians do not believe us. They say that **Asclepius** was the son of **Apollo**, that in return for gold he cured a rich man who was at death’s door, and that for this he was struck by lightning. What we have said so far does not allow us to believe both parts of their story. If he was the son of a god, we shall say, then he was not mercenary. If he was mercenary, then he was not the son of a god."
- **Glaucon**: "I quite agree with you, as far as that goes."

**Extracted Argument Structure** (Reconciling Myth with **Ethics**):
- **Premise 1**: Myths (**Pindar**, tragedians) depict **Asclepius** as greedy, struck by lightning.
- **Premise 2**: As son of **Apollo** (god), he cannot be mercenary; greed contradicts divine nature.
- **Conclusion**: Myth's second part (greed) is false; **Asclepius** acted for societal **good**, not gold (<cross-ref: critique of poetry in Book 10>).

**Entities**:
- **Figures**: **Pindar**, **Asclepius**, **Apollo**
- **Concepts**: **Ethics**, **Mercenary**

### Section 408d–410a: Qualifications for Doctors and Judges
**Citation**: Plato, *Republic* 3.408d–410a (pp. 99–100, Book 3 408b–410a)  
**Summary**: Best doctors/judges need experience with ills/wrongs but healthy/moral minds; judges use mind to rule mind, avoiding corruption (<cross-ref: **knowledge** vs. experience in epistemology>).

**Dialogue**:
- **Glaucon**: "But there’s another question I’d like to ask you, **Socrates**. We need good doctors in our city, don’t we? And I imagine the best doctors will be the ones who have treated the greatest number of healthy and sick people. Similarly, the best judges will be those who have associated with all kinds of characters."
- **Socrates**: "We certainly do need doctors. Good ones, that is. And do you know who I think the good ones are?"
- **Glaucon**: "I will if you tell me."
- **Socrates**: "I’ll try. But you’re asking about two quite different things in the same question."
- **Glaucon**: "Why is that?"
- **Socrates**: "Doctors will become most skilled if from their earliest years they not only learn the art of **medicine**, but also come into contact with the largest possible number of the most diseased bodies, and if they have themselves suffered from all illnesses, and are by their nature far from healthy. The reason for this, I believe, is that they do not use the body to treat the body. If they did, it would not be allowable for a doctor’s body ever to be, or get itself into, a bad condition. No, they use the mind to treat the body, and it is not permitted for a mind which has become diseased, and is still in bad shape, to treat anything successfully."
- **Glaucon**: "True."
- **Socrates**: "A judge, on the other hand, uses the mind to rule the mind. So it is not allowable for a judge’s mind, from its earliest years, to be brought up in close contact with minds which are no good, or for it to have done a complete course in all forms of wrongdoing for itself, so that it can readily draw on its own experience in dealing with the wrongdoings of others."

**Extracted Argument Structure** (Expertise in **Medicine** and **Justice**):
- **Premise 1 (Doctors)**: Skill from treating many bodies/illnesses, but via healthy mind (not diseased body).
- **Premise 2 (Judges)**: Skill from observing wrongs, but via uncorrupted mind (not personal wrongdoing).
- **Conclusion**: True **knowledge** requires pure mind; experience alone corrupts **justice** (<cross-ref: philosopher-kings' education>).

**Entities**:
- **Concepts**: **Medicine**, **Judge**, **Mind**, **Knowledge**, **Wrongdoing**
- **Figures**: **Socrates**

## Section 1: The Ideal Judge (408e–410a)
**Text Type**: Dialogue excerpt.  
**Argument Structure**: Main argument on the qualities of a <entity type="concept">good judge</entity>: Experience of <entity type="concept">evil</entity> corrupts judgment; purity through <entity type="concept">education</entity> enables true discernment.  
**Cross-References**: Links to soul's tripartite nature [ref: 435a–441c]; contrasts with earlier medical analogy for soul care [ref: 403c–407e, footnote 58].

### Dialogue Separation
- **Socrates** (408e–409a): "Like a doctor drawing on his experience of the body when he treats disease. No, if it is to be fine and noble, and able to judge questions of <entity type="concept">right and wrong</entity> in a healthy way, it must have had no experience—no taint—of <entity type="concept">evil natures</entity> when it was young. That’s why, when they are young, people who are morally <entity type="concept">good</entity> strike us as naive, and easily fooled by wrongdoers. They have no internal model corresponding to the behaviour of people who are no <entity type="concept">good</entity>."

- **Glaucon** (409a): "Yes, that’s exactly what happens to them."

- **Socrates** (409a–b): "For that reason, the <entity type="concept">good judge</entity> must be old, not young, a late developer when it comes to discovering the nature of <entity type="concept">injustice</entity>. He will not have seen it as something internal, in his own <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, but as something external, in the <entity type="concept">souls</entity> of others. He will have trained himself over a long period of time to see the kind of <entity type="concept">evil injustice</entity> is, relying on theoretical <entity type="concept">knowledge</entity>, not on personal experience."

- **Glaucon** (409b): "Yes, that certainly seems the noblest kind of judge."

- **Socrates** (409b–c): "And a _good_ judge, what is more. That was your question. After all, a <entity type="concept">good soul</entity> makes a <entity type="concept">good person</entity>. The person who is knowing and distrustful, with a long history of wrongdoing of his own, who regards himself as a criminal, but a clever one, can cope with people like himself when he meets them. His wariness makes him seem knowing, because he has the model of his own behaviour to refer to. But when he comes into contact with people who are <entity type="concept">good</entity>, older people, then he looks pretty silly. He is distrustful without reason, and cannot recognise a <entity type="concept">healthy nature</entity>, because he has no model of it. But because he encounters more people who are no <entity type="concept">good</entity> than <entity type="concept">good</entity>, he is regarded, by himself and by others, as <entity type="concept">wise</entity> rather than foolish."

- **Glaucon** (409c): "That is absolutely true."

- **Socrates** (409c–d): "In that case, if we are looking for a <entity type="concept">good and wise judge</entity>, he is not our man. We want the other sort. <entity type="concept">Evil</entity> can never understand either <entity type="concept">goodness</entity> or itself, whereas <entity type="concept">goodness</entity>, if its natural gifts are improved by <entity type="concept">education</entity>, will in time gain a <entity type="concept">knowledge</entity> both of itself and of <entity type="concept">evil</entity>. So though the <entity type="concept">good man</entity> can become <entity type="concept">wise</entity>, in my view, the bad man cannot."

- **Glaucon** (409d): "That’s my view, too."

- **Socrates** (409d–410a): "In which case, this is the kind of art of judging you will legislate for in your city, isn’t it, together with an art of medicine of the kind we described earlier? Between them they will care for the <entity type="concept">souls</entity> and bodies of those citizens who are naturally <entity type="concept">good</entity>. As for the ones who are not <entity type="concept">good</entity>, they will allow the physically defective to die, whereas those who have incurable faults of the <entity type="concept">soul</entity> they will themselves put to death."

- **Glaucon** (410a): "Yes. After all, it has been shown to be the best thing both for the individuals concerned and for the city." <footnote id="58">At 403c this conclusion was drawn concerning those whose physical ill-health precluded useful activity of either a manual or intellectual sort. There has been no previous discussion, however, of the treatment of the incurably criminal. [Cross-ref: 403c; relates to ethics of euthanasia in ideal state].</footnote>

### Extracted Argument: Qualities of the Good Judge

- **Premise 2**: Youthful exposure to <entity type="concept">evil</entity> corrupts the <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, making one naive if pure or cynical if experienced (408e–409a).
- **Reasoning**: True judgment requires theoretical <entity type="concept">knowledge</entity> from <entity type="concept">education</entity>, observing <entity type="concept">evil</entity> externally in old age, preserving the <entity type="concept">soul</entity>'s purity (409a–b). <entity type="concept">Goodness</entity> educated yields understanding of both <entity type="concept">good</entity> and <entity type="concept">evil</entity>; <entity type="concept">evil</entity> cannot (409c–d).
- **Conclusion**: The ideal <entity type="concept">judge</entity> is elderly, theoretically trained, and legislates alongside medicine to care for <entity type="concept">good souls</entity>, euthanizing incurable <entity type="concept">evil</entity> (409d–410a).
