## Section 2: Education and Self-Discipline (410a–411e)
**Text Type**: Dialogue excerpt.  
**Argument Structure**: <entity type="concept">Education</entity> in music/poetry and gymnastics fosters <entity type="concept">self-discipline</entity> in the <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, prioritizing <entity type="concept">soul</entity> over body.  
**Cross-References**: Ties to earlier education patterns [ref: 376c–403c, footnote 59]; soul's spirited/philosophical parts [ref: 435a–441c].

### Dialogue Separation
- **Socrates** (410a–b): "Of course, our young people will clearly be reluctant to resort to the law, if they receive the simple musical and poetic <entity type="concept">education</entity> we described, the one we claimed bred <entity type="concept">self-discipline</entity>."

- **Glaucon** (410b): "Yes. What of it?"

- **Socrates** (410b–c): "Well, won’t the person with the right musical and poetic <entity type="concept">education</entity> take the same approach in his hunt for a physical <entity type="concept">education</entity>? Won’t he end up, if he so chooses, gaining independence from medicine except in emergencies?"

- **Glaucon** (410c): "Yes, I think he will."

- **Socrates** (410c–d): "His actual physical training, his exercises, are things he will do with a view to arousing the spirited part of his <entity type="concept">nature</entity> rather than developing his strength—unlike most athletes, whose diet and exercise is aimed at improving their physique."

- **Glaucon** (410d): "Exactly."

- **Socrates** (410d–e): "In that case, Glaucon, when people establish a system of artistic and physical <entity type="concept">education</entity>, isn’t their reason for doing so different from the one usually attributed to them—that one cares for the body, and the other for the <entity type="concept">soul</entity>?"

- **Glaucon** (410e): "What _is_ the reason, then?"

- **Socrates** (410e–411a): "I suspect both are established principally for the benefit of the <entity type="concept">soul</entity>."

- **Glaucon** (411a): "Explain."

- **Socrates** (411a–b): "Have you never observed the mentality of those who spend all their time on physical <entity type="concept">education</entity>, to the exclusion of musical and poetic <entity type="concept">education</entity>? Or those whose way of life is the opposite?"

- **Glaucon** (411b): "What have you in mind?"

- **Socrates** (411b–c): "Savagery and hardness, in the one case. Weakness and gentleness, in the other."

- **Glaucon** (411c): "Yes, I have noticed that those whose <entity type="concept">education</entity> is purely physical turn out more savage than they should. Those who have only a musical and moral <entity type="concept">education</entity>, on the other hand, do become softer than is good for them."

- **Socrates** (411c–d): "What is more, the fierce element comes from the spirited part of their <entity type="concept">nature</entity>. Correctly brought up, it would be brave, but when it is developed to a higher pitch than is necessary, it is likely to become harsh and unmanageable."

- **Glaucon** (411d): "Yes, I think that’s right."

- **Socrates** (411d–e): "What about the gentle element? Isn’t it a property of the wisdom-loving or philosophical <entity type="concept">nature</entity>? Undue relaxation makes it too soft, doesn’t it, whereas the right upbringing makes it gentle and well-behaved."

- **Glaucon** (411e): "Yes."

### Extracted Argument: Purpose of Education
- **Premise 1**: Pure physical <entity type="concept">education</entity> breeds savagery (spirited excess); pure musical <entity type="concept">education</entity> breeds softness (philosophical excess) (411a–c).
- **Premise 2**: Balanced <entity type="concept">education</entity> harmonizes spirited (brave) and philosophical (gentle) parts of the <entity type="concept">soul</entity> (411c–e).
- **Reasoning**: Both arts target the <entity type="concept">soul</entity>'s harmony, not just body/mind incidentally; guardians need both for <entity type="concept">self-discipline</entity> and bravery (410d–411e). <footnote id="59">375c–376c. [Cross-ref: Initial education discussion].</footnote>
- **Conclusion**: <entity type="concept">Education</entity> systems aim at <entity type="concept">soul</entity> benefit, producing harmonious, brave souls (411e).  
**Relationship**: Extends judge's theoretical training [ref: Section 1]; foreshadows guardian harmony [ref: Section 3, 411e–412a].

## Section 3: Harmony Through Education (411e–412a)
**Text Type**: Dialogue excerpt.  
**Argument Structure**: Imbalance in <entity type="concept">education</entity> leads to discord in the <entity type="concept">soul</entity>; balance yields <entity type="concept">virtue</entity>.  
**Cross-References**: Musical modes [ref: 398d–399e]; tripartite soul [ref: 435a–441c].

### Dialogue Separation
- **Socrates** (411e): "The guardians must have both these natural attributes, we say."

- **Glaucon** (411e): "Yes, they must."

- **Socrates** (411e–412a): "And these must be harmonised with one another?"

- **Glaucon** (412a): "Of course."

- **Socrates** (412a): "The <entity type="concept">soul</entity> of someone who is harmonised in this way is <entity type="concept">self-disciplined</entity> and brave, isn’t it?"

- **Glaucon** (412a): "Yes."

- **Socrates** (412a): "Whereas the <entity type="concept">soul</entity> of someone discordant is cowardly and uncivilised?"

- **Glaucon** (412a): "Exactly."

- **Socrates** (412a–b): "So if you give music the chance to play upon your <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, and pour into the funnel of your ears the sweet, soft, lamenting modes we were talking about a little while ago, if you spend your whole life humming them, bewitched by song, then the first effect on a <entity type="concept">nature</entity> with any spirit in it is to soften it, like heating iron, making it malleable instead of brittle and unworkable. But if you press on regardless, and are seduced by it, the next stage is melting and turning to liquid—the complete dissolution of the spirit. It cuts the sinews out of your <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, and turns it into a 'feeble warrior.'"

- **Glaucon** (412b): "Yes." <footnote id="60">Said of Menelaus in Homer, *Iliad* 17.588. [Cross-ref: Poetic critique, 595a–608b].</footnote>

- **Socrates** (412b–c): "If you start with a <entity type="concept">soul</entity> which is not very spirited by <entity type="concept">nature</entity>, this happens quite quickly. If you do have a spirited <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, you weaken the spirit and make it unstable—easily roused by trivial things, and as easily extinguished. People like this become hot-tempered and quick to anger rather than spirited; they are full of discontent."

- **Glaucon** (412c): "They certainly do."

### Extracted Argument: Effects of Musical Excess
- **Premise 1**: Excessive music softens the spirited <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, leading to malleability then dissolution (412a–b).
- **Premise 2**: In spirited natures, it creates instability and irritability (412b–c).
- **Reasoning**: Soft modes erode <entity type="concept">spirit</entity>, preventing <entity type="concept">harmony</entity> (412a–c).
- **Conclusion**: Discordant <entity type="concept">soul</entity> from imbalance yields cowardice/uncivilization; harmony yields <entity type="virtue">virtue</entity> (411e–412a).  
**Relationship**: Contrasts with physical excess [ref: Section 4]; part of broader <entity type="theme">ethics</entity> of balance.

## Section 4: Physical Education's Effects and Overall Harmony (412c–413e)
**Text Type**: Dialogue excerpt.  
**Argument Structure**: Physical excess without music leads to savagery and ignorance; both arts harmonize spirited/philosophical parts.  
**Cross-References**: Muse and learning [ref: 376e–377c]; guardian role [ref: 412b–414a].

### Dialogue Separation
- **Socrates** (412c–d): "What about the person who puts a lot of effort into his physical training, and eats like a horse, but has nothing to do with music or <entity type="concept">philosophy</entity>? At first, because his body is in good shape, isn’t he full of decision and spirit? Doesn’t he become braver than he was before?"

- **Glaucon** (412d): "Much braver."

- **Socrates** (412d–e): "But suppose that is all he does. Suppose he has no contact with the Muse. Even if he did have some love of learning in his <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, it gets no taste of learning or enquiry, and has no experience of rational argument or any artistic pursuit. As a result, since it never wakes up and has nothing to feed on, and since there is nothing to purify its senses, it becomes weak, and deaf, and blind, doesn’t it?"

- **Glaucon** (412e): "Yes, it does."

- **Socrates** (412e–413a): "Someone like this becomes an enemy of rational argument, I suspect, and an enemy of music and literature. He abandons any attempt at persuasion using rational argument, and does everything with savage violence, like a wild animal. He lives his life in ignorance and stupidity, without grace or rhythm."

- **Glaucon** (413a): "Yes, that’s exactly what he is like."

- **Socrates** (413a–b): "If you want my opinion, then, the two elements for which some god has given mankind two arts—one musical and poetic, the other physical—seem to be not the mind and the body, or only incidentally, but the spirited part of their <entity type="concept">nature</entity> and the philosophical part, so that these can be brought into <entity type="concept">harmony</entity> with one another through the appropriate tension and relaxation."

- **Glaucon** (412b): "Yes, those do seem to be the two elements."

- **Socrates** (412b): "In that case, we would be entitled to describe as perfectly musical and harmonious the person who best combines physical with musical and poetic <entity type="concept">education</entity>, and who introduces them into his <entity type="concept">soul</entity> in the most balanced way. Far more musical and harmonious than the person who tunes the strings of an instrument."

- **Glaucon** (412b): "Very likely, Socrates."

### Extracted Argument: Physical Excess and True Harmony
- **Premise 1**: Initial physical training boosts bravery but, without music/<entity type="concept">philosophy</entity>, dulls the rational <entity type="concept">soul</entity> (412c–e).
- **Premise 2**: Result: Savagery, rejection of reason, animal-like life (413a).
- **Reasoning**: Arts target spirited/philosophical parts for <entity type="concept">harmony</entity> via tension (physical) and relaxation (musical) (413a–b).
- **Conclusion**: Balanced <entity type="concept">education</entity> produces the most harmonious <entity type="concept">soul</entity>, superior to mere instrumental tuning (412b).  
**Relationship**: Completes education duality [ref: Section 2]; essential for city security [ref: Section 5].

## Section 5: Guardians and Rulers (412b–413e)
**Text Type**: Dialogue excerpt.  
**Argument Structure**: Rulers must be wise, devoted guardians selected for unyielding loyalty to the city.  
**Cross-References**: Earlier guardian traits [ref: 374e–376c]; belief loss [ref: 413a–e].

### Dialogue Separation
- **Socrates** (412b): "Well then, Glaucon, won’t we always need someone like this in our city to keep an eye on things, if our state is to be secure?"

- **Glaucon** (412b): "Yes, we shall. It will be our greatest need."

- **Socrates** (412b): "So much for the patterns of <entity type="concept">education</entity> and upbringing. We don’t have to go through the dances, modes of hunting and coursing, athletic events or horse races that go with them. It’s pretty obvious these must follow from the patterns, so there can’t now be any difficulty in discovering them."

- **Glaucon** (412b): "No, it probably wouldn’t be too difficult."

- **Socrates** (412b–c): "Very well, then. What is the next question we have to decide? Isn’t it which of these people are to rule, and which be ruled?"

- **Glaucon** (412c): "Unquestionably."

- **Socrates** (412c): "Is it obvious the rulers should be older, and those who are ruled younger?"

- **Glaucon** (412c): "Yes, it is."

- **Socrates** (412c–d): "And that the rulers should be the best among them?"

- **Glaucon** (412d): "That too."

- **Socrates** (412d): "Among farmers, aren’t the best ones the ones who most possess the attributes of a farmer?"

- **Glaucon** (412d): "Yes."

- **Socrates** (412d–e): "So in this context, since we are looking for the best of the <entity type="concept">guardians</entity>, must they not be the ones who most possess the attributes of a <entity type="concept">guardian</entity> of the city?"

- **Glaucon** (412e): "Yes."

- **Socrates** (412e): "And for this purpose, do they have to be <entity type="concept">wise</entity>, powerful and above all devoted to the city?"

- **Glaucon** (412e): "They do."

- **Socrates** (413a): "And people are most devoted to whatever it is they love."

- **Glaucon** (413a): "Bound to be."

- **Socrates** (413a): "And they love most what they believe to have the same interests as themselves, the thing whose success or failure they think results in their own success or failure."

- **Glaucon** (413a): "True."

- **Socrates** (413a–b): "Then we must select from the <entity type="concept">guardians</entity> the kind of men who on examination strike us most strongly, their whole lives through, as being utterly determined to do what is in the city’s interests, and as refusing to act in any way against its interests."

- **Glaucon** (413b): "Yes, they should be the people we want."

- **Socrates** (413b): "I think we should observe them at all ages, to make sure they are the <entity type="concept">guardians</entity> and defenders of this belief, and that neither magic nor force can make them forget, and jettison their conviction that they should do what is best for the city."

- **Glaucon** (413b): "What do you mean by this jettisoning?"

- **Socrates** (413b–c): "I’ll tell you. I think our minds can lose a belief either with or without our consent. With our consent when it’s a false belief and we learn better. Without our consent in the case of all true belief."

- **Glaucon** (413c): "I understand the loss which is with our consent, but the loss which is without our consent I need to have explained to me."

- **Socrates** (413c–d): "Really? Don’t you agree with me that what is <entity type="concept">good</entity> can be taken away from people only without their consent, whereas what is bad is taken away with their consent? Isn’t being deceived about the truth something bad, and knowing the truth something <entity type="concept">good</entity>? And don’t you think that having a belief which agrees with the way things are is knowing the truth?"

- **Glaucon** (413d): "You’re right. When people lose a true belief, it is without their consent."

- **Socrates** (413d–e): "And is that a question of theft, or magic, or force?"

- **Glaucon** (413e): "Once again, I’m afraid, I don’t see what you mean."

- **Socrates** (413e): "I seem to be making myself about as clear as a tragic poet. By theft I mean people who are talked into changing their minds, and people who forget. Either the passage of time or some process of argument takes away their belief without them realising it. You do see what I mean now, I hope?"

- **Glaucon** (413e): "Yes."

- **Socrates** (413e): "By force I mean those whom pain or grief causes to change their beliefs."

- **Glaucon** (413e): "Yes, I understand that as well. And I agree."

- **Socrates** (413e): "As for magic, you would also accept, I imagine, that there are people whose beliefs change because they are seduced by pleasure, or because there is something they are afraid of."

- **Glaucon** (413e): "Yes, all the things which deceive us do look like a form of magic."

- **Socrates** (413e): "So as I said just now,<footnote id="61">[Cross-ref: Earlier in dialogue, 412e].</footnote> we must look for those who are the best defenders of their conviction that in any situation they must do what they think is in the city’s best interests for them to do. From their earliest childhood we must watch them, and set them the kind of tasks which could most easily make them lose sight of this aim, and lead them astray. Then we must choose the ones who remember their aim and are not easily led astray. Those who are led astray we must reject, mustn’t we?"

- **Glaucon** (413e): "Yes."

### Extracted Argument: Selection of Rulers/Guardians
- **Premise 1**: Best rulers are oldest, wisest, most devoted <entity type="concept">guardians</entity>, loving the city's interests as their own (412c–413a).
- **Premise 2**: True beliefs (<entity type="concept">good</entity>) are lost involuntarily via theft (forgetting/argument), force (pain), or magic (pleasure/fear) (413b–e).
- **Reasoning**: Observe lifelong resistance to these losses; select those unswayed by tests (413e).
- **Conclusion**: Rulers are lifelong-tested <entity type="concept">guardians</entity> who defend city's <entity type="concept">good</entity> unwaveringly (413a–e).  
**Relationship**: Integrates education's harmony [ref: Sections 2–4] into political structure; epistemological focus on true belief preservation [ref: *Meno* 97e–98a].

### Section: *Republic* 414a–c (Selection of Rulers/Guardians)
**Narrative Context**: Socrates outlines criteria for appointing <entity>guardians</entity> after lifelong testing, emphasizing <entity>virtue</entity> and <entity>justice</entity>. Transition to distinguishing <entity>full guardians</entity> from <entity>auxiliaries</entity>.

**Dialogue Separation**:
- **Socrates**: "414 under constant testing emerges as pure is the one who should be appointed as a ruler and guardian of our city. We should heap honours on him, in life and in death, and when it comes to burial and other memorials he should receive the greatest tributes. The one who fails the tests we should reject. Well, Glaucon, so much for my views on the selection and appointment of the rulers and guardians. It’s only a general outline, of course, not a precise specification."
- **Glaucon**: "I think my views are pretty much the same as yours."
- **Socrates**: "In that case, aren’t these really the people who can most accurately be called full guardians - making sure friends within do not _want_ to harm it, and enemies without are not _able_ to harm it? The young people whom we have been calling guardians up to now we can call auxiliaries, the defenders of the rulers’ beliefs." [Annotation: Footnote 62 – "Auxiliaries" also denotes mercenaries or tyrant's bodyguards; cf. Adeimantus at 419a.]
- **Glaucon**: "I agree."

**Extracted Argument: Selection and Role of Guardians**  
- **Premises**:  
  1. Lifelong <entity>testing</entity> ensures purity and <entity>virtue</entity> in <entity>rulers</entity>/<entity>guardians</entity> (414a).  
  2. <entity>Honours</entity> (life/death) incentivize <entity>justice</entity>; failures are rejected to protect the city.  
  3. <entity>Full guardians</entity> prevent internal desire for harm and external capability for harm (414b).  
- **Evidence**: Analogical reasoning from education/training (cross-ref: earlier guardian education, 376e–412a).  
- **Conclusion**: Distinguish <entity>full guardians</entity> (rulers) from <entity>auxiliaries</entity> (defenders of beliefs); this structure upholds <entity>justice</entity> in the city.  
**Relationships**: Links to <entity>happiness</entity> theme (guardians' role in collective eudaimonia); foreshadows noble lie for cohesion.

### Section: *Republic* 414c–d (Introduction of the Noble Lie)
**Narrative Context**: Socrates proposes a "<entity>noble lie</entity>" (gennaios pseudos) to unify the city, rooted in myth. [Annotation: Footnote 63 – "Noble" due to civic purpose; cf. 382c–d for necessity of falsehoods in education.]

**Dialogue Separation**:
- **Socrates**: "In that case, how can we contrive to use one of those necessary falsehoods we were talking about a little while back? [cross-ref: 382c–d] We want one single, grand lie which will be believed by everybody - including the rulers, ideally, but failing that the rest of the city."
- **Glaucon**: "What kind of thing do you mean?"
- **Socrates**: "A very familiar story, of Phoenician origin. It has happened in the past, in several places. So the poets tell us, and they have found believers. But it has not happened in our time, and I don’t even know if it _could_ happen. People would take a lot of persuading."
- **Glaucon**: "You seem a bit reluctant to tell your story."
- **Socrates**: "With good reason - as you will see when I do tell you."
- **Glaucon**: "Don’t worry. Tell it."
- **Socrates**: "Very well. I will. Though I don’t know how I shall have the nerve, or find the right words. I have to try and persuade first of all the rulers themselves and the soldiers, and then the rest of the city, that the entire upbringing and education we gave them, their whole experience of it happening to them, was after all merely a dream, something they imagined, and that in reality they spent that time being formed and raised deep within the earth — themselves, their weapons and the rest of the equipment which was made for them. When the process of making them was complete, the earth their mother released them, and now it is their duty to be responsible for defending the country in which they live against any attack - just as they would defend their mother or nurse - and to regard the rest of the citizens as their brothers, born from the earth."

**Extracted Argument: The Myth of Earth-Born Citizens (First Part of Noble Lie)**  
- **Premises**:  
  1. A unifying myth is needed for belief in shared origins (414c).  
  2. Phoenician/Poetic tradition (autochthonous birth) fosters loyalty (414d).  
  3. <entity>Guardians</entity> must view citizens as <entity>brothers</entity> to defend the city as <entity>mother</entity>.  
- **Evidence**: Mythical narrative (dream-like education inside earth); persuasion targets rulers/soldiers first.  
- **Conclusion**: This "<entity>grand lie</entity>" promotes civic unity and <entity>justice</entity> by instilling fraternal duty.  
**Relationships**: Ties to <entity>epistemology</entity> (myth as necessary belief vs. true <entity>knowledge</entity>); cross-ref to Hesiodian traditions (footnote 64).

### Section: *Republic* 414e–415d (Myth of Metals)
**Dialogue Separation**:
- **Glaucon**: "No wonder you were so embarrassed about telling us your lie."
- **Socrates**: "Yes, I had good reason. But you must listen to the second half of the story as well. 'You are all brothers,' our story will tell them, 'all of you in the city. But when god made you, he used a mixture of gold in the creation of those of you who were fit to be rulers, which is why they are the most valuable. He used silver for those who were to be auxiliaries, and iron and bronze for the farmers and the rest of the skilled workers. Most of the time you will father children of the same type as yourselves, but because you are all related, occasionally a silver child may be born from a golden parent, or a golden child from a silver parent, and likewise any type from any other type. The first and most important instruction god gives the rulers is that the thing they should be the best guardians of, the thing they should keep the most careful eye on, is the compound of these metals in the souls of the children. If their own child is born with a mixture of bronze or iron in him, they must feel no kind of pity for him, but give him the position in society his nature deserves, driving him out to join the skilled workers or farmers. On the other hand, any children from those groups born with a mixture of gold or silver should be given recognition, and promoted either to the position of guardian or to that of auxiliary. There is a prophecy, god tells them, that the end of the city will come when iron or bronze becomes its guardian.'" [Annotation: Footnote 64 – Draws from Hesiod's *Works and Days* 109–201; contrasts successive decay with class mobility here; cf. Book 8, 546a–547a.]
- **Socrates**: "Well, that’s the story. Can you think of any possible way of getting people to believe it?"
- **Glaucon**: "No. Not the actual people you tell it to. But their children might, and _their_ children after them, and the rest of the population in later generations."
- **Socrates**: "Even that might help them to care more about the city and one another. I think I see what you’re getting at. Anyway, let that turn out as popular belief and tradition will have it."

**Extracted Argument: Myth of Metals (Social Hierarchy and Vigilance)**  
- **Premises**:  
  1. Divine mixture of metals in souls determines class: gold (<entity>rulers</entity>), silver (<entity>auxiliaries</entity>), iron/bronze (workers) (415a–b).  
  2. Intergenerational mobility requires <entity>testing</entity> of offspring natures (415b–c).  
  3. Rulers must guard against degradation to prevent city's fall (prophecy of iron/bronze guardians).  
- **Evidence**: Mythical allegory (god's creation); promotes <entity>justice</entity> via merit-based assignment.  
- **Conclusion**: The noble lie ensures class stability and vigilance, preserving <entity>virtue</entity> in the city.  
**Relationships**: Connects to <entity>metaphysics</entity> (soul composition); reinforces <entity>education</entity> as key to discerning natures.

### Section: *Republic* 415d–416a (Camp and Housing for Guardians)
**Dialogue Separation**:
- **Socrates**: "Our job now is to arm these earth-born warriors of ours, and lead them forth, with the rulers at their head. Let them go and look for the best place in the city to put their camp, a place from which they can most easily control their own citizens, if any of them refuse to obey the laws, or repel any external threats, in the event of some enemy coming down on them 'like a wolf on the fold.' When they have set up their camp, they can sacrifice to the appropriate gods, and then organise their sleeping accommodation. Does that sound right?"
- **Glaucon**: "Yes."
- **Socrates**: "Should it be the kind of accommodation which will give them adequate shelter both in winter and summer?"
- **Glaucon**: "Of course. This is their home you are talking about, I take it."
- **Socrates**: "Yes. But a home fit for soldiers, not for businessmen."

**Extracted Argument: Practical Setup for Guardians**  
- **Premises**: Armed <entity>guardians</entity> need strategic camps for internal/external defense (415d–e).  
- **Evidence**: Analogy to wolves on sheep (416a); sacrifices to gods for legitimacy.  
- **Conclusion**: Communal, soldierly housing ensures readiness and <entity>discipline</entity>.  
**Relationships**: Builds on noble lie for unity; links to <entity>ethics</entity> of communal life.

### Section: *Republic* 416a–417b (Education and Lifestyle of Guardians)
**Dialogue Separation**:
- **Socrates**: "What is the difference, in your view? I’ll try and tell you. When shepherds are breeding dogs as protectors of their flocks, the worst possible disaster and disgrace, I imagine, is to breed dogs whose nature and training are such that lack of discipline, hunger or some fault of character leads them to try to attack the sheep themselves, and start behaving like wolves instead of dogs."
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, of course that is a disaster."
- **Socrates**: "In that case we must guard in every way we can against our auxiliaries doing the same sort of thing to the citizens. After all, they are stronger than the citizens. We don’t want them behaving like savage masters instead of friendly allies."
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, we must guard against that."
- **Socrates**: "Won’t the best insurance against this be for them to have received a really good education?"
- **Glaucon**: "But they _have_ received one."
- **Socrates**: "We can’t be sure of that, my dear Glaucon. What we _can_ be sure about is what we have just been saying, which is that when it comes to gentleness - both to themselves and to those under their protection - then the right education, whatever that may be, is the key."
- **Glaucon**: "Yes, we are right to be sure of that."
- **Socrates**: "In addition to this education, an intelligent observer may say, the guardians should be furnished with housing and a general standard of living which will not hinder them from becoming the best possible guardians, and which will give them no encouragement to do wrong in their dealings with the rest of the citizens."
- **Glaucon**: "He may say that. And he will be quite right."
- **Socrates**: "Well, then, do you agree with some suggestions about the way they should live and be housed if this is what we want them to be like? In the first place, no one is to have any private property beyond what is absolutely essential. Secondly, no one is to have the kind of house or storeroom which cannot be entered by anyone who feels like it. For their subsistence, which should meet the needs of self-disciplined and courageous warrior-athletes, they should impose a levy on the rest of the citizens, and receive an annual payment for their role as guardians which leaves them with neither a surplus nor a deficiency. They should live a communal life, eating together like soldiers in camp. As for gold and silver, they should be told they already have in their souls, all the time, the divine gold and silver given to them by the gods. They have no need of human gold in addition, and it is sacrilege to contaminate the divine gold they possess by adding to it a mixture of the perishable gold, since the gold in circulation among ordinary people has been the cause of much evil, whereas their own gold is pure. To them alone, out of the city’s population, is it forbidden to handle or touch gold or silver, or be beneath the same roof, or wear it as jewellery, or drink from gold or silver cups. In this way they will be kept safe, and they will keep the city safe. Once they start acquiring their own land, houses, and money, they will have become householders and farmers instead of guardians. From being the allies of the other citizens they will turn into hostile masters. They will spend their whole lives hating and being hated, plotting and being plotted against. Their fears of enemies inside the city will be much more numerous and more acute than their fears of enemies outside the city. Both they themselves and the city will be heading at full speed towards imminent destruction. For all these reasons, shall we say that our guardians are to be provided with the housing and way of life we have described? Are these the laws we should enact, or not?"
- **Glaucon**: "They certainly are."

**Extracted Argument: Communal Living to Prevent Corruption**  
- **Premises**:  
  1. Analogy: Guardians as dogs must not become wolves via poor <entity>education</entity> or lifestyle (416a–b).  
  2. No private property/gold/silver prevents greed and internal enmity (416d–417a).  
  3. Communal life (levies, shared housing) aligns with <entity>virtue</entity> of warrior-athletes.  
- **Evidence**: Shepherd-dog analogy; prophecy of destruction from wealth (ties to myth of metals).  
- **Conclusion**: <entity>Communal living</entity> ensures <entity>guardians</entity> remain allies, safeguarding <entity>justice</entity> and city stability.  
**Relationships**: Central to <entity>ethics</entity> (virtue through austerity); cross-ref to noble lie's fraternal bonds.

### Book 4 Transition: *Republic* 419a–421b (Defense Against Charge of Guardian Unhappiness)
**Narrative Context**: Adeimantus challenges the <entity>happiness</entity> of <entity>guardians</entity>, prompting Socrates' response on collective <entity>justice</entity>.

**Dialogue Separation**:
- **Adeimantus**: "At this point... How will you defend yourself, Socrates, against the charge that you are not making these men very happy, and that they have only themselves to blame? The city in fact belongs to them, yet they derive no benefit from it. Other people have acquired land, built themselves beautiful great houses, and are now collecting the furniture to go with them; they make their own sacrifices to the gods; they entertain foreign visitors; and they are also the owners of the things you’ve just been talking about — gold, silver and everything which is regarded as necessary for people who are going to be happy. Our men just seem to sit there in the city, like hired bodyguards. All they do is guard it." (419a–420a)
- **Socrates**: "Yes, and working just for their keep at that. Unlike the others, they receive no pay over and above their food, so if they feel like going abroad as private individuals, they won’t be able to. They can’t give presents to mistresses, or spend money on anything else they choose, on the things people who are generally regarded as happy spend money on. You left that, and a whole lot more along the same lines, out of your accusation." (420a)
- **Adeimantus**: "Very well, you can take those as being part of the accusation as well."
- **Socrates**: "What is our defence, then? Is that your question?" (420b)
- **Adeimantus**: "Yes."
- **Socrates**: "We shall find our answer, I think, if we carry on down the same road. We shall say that we wouldn’t be at all surprised if even our guardians were best off like this, but that in any case our aim in founding the city is not to make one group outstandingly happy, but to make the whole city as happy as possible. We thought we would be most likely to find <entity>justice</entity> in a city of this kind, and most likely to find injustice in the city with the worst institutions, and that looking at these would give us the answer to our original question. What we are doing at the moment, we believe, is not separating off a few of the inhabitants, and making _them_ happy, but constructing a complete city, and making that happy. We’ll have a look at its opposite later. Imagine we were putting the colours on a statue of a man, and someone came along and told us we were doing it wrong, since we weren’t using the most beautiful colours for the most beautiful parts of the living creature. The eyes, the most beautiful feature, had been coloured black, not purple. We would regard it as a quite reasonable defence to say to him: 'Hang on a minute. You surely don’t think, do you, that we should make the eyes - or any of the other parts of the body - so beautiful that they don’t even look like eyes. The thing to ask yourself is whether by giving the right colours to everything we are making the whole thing beautiful.' It’s the same with us. You mustn’t start forcing us to give the guardians the kind of happiness which will turn them into anything other than guardians. We could perfectly easily dress our farmers in purple robes, and give them gold jewellery to wear, and tell them to work the land when they feel like it. We could let our potters recline on banqueting couches, passing the wine to the right and feasting in front of their fire, with their potters’ wheels beside them for when they really felt like doing some pottery. We could make everyone else happy in the same kind of way, so that the whole city would be happy. You mustn’t ask us to do that. If we do as you suggest, the farmer will not be a farmer, the potter will not be a potter, nor will anyone else continue to fulfil any of the roles which together give rise to a city. For most of the population it is not that important. If our cobblers are no good, if they stop being proper cobblers and only pretend to be when they are not, the city won’t come to much harm. But if the guardians of our laws and our city give the impression of being guardians, without really _being_ guardians, you can see that they totally destroy the entire city, since they alone provide the opportunity for its correct management and prosperity. If we are making real guardians, people who are incapable of harming the city, whereas the person who criticises us is making them into farmers of some kind, who are not so much running a city as presiding over a chaos of mutual grievances." (420b–421b) [Annotation: Footnote 1 – Greek statues were painted; image critiques disproportionate happiness.]

**Extracted Argument: Collective Happiness Over Individual**  
- **Premises**:  
  1. Guardians' austerity (no wealth) serves the whole city, not personal gain (419a–420a).  
  2. Aim is holistic <entity>happiness</entity> and <entity>justice</entity>, not class-specific luxury (420b–c).  
  3. Analogy: Statue painting – parts must fit the whole for beauty (420d–e); role specialization prevents chaos (421a–b).  
- **Evidence**: Critique of critics (e.g., making potters idle destroys functions); guardians as true protectors.  
- **Conclusion**: True <entity>justice</entity> emerges in a balanced city; individual "happiness" via wealth corrupts roles and leads to destruction.  
**Relationships**: Core to <entity>ethics</entity> (justice as harmony); cross-ref to original question (Books 1–2); foreshadows unjust cities (Books 8–9).

Not in reputation, I don’t mean, but great in fact, even if it is a <entity type="concept">city</entity> with only a thousand men to fight for it. You will have a job to find a single <entity type="concept">city</entity> which is great in this way, either among Greeks or non-Greeks, though you will find plenty, many times the size of this one, which give the illusion of greatness. Don’t you agree?"  
    - <entity type="person">Adeimantus</entity>: "Emphatically."
  - <entity type="person">Socrates</entity>: "In that case, this could also be an excellent marker, or limit, for our rulers, to show them how big they should make the <entity type="concept">city</entity>, and the amount of land they should mark out for a <entity type="concept">city</entity> this size, before saying 'no' to any more."

### Section 1: 427a–427e (Modern p. 120; Speakers: Socrates, Adeimantus, Glaucon)
**Summary Chunk for RAG**: Discussion of flawed cities mirroring sick patients; introduction to <entity>justice</entity> search via city virtues. Argument: Bad governance as self-deception, contrasting true statesmen.

**Dialogue**:
<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: "Yes, that’s exactly what life is like for patients of that sort," he said. "And what about their equally charming habit of reserving their greatest hostility for the person who tells them the truth, which is that until they give up drinking, over-eating, sex and idleness, no medicine, cauterisation or surgery, no charms, amulets or anything of that kind, will do them the slightest good."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "It’s not a charming habit in the least," he said. "There’s nothing charming about getting angry with people who tell you the truth."

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: "You don’t seem to be a great admirer of people like this," I said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Emphatically not."

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: "So you won’t be impressed if, as we were just saying, the <entity>city</entity> as a whole behaves like this. Don’t you think this is just what <entity>cities</entity> are doing when they are badly governed, and yet forbid their citizens to make any change at all in the constitution, telling them they will be put to death if they do? Rather it is the person who takes the <entity>city</entity> as it is, who is the people’s most beguiling servant and flatterer, who creeps into their good graces, who anticipates their wishes and is adept at satisfying them - this person they will declare a fine man, a man profoundly wise. This man they will honour."[^9]

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes, I think it’s exactly what <entity>cities</entity> are doing. And I can see nothing to be said for it."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "How about those who are willing and eager to be the servants of <entity>cities</entity> like this? Don’t you admire their courage and readiness?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes, I do," he said. "Apart from the ones who let the approval of the majority fool them into thinking they really are statesmen."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Are you saying you can’t find any excuse for these people? If a man knows nothing about measurement, and lots of people who also know nothing tell him he is six feet tall, do you suppose it is possible for him to avoid thinking that’s what he is?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "No, I don’t."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Don’t let it annoy you, then. After all, surely people like this are the most entertaining of all, passing and amending the kind of laws we were describing just now, in the constant belief that they will find an answer to dishonesty in business dealings and all the areas I have just been talking about. They don’t realise they are cutting off the <entity>Hydra</entity>’s head."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Though that’s exactly what they _are_ doing," he said.

**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: Flawed <entity>cities</entity> resist truth like sick patients reject remedies (analogy: bodily vices → constitutional flaws).
- **Premise 2**: Flatterers gain honor by indulging wishes, while truth-tellers face hostility (cross-ref: democratic flaws in <entity>city</entity>-soul analogy).
- **Conclusion**: True <entity>lawgivers</entity> avoid minor reforms in bad <entity>cities</entity>; focus on foundational <entity>virtues</entity> (leads to 427b search for <entity>justice</entity>).
- **Relationship**: Sets up <entity>justice</entity> as non-flattering virtue; contrasts with <entity>knowledge</entity>-based statesmanship.

[^9]: Although the Athenian political system made it quite easy for citizens to propose new laws or decrees for action, it hedged the procedure by making liable to prosecution and severe penalty anyone whose proposal was found to contravene existing law. The rhetoric used in such cases tended to present the laws as ancestral and permanent. In practice, new laws and decrees were most often proposed by the leading politicians, who became adept at surviving the legal hazards.

### Section 2: 427b–427d (Modern p. 120–121; Speakers: Socrates, Glaucon)
**Summary Chunk for RAG**: Transition to founding the ideal <entity>city</entity>; deferral to Apollo for religious laws. Argument: <entity>Lawgivers</entity> focus on essentials, not details.

**Dialogue**:
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Well, if it were up to me," I said, "I wouldn’t have thought the true <entity>lawgiver</entity> should concern himself with these details of the laws and the constitution - either in a badly-governed or a well-governed <entity>city</entity>. In one it is pointless, and achieves nothing; in the other, some of the legislation can be devised by absolutely anyone, while the rest follows automatically from our previous arrangements."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "In that case," he asked, "what area of lawmaking have we still got left?"

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: " _We_ haven’t got any. But Apollo at Delphi has — the most important, the finest and the most fundamental pieces of legislation."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "What are those?"

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "The foundation of temples. Sacrifices. Other acts of service performed for gods, demigods and heroes. The burial places of the dead, and the observance which must be paid to those below to keep them favourable. We do not know about this kind of thing, and when we found our <entity>city</entity>, if we have any sense, the only advice we shall follow, the only authority we shall recognise, is the traditional authority. And I take it that in these matters Apollo, making his pronouncements seated on the stone which forms the earth’s navel, is the ancestral authority for the whole of mankind."[^10]

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "You are right," he said. "That must be our approach."

**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: Minor laws useless in bad <entity>cities</entity>, automatic in good ones (from prior founding; cross-ref: 427a).
- **Premise 2**: Humans lack <entity>knowledge</entity> of divine matters; defer to oracle (epistemological humility).
- **Conclusion**: Ideal <entity>city</entity> founded on religious foundations via Apollo (metaphysical: ties ethics to divine order).
- **Relationship**: Bridges to <entity>justice</entity> search (427d); contrasts human <entity>lawgivers</entity> with divine authority.

[^10]: The oracle of Apollo at Delphi was authoritative on religious questions for the entire Greek world — questions which were not as a rule so sharply differentiated from other kinds of political questions as they are in this passage. It was also consulted before the founding of any colony. The sanctuary contained a stone, the ‘navel-stone’, which was thought to mark the centre of the earth.

### Section 3: 427d–428b (Modern p. 121; Speakers: Socrates, Glaucon)
**Summary Chunk for RAG**: Launch of <entity>justice</entity> inquiry via four <entity>virtues</entity> (wisdom, courage, self-discipline, justice). Argument: Identify three to reveal the fourth by remainder.

**Dialogue**:
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "In that case, son of Ariston, your <entity>city</entity> can now be regarded as founded. The next step is to look inside it, and for that you are going to need a pretty powerful light. You can provide your own, or get your brother and Polemarchus and the others to help you. Then perhaps we shall find some way of seeing just where in the <entity>city</entity> <entity>justice</entity> is, where injustice is, what the difference is between the two, and which of them people who are going to be happy must possess, whether all the gods and all mankind realise they possess it or not."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Oh, no, you don’t," said Glaucon. "You told us _you_ were going to look for <entity>justice</entity>. You said it was impious not to do everything you possibly could to support <entity>justice</entity>."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "That’s true," I said. "Thank you for reminding me. I must do what I promised. But you must do your bit as well."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "We will."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "In that case," I said, "here’s how I hope to find the answer. I take it our <entity>city</entity>, if it has been correctly founded, is wholly good."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "It can’t help being."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Clearly, then, it is wise, courageous, self-disciplined and just."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Clearly."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Then as we find each of these elements in it, those we have not yet found will constitute the remainder."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Of course."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "With any four things, if we were looking for one of them in some place or other, and it was the first thing we caught sight of, that would be enough for us. But if we identified the other three first, then the one we were looking for would _ipso facto_ have been identified as well, since clearly it could then only be whatever was left."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "You are right," he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "It’s the same for us now. Since there actually are four elements, should we conduct our search in the same way?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes. Obviously."

**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: Good <entity>city</entity> embodies four <entity>virtues</entity> (wisdom, courage, self-discipline, justice; cross-ref: traditional Greek virtues).
- **Premise 2**: Locating three reveals the fourth by elimination (logical method: remainder principle).
- **Conclusion**: Proceed to identify <entity>wisdom</entity> first (leads to 428b; epistemological strategy for <entity>justice</entity>).
- **Relationship**: Frames entire inquiry; ties to happiness and piety (ethics-metaphysics link).

### Section 4: 428b–429a (Modern p. 121–122; Speakers: Socrates, Glaucon)
**Summary Chunk for RAG**: Definition of <entity>wisdom</entity> in the <entity>city</entity> as rulers' <entity>knowledge</entity> of the whole. Argument: Wisdom not in productive arts, but deliberative judgment.

**Dialogue**:
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Well, I think the first one to catch the eye is <entity>wisdom</entity>. And it seems to have an unusual feature."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "What is that?"

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "It is truly wise, I think, this <entity>city</entity> we have described. It has good judgment, doesn’t it?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Now this thing, judgment, is clearly <entity>knowledge</entity> of some sort. Good decisions, I take it, are the result of <entity>knowledge</entity>, not ignorance."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Obviously."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "But our <entity>city</entity> contains many types of <entity>knowledge</entity>, of very different kinds."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Of course it does."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Is it the <entity>knowledge</entity> possessed by its carpenters which entitles us to call our <entity>city</entity> wise, and say it possesses good judgment?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Certainly not," he said. "That merely entitles us to call it good at carpentry."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "So a <entity>city</entity> is not to be called wise because of its <entity>knowledge</entity> and judgment in making the best possible wooden furniture."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Absolutely not."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "How about its <entity>knowledge</entity> of making things out of bronze, or any other <entity>knowledge</entity> of that kind?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "No, nothing like that," he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Nor the <entity>knowledge</entity> of how to grow crops from the soil, since that’s called farming."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "So I believe."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Is there, then," I asked, "among any of the citizens of this <entity>city</entity> we have just founded, _any_ branch of <entity>knowledge</entity> which makes decisions about the <entity>city</entity> as a whole - deciding on the best approach to itself and to other <entity>cities</entity> - and not about one particular element in the <entity>city</entity>?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "There most certainly is."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "What is this <entity>knowledge</entity>, and in which group is it to be found?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "It is the <entity>knowledge</entity> possessed by the <entity>guardians</entity>," he said. "And it is to be found in the rulers, whom we have just been calling the perfect <entity>guardians</entity>."[^11]

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "And what is the label you give your <entity>city</entity> on the strength of this <entity>knowledge</entity>?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "I call it sound in judgment, and truly wise."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "So which do you think our <entity>city</entity> will have more of? Metalworkers, or these true <entity>guardians</entity>?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Metalworkers," he said. "Far more."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Of all the groups which have a branch of <entity>knowledge</entity> of their own, and which are identified as a group, wouldn’t the <entity>guardians</entity> be the smallest?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Easily the smallest."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "In which case, the <entity>wisdom</entity> of a <entity>city</entity> founded on natural principles depends entirely on its smallest group and element - the leading and ruling element - and the <entity>knowledge</entity> that element possesses. The class which can be expected to share in this branch of <entity>knowledge</entity>, which of all branches of <entity>knowledge</entity> is the only one we can call <entity>wisdom</entity>, is by its nature, apparently, the smallest class."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "That’s very true," he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Well, that’s one of the four things we were looking for. And we’ve not only found it, I’m not quite sure how, but also found whereabouts in the <entity>city</entity> it is located."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Nothing much wrong with the way it was found as far as I’m concerned," he said.

**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: <entity>City</entity>'s <entity>wisdom</entity> = <entity>knowledge</entity> of the whole, not partial crafts (elimination: carpentry, metallurgy, farming excluded).
- **Premise 2**: Only <entity>guardians</entity> (rulers) possess deliberative <entity>knowledge</entity> for <entity>city</entity>-wide decisions (cross-ref: 414b).
- **Conclusion**: <entity>Wisdom</entity> resides in smallest class (epistemological: true <entity>knowledge</entity> is rare and elite).
- **Relationship**: First virtue identified; advances remainder method toward <entity>justice</entity> (cross-ref: soul's rational part).

[^11]: They were distinguished as ‘full guardians’ at 414b.

### Section 5: 429a–430c (Modern p. 122–123; Speakers: Socrates, Glaucon)
**Summary Chunk for RAG**: Definition of <entity>courage</entity> as preservation of lawful opinion on fear. Argument: Located in warrior class; dye analogy for fixity.

**Dialogue**:
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Courage, next. It is not hard to see both the thing itself and the part of the <entity>city</entity> in which it is located, the part which gives the <entity>city</entity> the name 'courageous.'"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Explain."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "No one classifying a <entity>city</entity> as cowardly or brave would look at any other part of it than the part which makes war in the <entity>city</entity>’s defence, and serves in its army."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes, that’s the only part anyone would look at," he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "I think the reason for that," I said, "is that the cowardice or bravery of the rest of the population would not be enough to make the <entity>city</entity> itself cowardly or brave."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "No, it wouldn’t."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Does that mean a <entity>city</entity>’s <entity>courage</entity>, as well as its <entity>wisdom</entity>, lies in a part of itself, because it has in that part a power capable of preserving, in all situations, the opinion that what is to be feared is just what the <entity>lawgiver</entity> listed and classified as such in the course of their education? Or isn’t that what you call <entity>courage</entity>?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "I didn’t altogether follow that. Say it again."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "I mean that <entity>courage</entity> is a kind of preservation," I said.

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Preservation? Of what?"

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Of the opinion formed by education, under the influence of law, about which things are to be feared. When I talked about its preservation in all situations, I meant keeping it intact, through pains, pleasures, desires and fears, without rejecting it. I can give you an analogy, if you would like."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "I would."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "When dyers want to dye wool purple," I said, "you know they start by selecting, from wools of various colours, the ones which are naturally white. They give these a lengthy preliminary preparation, so that they will absorb as much of the colour as possible. Only then do they do the dyeing. Anything dyed in this way is colour-fast. No washing, with or without detergent, can remove the colour from it. But when things are dyed in some other way, whether the wool is some other colour, or whether it is white but dyed without preparation, you know what happens."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes," he said. "They look faded and ridiculous."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "That’s the kind of thing you must imagine we too were doing, to the best of our ability, when we selected our soldiers and gave them their musical, poetic and physical education. You must realise that all we were trying to do was organise things so that they would absorb our laws as completely as possible, like a dye. We wanted them to possess the right character and upbringing, so that their views on danger and other things would be colour-fast, incapable of being washed out by any of the detergents which are such good solvents. Not by pleasure, which is a better solvent than any soda or lye. Nor by pain, fear or desire, which are stronger than any other detergent. This kind of power and preservation I call <entity>courage</entity> - the preservation, in all situations, of correct and lawful belief about what is to be feared and what is not. That’s my definition, unless you have some objection to it."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "No, I have no objection," he said. "I take it that when a slave or an animal has a correct opinion on these subjects, an opinion which is not the result of education, you do not regard this as properly lawful,"[^12] "and you give it some name other than <entity>courage</entity>."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Precisely," I said. "In that case, I accept your definition of <entity>courage</entity>."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Take it as a definition of <entity>courage</entity> _in a city_," I said, "and you will be right. We can give a better account of <entity>courage</entity> some other time, if you like. At the moment, though, we are investigating <entity>justice</entity>, not <entity>courage</entity>. And for that purpose I think this is enough."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes. You are right."

**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: <entity>Courage</entity> in warrior class (auxiliaries), not whole <entity>city</entity> (parallels <entity>wisdom</entity> in rulers).
- **Premise 2**: = Preservation of educated opinion on fear/danger through trials (analogy: dye fixity against solvents like pleasure/pain; cross-ref: Book 3 education).
- **Conclusion**: <entity>Courage</entity> as lawful belief, not mere instinct (distinguishes from animal bravery; ethical: ties to <entity>lawgiver</entity>'s education).
- **Relationship**: Second virtue; provisional for <entity>city</entity> (foreshadows soul application); advances to self-discipline.

[^12]: A less secure manuscript reading would be translated ‘not properly permanent’ rather than ‘not properly lawful’.

### Section 6: 430d–431c (Modern p. 123–124; Speakers: Socrates, Glaucon)
**Summary Chunk for RAG**: Introduction to <entity>self-discipline</entity> as harmony/mastery. Argument: Better rules worse in <entity>city</entity>/soul; critique of "master of himself."

**Dialogue**:
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "That leaves two things to for us to identify in our <entity>city</entity>," I said. "One is <entity>self-discipline</entity>. The other is the object of our entire investigation, <entity>justice</entity>."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Well, is there some way we can find <entity>justice</entity> without having to bother about <entity>self-discipline</entity>?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "I don’t know," he said. "I wouldn’t want it to make its appearance too soon, if that means giving up the search for <entity>self-discipline</entity>. If I have any say in the matter, please examine <entity>self-discipline</entity> first."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Well, if it’s not wrong of me, I’m quite happy to do that?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Start looking, then."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "I shall have to," I said. "My first impression is that it is more like a harmony or musical mode than the other two."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "In what way?"

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: " <entity>Self-discipline</entity>, I take it, is a kind of order. They say it is a mastery of pleasures and desires, and a person is described as being in some way or other master of himself. And there are other clues of the same sort in the way it is talked about, aren’t there?"

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Indeed there are," he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "But isn’t the phrase 'master of himself' an absurdity?"[^13] "The master of himself must surely also be slave to himself, and the slave to himself must be master of himself. It’s the same person being talked about all the time."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Of course."

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "What this way of speaking seems to me to indicate is that in the <entity>soul</entity> of a single person there is a better part and a worse part. When the naturally better part is in control of the worse, this is what is meant by 'master of himself.' It is a term of approval. But when as a result of bad upbringing or bad company the better element, which is smaller, is overwhelmed by the mass of the worse element, this is a matter for reproach. They call a person in this condition a slave to himself, undisciplined."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes, I think that is what it indicates," he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: "Now, if you take a look at this new <entity>city</entity> of ours, you will find one of these situations prevailing. You will admit that it can quite legitimately be called master of itself, if something in which the better rules the worse can be called <entity>self-disciplined</entity> and master of itself."

<speaker>Glaucon</speaker>: "Yes, when I take a look at our <entity>city</entity>," he said, "you are right."

**Argument Structure**:
- **Premise 1**: <entity>Self-discipline</entity> as order/harmony, not literal self-mastery (linguistic critique: paradox of one ruling oneself implies parts).
- **Premise 2**: In <entity>soul</entity>, better (rational) part rules worse (appetitive); mirrors <entity>city</entity> (rulers over masses; cross-ref: tripartite soul, 435b).
- **Conclusion**: <entity>City</entity> exhibits <entity>self-discipline</entity> via better ruling worse (ethical: approval for order, reproach for vice; leads to <entity>justice</entity> as mutual harmony).
- **Relationship**: Third virtue; introduces soul analogy fully; remainder leaves <entity>justice</entity> (cross-ref: 431d–e for completion).

[^13]: The literal meaning of the phrase translated ‘master of himself’ here and throughout.
