### Section 531a–531d: Reforming Astronomy and Introducing Harmonics
**Socrates**: "Part in true <entity>astronomy</entity>, and make the naturally rational part of the <entity>soul</entity> useful instead of useless, we shall forget about the <entity>heavenly bodies</entity>."

**Glaucon**: "That’s a much, much larger task you are requiring of us, compared with the way <entity>astronomy</entity> is done at the moment."

**Socrates**: "Yes, and if we are going to be any use as <entity>lawgivers</entity>, I think we shall have to impose the same requirements in other subjects as well. Can you suggest any other subjects that might be useful?"

**Glaucon**: "No, I can’t. Not on the spur of the moment."

**Socrates**: "Well, I’m sure <entity>motion</entity> doesn’t take just a single form. It takes several. No doubt an expert could give you a comprehensive list. But there are two which are obvious even to us."

**Glaucon**: "What are they?"

**Socrates**: "The one we’ve just been talking about [<entity>astronomy</entity>], and its counterpart."

**Glaucon**: "What is its counterpart?"

**Socrates**: "The chances are that our ears can be fixed on <entity>harmonic motion</entity> in the same way as our eyes on <entity>astronomical motion</entity>. These may well be in some sense sister sciences. That’s what the <entity>Pythagoreans</entity> say, and you and I agree with them, <entity>Glaucon</entity>. Or do we not?"

**Glaucon**: "We do."

*(Cross-reference: <entity>Astronomy</entity> and <entity>harmonics</entity> as kin via numerical ratios in <entity>motion</entity>; prelude to <entity>dialectic</entity> [cf. 531e].)*

### Section 531d–532a: Maxim for Education; Critique of Empirical Harmonics
**Socrates**: "Very well. It’s a massive task, so let’s ask them what they have to say on the subject—and possibly other subjects as well. Meanwhile we will stick to our maxim throughout."

**Glaucon**: "What maxim is that?"

**Socrates**: "We should not allow the people for whose upbringing we are responsible ever to try and learn any pointless part of the subject, any part that is not constantly leading them to the goal that all things must reach—as we were proposing in the case of <entity>astronomy</entity> just now [531a–d]. You must be aware that students of <entity>harmonics</entity> behave in more or less the same way. In trying to make comparative measurements of the <entity>harmonies</entity> and sounds which can be heard, they set themselves an endless task, just as the <entity>astronomers</entity> do."

**Glaucon**: "Good god, yes. They certainly do. They make complete fools of themselves with their 'close' intervals, applying their ears to the instrument as if they were eavesdropping on their neighbours. One group claims it can still distinguish an intermediate sound, and says this is the smallest interval which should be used as a unit of measurement. Others disagree. They say the two sounds are the same. Both groups trust their ears in preference to their reason."

**Socrates**: "You mean the worthy individuals who make life a misery for their strings by torturing them and using pegs to stretch them on the rack. I don’t want to labour the metaphor—the plectrum striking and accusing, the strings refusing to speak or noisily defiant [Footnote 12: Metaphor from lawcourts, where evidence of slaves was taken under torture]—so I’ll abandon it, and simply say that those aren’t the people I mean. The people I’m talking about are the ones we said just now we would ask about <entity>harmonics</entity> [531d]. What they do is the same as what the <entity>astronomers</entity> do. They look for the numerical ratios in these <entity>harmonies</entity> which can be heard, without ever rising above those to an approach based on problems. They don’t investigate which ratios are <entity>harmonious</entity>, which are not, and why."

**Glaucon**: "That would be a superhuman task."

**Socrates**: "Well, it would certainly be a useful one, in the pursuit of the <entity>beautiful</entity> and the <entity>good</entity>. Pursued for any other reason it is useless."

**Glaucon**: "Very likely."

*(Argument Structure: Critique of sensory-based sciences—empirical <entity>astronomy</entity>/<entity>harmonics</entity> as "useless" without rational ascent to <entity>forms</entity> [ratios as <entity>problems</entity>, not measurements]. Goal: Utility for <entity>soul</entity>'s rational part in guardian education. Relationship: Both sciences share <entity>motion</entity>; empirical method trusts <entity>senses</entity> over <entity>reason</entity>, leading to endless tasks.)*

### Section 532a–532e: Kinship of Sciences; Prelude to Dialectic
**Socrates**: "It’s my opinion that if the investigation of all these subjects we’ve outlined arrives at what they have in common with one another, their kinship with one another, and if it can work out how they are related to one another, then it’s not a pointless task. It’s an activity which contributes to what we are trying to achieve. Otherwise it is pointless."

**Glaucon**: "I agree. I have the same presentiment myself. But it’s an enormous task you’re proposing, <entity>Socrates</entity>."

**Socrates**: "And that’s merely the prelude. Or don’t you agree? Are we in any doubt that all these subjects are merely preludes to the main theme we have to learn? [Footnote 13: Musical metaphor; *nomos* means 'theme' or 'law'] After all, you presumably don’t regard people as <entity>dialecticians</entity> just because they are good at these subjects."

**Glaucon**: "Good heavens, no. A very few perhaps of those I’ve ever come across."

**Socrates**: "And did you think that people who were incapable of explaining or understanding the basis of their subject were ever going to know any of the things we say they need to know?"

**Glaucon**: "Again, the answer is no."

**Socrates**: "Well, <entity>Glaucon</entity>, isn’t this finally the true tune or theme which the study of <entity>dialectic</entity> plays? It is in the realm of <entity>thought</entity>, though the power of sight can imitate it, as when we said that sight attempts to look at <entity>animals</entity> themselves, and <entity>stars</entity> themselves, and even finally at the <entity>sun</entity> itself [Footnote 14: 516a–b]. In the same way, when someone tries to use <entity>dialectic</entity> to arrive at what each thing itself is, by means of <entity>reason</entity>, without using any of the <entity>senses</entity>, and does not give up the attempt until he grasps what <entity>good</entity> itself is, by means of <entity>thought</entity> itself, then he has come to the true end or goal of the <entity>intelligible</entity>, just as the man in the <entity>cave</entity>, in our earlier example, came to the true end or goal of the <entity>visible</entity> [Cross-reference: Cave Analogy, 514a–520a]."

**Glaucon**: "Exactly."

**Socrates**: "Very well. Isn’t '<entity>dialectic</entity>' the name you give to this journey?"

**Glaucon**: "Of course."

*(Argument Structure: Mathematical sciences (<entity>astronomy</entity>, <entity>harmonics</entity>, geometry) as "preludes" to <entity>dialectic</entity>, which grasps <entity>forms</entity> (e.g., <entity>good itself</entity>) via pure <entity>reason</entity>. Relationship: Ascent parallels Cave (shadows → fire → sun) and Divided Line (<entity>visible</entity> → <entity>intelligible</entity>). Non-dialecticians lack true <entity>knowledge</entity> of essences.)*

### Section 532e–533c: Dialectic as Release and Ascent
**Socrates**: "And the release from chains? The turning away from the shadows towards the images and the firelight? The upward path from the underground <entity>cave</entity> to the daylight, and the ability there to look, not in the first instance at <entity>animals</entity> and plants and the light of the <entity>sun</entity>, but at their divine reflections in water and the shadows of real things, rather than the shadows of models cast by a light which is itself a shadow in comparison with the <entity>sun</entity>? All this practice of the sciences we have just outlined has precisely this power to direct the best element in the <entity>soul</entity> upwards, towards the contemplation of what is best among the things that are—just as earlier on the clearest element in the body was directed to the contemplation of what was brightest in the corporeal and <entity>visible</entity> region [Cross-reference: 516a–b]."

**Glaucon**: "Personally speaking, I accept that, though I find it extremely hard. But then again, in another way it is very hard *not* to accept. Still, this won’t be our only opportunity to hear what you have to say on the subject. We shall often have to return to it in the future. So let’s take it these things are as we have just said they are, and go on to the main theme itself, and describe that in the same way we described the prelude. Tell us, how does it operate, this power of <entity>dialectic</entity>? Into what forms is it divided? And by what routes, again, does it progress? After all, it is these routes which can apparently take a man to the destination which is his place of rest after the road, and the end of his journey."

**Socrates**: "My dear <entity>Glaucon</entity>, you will not be able to follow me that far—though not for any want of enthusiasm on my part. From now on what you would be seeing would not be an image or model of what we are talking about, but the truth itself—at least as it seems to me. Whether it’s precisely like this doesn’t seem worth insisting on. But that there is something *like* this to see—that we must insist on, mustn’t we?"

**Glaucon**: "Of course."

**Socrates**: "Do we insist also that the power of <entity>dialectic</entity> is the only power which can reveal this? That it reveals it to the person who is expert in the subjects we have just been talking about? And that it is impossible in any other way?"

**Glaucon**: "Yes, these are things we should insist on."

*(Argument Structure: <entity>Dialectic</entity> as "release from chains" (Cave metaphor), using sciences as "allies" to turn <entity>soul</entity>'s eye upward to <entity>good</entity>. Exclusive path to truth; others (senses, assumptions) fail. Relationship: Sciences dream of <entity>being</entity>; <entity>dialectic</entity> awakens to it.)*

### Section 533c–534e: Dialectic vs. Other Arts; Divided Line Recap
**Socrates**: "At the very least, then, no one will quarrel with us if we claim it is a distinct and separate inquiry which systematically and universally attempts, for each thing just by itself, to grasp what that thing is. All other arts and sciences, without exception, are directed either towards human <entity>opinions</entity> and desires, or towards creation or manufacture, or towards the care of things which are growing or being manufactured. As for the subjects which we said *did* grasp some part of what really is—studies in <entity>geometry</entity> and the disciplines which go with <entity>geometry</entity>—we can now see that as long as they leave the assumptions they use untouched, without being able to give any justification for them, they are only dreaming about what is. They cannot possibly have any waking awareness of it [Footnote 15: Recalling 510c–511a]. After all, if the first principles of a subject are something you don’t know, and the endpoint and intermediate steps are interwoven out of what you don’t know, what possible mechanism can there ever be for turning a coherence between elements of this kind into <entity>knowledge</entity>?"

**Glaucon**: "None."

**Socrates**: "Very well. The <entity>dialectical</entity> method is the only one which in its determination to make itself secure proceeds by this route—doing away with its assumptions until it reaches the first principle itself. <entity>Dialectic</entity> finds the eye of the <entity>soul</entity> firmly buried in a kind of morass of philistinism. Gently it pulls it free and leads it upwards, using the disciplines we have described as its allies and assistants in the process of conversion. We have generally followed convention in calling these disciplines branches of <entity>knowledge</entity>, but they really need some other name. Something clearer than <entity>opinion</entity>, but more obscure than <entity>knowledge</entity>. We may have used the term '<entity>thinking</entity>' at some point earlier on [Footnote 16: 511d–e]. But I don’t think people need argue about names when they have as many important matters still to investigate as we have."

**Glaucon**: "No, they needn’t."

**Socrates**: "We’ll be happy enough, then, to do what we did before. We’ll call the first section or category <entity>knowledge</entity>, the second <entity>thinking</entity>, the third <entity>belief</entity>, and the fourth <entity>conjecture</entity>. Three and four taken together we can call <entity>opinion</entity>, and one and two taken together, <entity>understanding</entity>. We’ll say that <entity>opinion</entity> has to do with <entity>becoming</entity>, whereas <entity>understanding</entity> has to do with <entity>being</entity>; that as <entity>being</entity> is to <entity>becoming</entity>, so <entity>understanding</entity> is to <entity>opinion</entity>; and as <entity>understanding</entity> is to <entity>opinion</entity>, so <entity>knowledge</entity> is to <entity>belief</entity>, and <entity>thinking</entity> is to <entity>conjecture</entity>. As for the proportions holding between the objects in these categories, and the division of the objects of <entity>opinion</entity> or the objects of <entity>understanding</entity> into two parts, let’s leave all that on one side, <entity>Glaucon</entity>. Otherwise it will overwhelm us with a discussion many times as long as the one we’ve had so far [Cross-reference: Divided Line, 509d–511e]."

**Glaucon**: "Very well. But as far as the rest of it goes, I for one agree with what you say. As far as I can follow it, that is."

*(Argument Structure: <entity>Dialectic</entity> unique in hypothesizing to first principles (unlike <entity>geometry</entity>, which assumes); other arts deal with <entity>becoming</entity>/<entity>opinion</entity>. Recap: Line divisions (<entity>knowledge</entity> > <entity>thinking</entity> > <entity>belief</entity> > <entity>conjecture</entity>). Relationship: <entity>Being</entity>/<entity>understanding</entity> superior to <entity>becoming</entity>/<entity>opinion</entity>; sciences aid but do not achieve full <entity>knowledge</entity>.)*

### Section 534e–535d: The Dialectician; Grasp of the Good
**Socrates**: "In which case, is '<entity>dialectician</entity>' the name you give to the person who grasps the explanation of the <entity>being</entity> of each thing? As for the person who has no explanation, will you say that to the extent that he is unable to give an account of it, to himself or to anyone else, he has no intelligent <entity>understanding</entity> of it?"

**Glaucon**: "Of course I will."

**Socrates**: "The same goes for the <entity>good</entity>. Anyone who cannot use <entity>reason</entity> to distinguish the <entity>form</entity> of the <entity>good</entity> from everything else, who cannot fight his way through all attempts to disprove his theory in his eagerness to test it by the standard of <entity>being</entity> rather than the standard of <entity>opinion</entity>, who cannot make his way through all these dangers with his explanation unscathed—won’t you say that a person who is in this state knows neither the <entity>good</entity> itself nor any other good? That if at any point he does lay hold of some image of it, he does so using <entity>opinion</entity>, not <entity>knowledge</entity>? That he is dreaming and dozing away his life on earth, and that one day he will come to <entity>Hades</entity> and go to sleep for good, without ever waking up here at all?"

**Glaucon**: "Yes, all that is exactly what I shall say. And with some emphasis."

**Socrates**: "These children of yours, then, for whom you are providing this theoretical upbringing and education—suppose one day you found yourself bringing them up in real life. If they had as little <entity>reason</entity> to them as incommensurable lines in <entity>mathematics</entity> [Footnote 17: 'Incommensurable' lines are *alogos* ('irrational') in Greek], don’t imagine you would still allow them to be rulers in your city and exercise control over matters of the greatest importance."

**Glaucon**: "No, I wouldn’t."

**Socrates**: "Will you enact a law, then, requiring them to have a particularly good grasp of that branch of education which will give them the ability to ask and answer questions in the most expert way?"

**Glaucon**: "Yes. I will enact such a law—with your help."

*(Argument Structure: True <entity>dialectician</entity> explains <entity>essences</entity>/<entity>forms</entity> (esp. <entity>good</entity>); without this, one lives in "dream" (<entity>opinion</entity>). For rulers: Mandatory <entity>dialectic</entity> to ensure <entity>justice</entity>/<entity>wisdom</entity>. Relationship: Ties to philosopher-kings; failure = eternal "sleep" vs. awakening to <entity>being</entity>.)*

### Section 535d–536c: Dialectic as Capstone; Selection of Students
**Socrates**: "Would you say, in that case, that <entity>dialectic</entity> sits as a kind of coping-stone on the top of our educational edifice, and that there is no other subject left which we’d be justified in putting on top of it? Do you think our list of subjects for study is now complete?"

**Glaucon**: "I do."

**Socrates**: "That just leaves you with the question of allocation, then. Who are we going to give these subjects to? And how are we going to give them?"

**Glaucon**: "Yes, that obviously needs to be decided."

**Socrates**: "Do you remember our selection of rulers earlier on? Do you remember the kind of people we selected? [Footnote 18: 374e–376c (guardians); 412b–414a (testing); 485a–487a (philosophers); etc.]"

**Glaucon**: "Of course I do."

**Socrates**: "Well, you can take it that in general those must be the natures we should select. We must choose the most steadfast, the bravest and as far as possible the best-looking. In addition, not only must we look for noble and virile character; we also need people with a natural talent for this kind of education."

**Glaucon**: "What talent is that?"

**Socrates**: "I tell you, they must be like razors when it comes to studying, and they must find learning easy. The <entity>soul</entity> gives up much more easily during hard study than it does during physical exercise, since when it is studying the pain is more its own—specific to it, not shared with the body."

**Glaucon**: "True."

**Socrates**: "The person we are looking for must also have a good memory, great resilience and tremendous energy. How else, do you suppose, will anyone be prepared both to endure the physical hardships and to complete such an extensive course of study and training?"

**Glaucon**: "I don’t suppose anyone will be prepared to. Not unless he is altogether exceptional."

**Socrates**: "The trouble at the moment, the reason why <entity>philosophy</entity> has fallen into disrepute, as I was saying a little while ago, is that the wrong kind of people are taking it up [Footnote 19: 495c–496a]. We didn’t want bastard, or illegitimate, philosophers taking it up. We wanted legitimate philosophers."

**Glaucon**: "What do you mean by 'legitimate'?"

**Socrates**: "Well, take love of hard work, for a start. It’s no good having a gammy leg if you’re going to take up <entity>philosophy</entity>. No good working really hard in one half of the subject, and doing no work in the other half. That’s what..."

*(Argument Structure: <entity>Dialectic</entity> as educational "coping-stone" (complete curriculum). Selection: <entity>Virtue</entity> (bravery, nobility) + talent (sharp mind, endurance) for guardians/philosophers. Critique: <entity>Philosophy</entity>'s disrepute from "illegitimate" practitioners. Relationship: Ensures <entity>justice</entity> in city via wise rulers; balances body/soul training.)*

## Extracted Philosophical Arguments (Structured Outline)
For RAG retrieval: Arguments chunked by core claim, premises, conclusion, and links.

1. **Argument for Reforming Sciences (Astronomy/Harmonics)**:
   - Premises: Current methods rely on <entity>senses</entity> (ears/eyes), leading to endless empirical tasks; ignore rational <entity>problems</entity> (ratios/forms).
   - Conclusion: True study must ascend to <entity>kinship</entity> (numerical essences) for <entity>soul</entity>'s utility; otherwise useless for <entity>lawgivers</entity>.
   - Links: Prelude to <entity>dialectic</entity>; <entity>Pythagorean</entity> influence.

2. **Argument for Dialectic as Path to Knowledge**:
   - Premises: Other arts/sciences assume unproven principles (dreaming); deal with <entity>becoming</entity>/<entity>opinion</entity>. <entity>Dialectic</entity> hypothesizes to first principles via <entity>reason</entity> alone.
   - Conclusion: Only <entity>dialectic</entity> reveals <entity>forms</entity> (e.g., <entity>good itself</entity>), achieving <entity>understanding</entity> of <entity>being</entity>; parallels Cave ascent.
   - Links: Divided Line; exclusive for philosopher-rulers.

3. **Argument for Educational Allocation**:
   - Premises: Rulers need <entity>virtue</entity> + intellectual talent (memory, energy); <entity>philosophy</entity> disreputed by unfit students.
   - Conclusion: Select "legitimate" natures for <entity>dialectic</entity>-capped education to ensure <entity>justice</entity>/<entity>wisdom</entity> in governance.
   - Links: Guardian selection; <entity>soul</entity>-body harmony.

This format enables efficient retrieval (e.g., query "<entity>dialectic</entity>" retrieves sections/arguments) while preserving Plato's content. Total length optimized for context windows.

‘Nowhere else,’ he said.
‘I imagine he’ll be thought to have changed from a law-abiding citizen
into a criminal.’

‘Bound to be.’

‘Isn’t that just what you’d expect to happen to people who take up argu­

‘Yes, and pity,’ he said.
‘Very well, then. If you don’t want your thirty-year-olds to qualify for

‘I certainly will.’
b ‘Isn’t one very effective safeguard not to let them get a taste for argu­
ment while they are young? You can’t have forgotten what adolescents are
like, the first time they get a taste of it. They regard it as a kind of game
to be constantly turning arguments into their opposites. They imitate
those they hear proving other people wrong by going out and doing the
same thing themselves. They’re like puppies in the delight they take in
tugging at anyone within reach, and tearing them to pieces with their
arguments.’
‘Yes, they really do overdo it, don’t they?’
‘And when they have themselves often proved other people wrong, and
c often been proved wrong, they suffer a sudden and disastrous lapse into
the state of not believing any of the things they believed before. The result
is that they themselves come in for a lot of criticism in the eyes of the
world - and so does everything to do with philosophy.’
‘That’s absolutely true,’ he said.
‘An older man would refuse to take part in that kind of madness. He
will imitate the person who chooses to employ dialectic in the search for
truth, rather than the person who engages in a game of contradiction for
d entertainment’s sake. He will be a more balanced person himself, and will
make philosophy more respected, not less respected.’
‘Rightly so.’
‘Hasn’t everything that has been said so far been said precisely with a
view to making sure that only people with orderly and reliable natures are
to be introduced to argument? Not like now, when anybody at all, however

## Section 1: Completion of the Ideal City and Individual (Book 7, 541a–b)
**Text Type**: Dialogue continuation; narrative proposal for regime implementation.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- **Main Argument**: The ideal <entity type="regime">aristocratic city</entity> is possible only through radical restructuring led by <entity type="character">philosophers as rulers</entity>, prioritizing <entity type="concept">justice</entity> over honors.  
  - **Premise 1**: Philosophers must rule, despising false honors and valuing <entity type="concept">justice</entity>.  
  - **Premise 2**: Isolate and re-educate the young to instill proper values.  
  - **Conclusion**: This ensures the city's happiness and benefits the nation.  
- **Relationship**: Builds on earlier descriptions of education and guardianship; cross-ref to [Republic 5.449b–502c] for philosopher-rulers.

**Dialogue Separation**:

**Socrates**: Impossible. However, it is possible only in the way we have described, when true <entity type="character">philosophers</entity>—it might be a number of them, or it might be just one—become rulers in our city. They will show their contempt for what are now regarded as honours, believing them to be worthless and demeaning. They will set the highest possible value on what is right, and the honours resulting from it. Their most important and demanding guide will be <entity type="concept">justice</entity>. They will serve <entity type="concept">justice</entity>, watch over its growth, and in this way keep their city on the right lines. [Republic 7.540d–541a]

**Glaucon**: How will they do that? [Republic 7.541a]

**Socrates**: Let them send everyone in the city over the age of ten into the countryside. Then they can isolate these people’s children from the values they hold at the moment—their parents’ values—and bring the children up according to their own customs and laws, which are of the kind we described earlier. Don’t you agree that this will be the quickest and simplest way for the city and regime we were talking about to come into being, making itself happy and bringing a large number of benefits to the nation in which it originates? [Republic 7.541a–b]  
*[Footnote 24: Banishing elements of a population from a city to the surrounding countryside was not without historic parallel (see pp. xv–xvii of the introduction), and in the Greek world in general populations were relocated with what to us would seem alarming frequency. But there was no historic parallel for removing a whole class of parents to the countryside without their children.]*

**Glaucon**: Yes. Much the quickest and simplest. I think you have given us a good idea, Socrates, of the way it would come about, if it ever did come about. [Republic 7.541b]

**Socrates**: In that case, isn’t our discussion of this city, and the corresponding individual, now complete? After all, I imagine it’s pretty clear what we are going to say that individual should be like. [Republic 7.541b]

**Glaucon**: Yes, it is clear. And in reply to your question, I do think this subject of discussion is complete. [Republic 7.541b]  
**Speakers**: _Socrates, Glaucon_  
**Chunk ID**: REP-7-541-Completion

## Section 2: Agreed Characteristics of the Ideal City (Book 8, 543a–d)
**Text Type**: Dialogue recap; summary of aristocratic regime features.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- **Main Argument**: The peak <entity type="regime">aristocratic city</entity> requires communal structures to foster <entity type="concept">virtue</entity> and <entity type="concept">justice</entity>.  
  - **Premise 1**: Community of women, children, education, and daily life.  
  - **Premise 2**: Rule by best <entity type="character">philosopher-warriors</entity>; guardians receive only necessary maintenance.  
  - **Conclusion**: This prevents corruption and ensures protection of the city.  
- **Relationship**: Recaps Books 5–7; cross-ref to [Republic 5.457b–471c] (communal living), [Republic 3.416d–417b] (guardian possessions). Transitions to degeneration of regimes.

**Dialogue Separation**:

**Socrates**: Very well, <entity type="character">Glaucon</entity>. The agreed characteristics of the city which is to reach the peak of political organisation are <entity type="concept">community of women</entity>, community of children and the whole system of education, community likewise of everyday life, both in wartime and peacetime, and the kingship of those among them who have developed into the best <entity type="character">philosophers</entity>, and the best when it comes to war. [Republic 8.543a]

**Glaucon**: Yes, those are the agreed characteristics. [Republic 8.543a]

**Socrates**: What is more, we also agreed that when the rulers assume power, they will take the soldiers and move them to housing of the kind we described earlier—common to all of them, and offering no private property to anyone.^1 And in addition to the nature of their housing, we even reached agreement, if you recall, on the kind of possessions they will have.^2 [Republic 8.543b]  
*[Footnote 1: See [Republic 5.416d–417b].]*  
*[Footnote 2: See [Republic 3.416e–417b].]*

**Glaucon**: I do recall. We thought that none of them should have any of the possessions which most people nowadays have. They should be <entity type="character">guardians</entity> and warrior-athletes of some sort, receiving from the rest of the citizens, as annual pay for their guardianship, just as much maintenance as they need for this purpose. Their duty would be to protect themselves and the rest of the city. [Republic 8.543b–c]

**Socrates**: You are right. But after we’d finished dealing with all that, can we remember the point where we began this digression, so that we can carry on from the same place? [Republic 8.543c]

**Glaucon**: That’s easy enough. You were talking, in pretty much the way you are talking now, as if you had completed your account of the city. You were saying you regarded the kind of city you had just described— [Republic 8.543d]  
**Speakers**: _Glaucon, Socrates_

## Section 3: Transition to Degenerate Regimes (Book 8, 544a–545b)
**Text Type**: Dialogue; recap and outline of regime degeneration.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- **Main Argument**: To judge <entity type="concept">justice</entity> vs. <entity type="concept">injustice</entity>, examine five regimes and corresponding soul-types, from best (<entity type="regime">aristocracy</entity>) to worst (<entity type="regime">tyranny</entity>).  
  - **Premise 1**: Regimes arise from individual characters; five city-types imply five soul-dispositions.  
  - **Premise 2**: Start with <entity type="regime">timocracy</entity> (honor-loving, Spartan/Cretan), then oligarchy, democracy, tyranny.  
  - **Conclusion**: This allows comparison of happiness in just vs. unjust lives; counters Thrasymachus [Republic 1.338c].  
- **Relationship**: Cross-ref to interruption by Polemarchus/Adeimantus [Republic 5.449b]; initial plan [Republic 368d–369a]; Thrasymachus' view [Republic 1.338a–c].

**Dialogue Separation**:

**Socrates** (continued from 543d): —and the individual who resembled it—as a good one, despite the fact that you apparently had an even finer city and individual to tell us about. You certainly said that if this was the right sort of city, then the others must have something wrong with them. And you said, if I remember rightly, that there were four other kinds of regime—or four others worthy of discussion, at any rate. You said we should look at their faults, and at the individuals who resemble them, so that when we had examined all the individuals, and reached agreement on which was the best and which was the worst, we could ask whether the best individual is the happiest and the <entity type="concept">worst the most wretched</entity>, or whether that’s all a mistake. I asked you which four regimes you meant, but then <entity type="character">Polemarchus</entity> and <entity type="character">Adeimantus</entity> interrupted, and that started you on the discussion which has brought you here.^3 [Republic 8.544a–b]  
*[Footnote 3: See the transition between Books 4 and 5 (445a–449b).]*

**Socrates**: What an excellent memory! [Republic 8.544b]

**Glaucon**: In which case, could you do what a wrestler does when he offers his opponent the same hold again? If I ask the same question again, try and give me the answer you were going to give me then. [Republic 8.544b]

**Socrates**: Certainly, assuming I can, that is. Apart from anything else, I have reasons of my own for wanting to know which four regimes you meant. [Republic 8.544b–c]

**Glaucon**: There will be no difficulty in telling you that. They even have names, the ones I’m talking about. There’s the one which is pretty generally approved, the <entity type="regime">Cretan or Spartan</entity>^4. Next—and next in the scale of general approval—is the one called <entity type="regime">oligarchy</entity>, a form of government filled with all sorts of evils. In contrast to oligarchy, and the form of government which arises next, is <entity type="regime">democracy</entity>. And then there is the wonderful institution of <entity type="regime">tyranny</entity>, standing head and shoulders above all the others, the fourth and last diseased state of the city. Can you think of any other kind of regime which forms a distinct category of its own? I take it that hereditary rule by families, kingships which go to the highest bidder, and other similar regimes, which you will find are no less common among the barbarians than among the Greeks, are all intermediate between the forms I have mentioned. [Republic 8.544c–d]  
*[Footnote 4: At 545b these relatively parochial terms will be replaced by the coinages ‘timocracy’ or ‘timarchy’. For historical information see ‘Crete’ and ‘Sparta’ in the glossary.]*

**Glaucon**: Yes, we certainly do hear about plenty of extraordinary regimes. [Republic 8.544d]

**Socrates**: Well, then, are you aware that for individuals also there must necessarily be as many kinds of character as there are kinds of regime? Or do you think that regimes somehow come into being “from oak or stone”?^5 Isn’t it rather from the characters of people in the city, which tip the scale, as it were, taking the rest with them? [Republic 8.544e]  
*[Footnote 5: The phrase is proverbial of the fact that we all have ancestors, and is so used in Homer’s *Odyssey* (19.163) and Plato’s *Apology* (34d).]*

**Glaucon**: No, I think it’s entirely the character of the inhabitants. [Republic 8.544e]

**Socrates**: In which case, if there are five types of city, then for individuals there will likewise be five <entity type="concept">dispositions of the soul</entity>. [Republic 8.544e]

**Glaucon**: Of course. [Republic 8.544e]

**Socrates**: Well, we have finished describing the person who resembles <entity type="regime">aristocracy</entity>. And we say, quite rightly, that he is good and just. [Republic 8.545a]

**Glaucon**: Yes. We have described him. [Republic 8.545a]

**Socrates**: Is the next thing, then, to describe the ones who are less good—the <entity type="character">lover of victory and honour</entity>, who corresponds to the <entity type="regime">Spartan regime</entity>, and then in turn the <entity type="character">oligarchic character</entity>, the <entity type="character">democratic</entity>, and the <entity type="character">tyrannical</entity>? That way we can contrast the most unjust, when we find him, with the most just. Our investigation into how pure <entity type="concept">justice</entity> fares, relative to pure <entity type="concept">injustice</entity>, in terms of the happiness or wretchedness of the person who possesses it, will be complete. And we can either follow <entity type="character">Thrasymachus’</entity> advice and pursue <entity type="concept">injustice</entity>, or follow the argument which is unfolding before us now, and pursue <entity type="concept">justice</entity>. [Republic 8.545a–b]

**Glaucon**: Yes, that’s exactly what we have to do. [Republic 8.545b]

**Socrates**: All right, then. In our earlier enquiry we started with the character of regimes rather than that of individuals, because we thought that would be clearer.^6 In the same way now, shall we start by taking a look at the honour-loving regime? I can’t think of another term in general use that would apply to it. Its name ought to be “<entity type="regime">timocracy</entity>” or “<entity type="regime">timarchy</entity>.”^7 Then we can look at the timocratic individual in relation to that regime—followed by oligarchy and the oligarchic individual. After that we can turn to democracy and study the democratic individual, and fourthly we can turn to the city which is ruled by a tyrant, and look at that, before studying the tyrannical soul. Will that be a way of trying to become competent judges of the question we have asked ourselves? [Republic 8.545b–c]  
*[Footnote 6: 368d–369a.]*  
*[Footnote 7: The etymological components of these coinages are ‘honour’ (‘timo-’), ‘power’ (‘-cracy’), and ‘rule’ (‘-archy’).]*

**Glaucon**: It would certainly be a logical way of going about our observations and judgments. [Republic 8.545c]

**Socrates**: Very well. Let’s try and describe the way in which <entity type="regime">timocracy</entity> might arise out of <entity type="regime">aristocracy</entity>. Is it a general rule that the cause of change in any regime is to be found in the sovereign body itself—when civil war arises within this group? That as long as this group, however small it may be, remains united, it is impossible for the regime to be altered? [Republic 8.545c–d]

**Glaucon**: Yes, that’s true. [Republic 8.545d]

**Socrates**: In that case, <entity type="character">Glaucon</entity>, how will the regime of our city be altered? How will civil war break out either between our auxiliaries and our rulers, or among them? Do you want us, like <entity type="author">Homer</entity>, to invoke the <entity type="mythical">Muses</entity> to tell us “how first dissension fell upon them”?^8 Shall we imagine that they speak to us in high-flown, tragic tones, as if they were playing with little children and teasing them by pretending to be speaking seriously? [Republic 8.545d–e]  
*[Footnote 8: An adaptation of *Iliad* 16.112–113.]*

**Glaucon**: What would they say? [Republic 8.546a]

**Speakers**: _Socrates, Glaucon_

## Section 4: Myth of Regime Degeneration via Muses (Book 8, 546a–547a)
**Text Type**: Narrative invocation; mythical prophecy on cosmic cycles and decline.  
**Argument Structure**: 
- **Main Argument**: <entity type="regime">Aristocracy</entity> decays into <entity type="regime">timocracy</entity> due to flawed breeding, neglecting <entity type="concept">education</entity> and <entity type="concept">music</entity>, leading to class mixing and civil war.  
  - **Premise 1**: All things decay; leaders fail in calculating <entity type="concept">perfect numbers</entity> for births (divine vs. human cycles).  
  - **Premise 2**: This produces unfit rulers who undervalue Muses, philosophy, and metallic classes (<entity type="concept">gold/silver vs. bronze/iron</entity>).  
  - **Conclusion**: Inequality breeds sedition; compromise introduces private property and slavery, shifting to honor-based rule.  
- **Relationship**: Mythical etiology; cross-ref to [Republic 3.415a–c] (metallic souls); Hesiod's classes; *Timaeus* for cosmic periods. Prefigures soul degeneration.

**Dialogue Separation** (Narrative within Socrates' speech):

**Socrates**: Something like this. “It is no easy matter for a city founded in this way to be altered. But since destruction awaits everything that has come to be, even a foundation of this kind will not survive for the whole of time. It will fall apart, and this will be the manner of its falling. Both for plants in the ground and for animals above the ground it is a fact that souls and bodies are produced or not produced when the cycles of begetting for each species complete their revolutions—short revolutions for short-lived species, and the opposite for long-lived species. In the case of your species, wise though the people you have educated as leaders of the city are, still they will not quite hit the mark when they apply calculation together with observation—to their programme of breeding and birth-control. Success will elude them, and they will sometimes produce children they should not produce. For the birth of a <entity type="metaphysical">divine being</entity> there is a period embraced by a <entity type="concept">perfect number</entity>,^9 while for a human being it is the first number in which increase to the power of roots combined with squares—taking on three dimensions and four defining limits—of the numbers which create likeness and unlikeness, and which wax and wane, makes all things conversable and rational with one another. Of these numbers the ones that form the basis of the musical fourth, when coupled with five and three times increased, produce two harmonies. The first harmony is a square, the product of equals, so many times 100. The second harmony is of equal length one way, but a rectangle. One side is the square of the rational diagonal of a five-by-five square, minus one, times 100, or the square of the irrational diagonal of a five-by-five square, minus two, times 100. The other side is three cubed times 100. Taken as a whole, this <entity type="concept">geometrical number</entity> is master of this domain—of better and worse births. When your <entity type="character">guardians</entity> fail to understand these births, and make injudicious unions of brides and grooms, the children will not have the right nature, and they will not be fortunate. The previous generation will select the best of them for office, but they will not deserve selection, and when they in their turn inherit the powers of their fathers, the first thing they will neglect as guardians will be us, the <entity type="mythical">Muses</entity>, since they will put too low a value on <entity type="concept">musical and literary education</entity>. And the second thing they will neglect will be <entity type="concept">physical education</entity>. The result will be a younger generation which has even less regard for us. And from their number rulers will be appointed who completely lack a guardian’s ability to discriminate between <entity type="author">Hesiod’s</entity> classes, or the classes in your city—<entity type="concept">gold</entity>, <entity type="concept">silver</entity>, <entity type="concept">bronze</entity> and <entity type="concept">iron</entity>.^10 When iron is compounded with silver, and bronze with gold, then you will get unlikeness and discordant inequality. And when you get those, wherever they occur, they always breed war and hostility. This is sedition’s noble line,^11 we have to say—always, and wherever it arises.” [Republic 8.546a–547a]  
*[Footnote 9: The divine being is presumably the cosmos. It is described in the *Timaeus* as a living creature, the most perfect of those made by the creator-god. It is unclear whether the period in question is a gestation-period (the time it took for the creator-god to bring the cosmos into being) or some cosmic period such as the Great Year (the time it takes for the various orbiting bodies in the cosmos to come back to the same positions relative to one another). For an explanation of the remainder of this paragraph, see the glossary under ‘Number’.]*  
*[Footnote 10: Originally described at 415a–c.]*  
*[Footnote 11: Socrates quotes the first part of a line that appears twice in Homer, to cap a hero’s description of his ancestry: ‘This is my line, my blood—and this my boast’ (*Iliad* 6.211, 20.241).]*

**Glaucon**: Yes, that is the answer the <entity type="mythical">Muses</entity> will give. And we cannot deny that they are right. [Republic 8.547a]

**Socrates**: They must be right, if they are <entity type="mythical">Muses</entity>. [Republic 8.547a]

**Glaucon**: In which case, what else do the <entity type="mythical">Muses</entity> have to say? [Republic 8.547a]

**Socrates**: When civil war breaks out, the classes or natures are divided into two. The iron and bronze draw the state towards commerce, and the possession of land and housing, of gold and silver. The other pair, by contrast, the gold and silver, since in their souls they are not poor, but naturally wealthy, lead the state towards <entity type="concept">virtue</entity> and the traditional order. In fighting and struggling against one another they arrive at a compromise. The land and housing is to be divided up and owned privately, and they agree to enslave those who were previously watched over by them as free men. [Republic 8.547a–c]

### Section 1: Origin and Characteristics of Timocracy (548a–549a)
**Speakers**: Socrates (primary), Glaucon (brief), Adeimantus (later entry)  
**Context**: Discussion of timocracy as a "halfway-house" regime between <entity>aristocracy</entity> and <entity>oligarchy</entity>, emphasizing shift to <entity>spirited element</entity> dominance.

**Original Content**:
> ‘friends and providers. They now hold them as serfs and slaves, while their role is to watch them, and conduct warfare.’  
> ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘I think that is the origin of this sort of change.’  
> ‘In which case,’ I said, ‘would this regime be a kind of halfway-house between <entity>aristocracy</entity> and <entity>oligarchy</entity>?’  
> ‘It certainly would.’  
> ‘That is how the change will take place, then. But how will the state be organised _after_ the change? It’s obvious, isn’t it, since it is midway between the two, that it will in some ways be modelled on the original regime, and in other ways on <entity>oligarchy</entity>, but that it will also have an element which is peculiar to itself?’  
> ‘Yes,’ he said.  
> ‘Very well. Will the points it has in common with the original regime be these: respect for the rulers; the disqualification of the warrior element in the state from <entity>agriculture</entity>, manual employment or any other kind of business; the establishment of communal living quarters; and the concentration on physical education and training for <entity>war</entity>?’  
> ‘Yes.’  
> ‘Whereas fear of putting the <entity>wise</entity> into positions of power - since the <entity>wise</entity> men it has are now complex, not simple and direct any more - a leaning towards people who are <entity>spirited</entity>, more straightforward and naturally cut out for <entity>war</entity> rather than peace, the value it places on military deceptions and stratagems, and the way it spends its entire time at <entity>war</entity> — will most of these characteristics be peculiar to itself?’  
> ‘Yes.’  
> ‘Now that they possess their own treasuries and strongrooms where they can put their gold and silver, and keep it hidden, people like this will be avaricious, like the members of an <entity>oligarchy</entity>, with a fierce and secret passion for gold and silver. And to protect it all they will have walls around their houses - real private nests where they can spend a fortune on women or anyone else they fancy.’  
> ‘Very true,’ he said.  
> ‘The value they put on money, and their inability to acquire it openly, will make them mean with their own money, while their desires and the secret pleasures they enjoy will make them extravagant with other people’s. They will run away from the law like children running away from their father, since their <entity>education</entity> will not have been a matter of conviction, but something imposed on them by force. This in turn is the result of neglecting the true Muse, the Muse of <entity>argument</entity> and <entity>philosophy</entity>, and setting a higher value on physical <entity>education</entity> than on <entity>education</entity> in the arts.’  
> ‘It’s certainly a mixed regime you are describing — partly bad and partly good.’  
> ‘Yes, it is a mixture,’ I said. ‘But it has one striking characteristic, which comes from the dominance of the <entity>spirited element</entity>. Love of victory and <entity>honor</entity>.’  
> ‘Absolutely.’

**Argument Structure** (Timocracy as Degenerate Regime):
- **Premise 1**: Origin via corruption of guardians (from friends/providers to serfs/slaves; focus on warfare oversight).  
  - Evidence: Shift from <entity>aristocracy</entity>'s communal harmony to possessive control (Citation: 548a).  
- **Premise 2**: Hybrid structure – Retains aristocratic elements (respect for rulers, warrior disqualification from business, communal quarters, military training) but adds oligarchic avarice (hidden wealth, private nests) and unique traits (fear of <entity>wise</entity>, preference for <entity>spirited</entity> warriors, constant <entity>war</entity>).  
  - Evidence: Midway modeling; neglect of <entity>philosophy</entity> leads to forced <entity>education</entity> and law evasion (Citation: 548b–c).  
- **Conclusion**: Timocracy is mixed (good: <entity>honor</entity>; bad: extravagance, secret passions) but dominated by <entity>spirited element</entity>, prioritizing victory over <entity>virtue</entity> (Cross-ref: Tripartite soul from Book 4).  

**Relationships**: Timocracy links <entity>aristocracy</entity> (ideal, rational) to <entity>oligarchy</entity> (wealth-based); individual mirrors city (Socrates' outline sketch for justice/unjustice comparison, 548d).

### Section 2: Timocratic Man and His Formation (549a–550c)
**Speakers**: Socrates, Adeimantus (Glaucon referenced)  
**Context**: Parallel between regime and individual soul; formation via family/societal influences.

**Original Content**:
> ‘So much for this regime, then. That’s how it would have come into existence, and that’s what it would be like. It’s just an outline sketch of the regime, without filling in the details, but even a sketch will give us a good enough picture of the completely just man and the completely unjust man. It’s an impossibly long task to describe every regime and every character without leaving anything out.’  
> ‘Quite right,’ he said.  
> ‘Well, then, who is the man corresponding to this regime? How did he come into existence, and what is he like?’  
> And Adeimantus replied, ‘When it comes to love of victory, I think he’s pretty close to Glaucon here.’  
> ‘Maybe he is,’ I said, ‘as far as that goes. But there are some ways in which I think his nature is different.’  
> ‘What ways are those?’  
> ‘He’d have to be more self-willed, and with less <entity>education</entity> in the arts, though still a lover of them. Interested in listening to speeches, but no speaker. He’ll be one of those people who are hard on his slaves, a man like this, since he doesn’t feel the superiority the truly <entity>educated</entity> man feels towards his slaves. He’ll be courteous towards free men, and his love of power and success will make him extremely deferential to those in authority. He is an avid hunter and loves physical exercise, and he feels entitled to rule not because of what he says, or anything like that, but because of his warlike deeds and achievements in <entity>war</entity>.’  
> ‘Yes, because this is the character of that regime.’  
> ‘As for money,’ I said, ‘someone like this would despise it in his youth, but the older he got, the more fond of it he would become. This is because he shares in the money-loving temperament, and is not purely directed towards <entity>virtue</entity>, since he has missed out on the finest of all guardians.’  
> ‘What guardian is that?’ Adeimantus asked.  
> ‘<entity>Reason</entity>, blended with musical and artistic <entity>education</entity>. <entity>Reason</entity> is the only thing which once it is born in a man, remains with him throughout his life as the protector of <entity>virtue</entity>.’  
> ‘You are right.’  
> ‘Well,’ I said, ‘that is undoubtedly what the timocratic man is like in his youth. He is very similar to the timocratic city.’  
> ‘Absolutely.’  
> ‘The way he comes into existence is something like this. You sometimes get the young son of a good man who lives in a badly governed state. The father avoids success, public office, the lawcourts, and all that kind of minding other people’s business. He’s prepared to settle for less than his due, in the interests of a quiet life.’  
> ‘How does the son become timocratic, then?’  
> ‘It happens when he starts listening to his mother complaining about her husband not being one of the ruling group, and her own failure, in consequence, to receive the respect she is entitled to from the other women. She can see that her husband is not particularly keen on money, that he does not fight, he is not argumentative - either as a private citizen in the lawcourts, or in public life - that he is indifferent to all this kind of thing. She notices that his attention is constantly directed towards himself, whereas for her he feels neither marked respect nor marked disrespect. The boy hears her complaining on all these counts, and saying that his father is a coward, far too easy-going, and all the rest of it. You know the kind of litany women tend to recite on these occasions.’  
> ‘I do indeed,’ Adeimantus said. ‘It’s a long litany, and all too typical.’  
> ‘And you’re aware too,’ I said, ‘that even the servants of men like this, the supposedly loyal servants, will sometimes say this kind of thing to the son behind the father’s back. If they see someone owing the father money, or doing him some other wrong, and the father not prosecuting him, they tell the son he must get his own back on all these kinds of people when he grows up, and be more of a man than his father. When he goes out, he hears and sees more of the same kind of thing. People who mind their own business in the city are called simpletons, and regarded as of little account, while those who don’t mind their own business are respected and admired. The young man is constantly hearing and seeing this kind of thing, but at the same time he listens to what his father says. He can observe his way of life close to, and compare it with other people’s way of life. At that point he is torn between the two, his father feeding the rational element in his soul, and making it grow, while the others feed the desiring and <entity>spirited</entity> elements. Since he is not a naturally bad man, but is influenced by the bad company he keeps, he is torn between these two extremes, and finishes up somewhere in the middle. He hands over power to the compromise candidate, the competitive and <entity>spirited</entity> element, and in this way becomes arrogant and ambitious.’  
> ‘Yes, I’m happy with that as an explanation of the way this man comes into being.’  
> ‘In that case,’ I said, ‘we have both our second regime and our second individual.’  
> ‘Yes, we have.’  
> ‘Should we move on, then, with apologies to Aeschylus, to “another man before another state”?12 Or would we rather, sticking to our original plan, deal with the state first?’  
> ‘By all means,’ he said.

**Argument Structure** (Formation of Timocratic Man):
- **Premise 1**: Character traits – Self-willed, less artistic <entity>education</entity>, <entity>spirited</entity> (hard on slaves, deferential to authority, war-focused); evolves to money-loving with age.  
  - Evidence: Lacks <entity>reason</entity> as <entity>virtue</entity>'s guardian (blended with arts; Citation: 549a–b).  
- **Premise 2**: Origin in dysfunctional influences – Father's quiet rationalism vs. mother's/servants'/society's push for ambition, <entity>war</entity>, revenge; tears soul between rational, <entity>desiring</entity>, and <entity>spirited</entity> elements.  
  - Evidence: Bad company compromises <entity>reason</entity>, elevating <entity>spirited element</entity> (Citation: 549c–550b; Cross-ref: Tripartite soul, Book 4).  
- **Conclusion**: Timocratic man mirrors timocratic city – Ambitious but incomplete <entity>virtue</entity>, leading to arrogance (Aeschylus pun transitions to next regime).  

**Relationships**: Individual soul degeneration parallels city (city-soul analogy); <entity>reason</entity>'s absence foreshadows oligarchy's wealth focus.

### Section 3: Transition to and Characteristics of Oligarchy (550c–553a)
**Speakers**: Socrates, Adeimantus  
**Context**: Oligarchy as wealth-based rule; faults include division, inefficiency, and social ills.

**Original Content**:
> ‘I imagine the next regime after the one we’ve just described would be <entity>oligarchy</entity>.’  
> ‘And what form of political organisation do you mean by <entity>oligarchy</entity>?’  
> ‘The regime based on property qualifications,’ I said. ‘The one where the rich rule, and a poor man is excluded from power.’  
> ‘I see.’  
> ‘Do we have to explain how the change from <entity>timocracy</entity> to <entity>oligarchy</entity> first takes place?’  
> ‘Yes.’  
> ‘Mind you,’ I said, ‘even a blind man could see how it happens.’  
> ‘How does it happen?’  
> ‘The regime we described is destroyed by the strongroom full of gold which each man possesses. They start by inventing extravagances for themselves, and then they bend the laws in that direction, since neither they nor their wives are prepared to obey them.’  
> ‘That’s likely enough.’  
> ‘The next step, I suppose, will have been for them to start eyeing one another and competing with one another, and in this way they would reduce the whole population to their own level.’  
> ‘Very likely.’  
> ‘After that, presumably, they would become still further involved in making money. And the higher the value they put on that, the lower the value they would put on <entity>virtue</entity>. Isn’t <entity>virtue</entity> always at odds with <entity>wealth</entity> in this way? As if they were in the two scales of a balance, always trying to move in opposite directions?’  
> ‘Exactly,’ he said.  
> ‘And as <entity>wealth</entity> and the wealthy are valued more in a city, so <entity>goodness</entity> and the good are valued less.’  
> ‘Obviously.’  
> ‘What is valued at any particular time becomes the common practice. What is not valued is neglected.’  
> ‘Yes.’  
> ‘Eventually, then, they stop being competitive and ambitious, and become mercenary and money-loving. They praise and admire the rich man, and admit him to positions of power. The poor man they treat with contempt.’  
> ‘Absolutely.’  
> ‘At that point they pass a law defining the oligarchic regime. They establish a wealth qualification — larger in an extreme <entity>oligarchy</entity>, smaller in a more moderate <entity>oligarchy</entity>—and declare that anyone whose property does not reach the prescribed value is debarred from the government. Either they put this into effect by force of arms, or else they’ve already established this kind of regime earlier by intimidation. Isn’t that how it’s done?’  
> ‘It is.’  
> ‘So that, more or less, is how it becomes established.’  
> ‘Yes,’ he said. ‘But what are the characteristics of this regime? And what are the kind of faults we said it possessed?’  
> ‘Well,’ I said, ‘the first fault is this very thing which defines its nature. Think what it would be like if you appointed ships’ captains in this way, on the basis of a property qualification, and refused a command to a poor man even if he was better qualified.’  
> ‘I think it’d be a sorry voyage they’d find themselves making,’ he said.  
> ‘And the same with any position of command over anything?’  
> ‘That’s certainly my opinion.’  
> ‘With the exception of a city? Or including a city?’  
> ‘It is especially true of a city,’ he said, ‘since the responsibility a city brings is the greatest and the most demanding.’  
> ‘This would be one great failing, then, possessed by <entity>oligarchy</entity>.’  
> ‘It looks like it.’  
> ‘What about its second failing? Is that any less serious?’  
> ‘What would it be, this second failing?’  
> ‘That a city of this kind is bound to be two cities, not one: a city of the poor and a city of the rich, living in the same place, but constantly scheming against one another.’  
> ‘That is, god knows, as big a failing as the first.’  
> ‘Nor is it much of a recommendation that they are unlikely to be able to fight any kind of <entity>war</entity>. They must necessarily either arm their own common people and use them, in which case they will fear them more than the enemy, or else not use them, and show themselves, when it comes to the actual fighting, to be true oligarchs, with few under their command.13 What is more, their love of money makes them reluctant to contribute to the cost of a <entity>war</entity>.’  
> ‘No, that’s not much of a recommendation.’  
> ‘What about the criticism we made some time ago,14 that in a regime of this kind the same people are farmers, businessmen and soldiers all at the same time - that they are jacks of all trades and masters of none? Do you think it is right for things to be like that?’  
> ‘Not in the least.’  
> ‘You must ask yourself, however, if this city isn’t also the first to introduce an evil which is greater than any of these.’  
> ‘What evil is that?’  
> ‘There is nothing to stop one person selling all his property, and a second person acquiring it.15 Nothing to stop the first person still living in the city after selling his property, without being one of the elements which make up the city. He is neither businessman nor skilled worker, neither cavalryman nor infantryman16 - just a poor man, what they call a man without means.’  
> ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘this city is the first to introduce this evil.’  
> ‘Certainly in cities with oligarchical regimes this kind of thing is not prohibited in any way. If it were, you wouldn’t get one group of people who are very rich, and the rest living in complete poverty.’  
> ‘That’s right.’  
> ‘And here’s another question you might ask yourself. At the point where someone like this was rich, and spending all his money, was he even at that time any use to the city for the purposes we’ve been talking about? Or was it an illusion, his being one of the rulers? Was he in truth neither a ruler nor a servant of the city, but merely a spendthrift?’  
> ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘it was an illusion. He was nothing more than a spendthrift.’  
> ‘Do you want us to say, then, that just as a drone born in a cell is a blight on the hive, so a man like this is born as a drone in a household, and is a blight on the city?’  
> ‘By all means, Socrates.’  
> ‘Well, then, Adeimantus, is it the case that god has made the winged variety of drone all stingless, whereas of these two-legged drones some are stingless, but others have very nasty stings? Do those who finish up as beggars in their old age come from the stingless class, and all those who are labelled criminals from the class with stings?’  
> ‘Yes, that’s true,’ he said.  
> ‘It’s obvious, then, that anywhere in a city you see beggars, there you can expect to find a secret nest of thieves, pickpockets, robbers of temples, and all these sorts of malefactors.’

**Argument Structure** (Oligarchy's Decline and Faults):
- **Premise 1**: Transition from timocracy – Gold hoarding leads to extravagance, law-bending, competition, and wealth prioritization over <entity>virtue</entity> (inverse balance: wealth up, <entity>goodness</entity> down).  
  - Evidence: Valued practices become norms; results in property-based rule (extreme/moderate variants; Citation: 550c–551b; Cross-ref: Footnote 12, Aeschylus).  
- **Premise 2**: Defining faults – (1) Incompetent leadership (wealth over qualification, e.g., ship captains analogy); (2) Internal division (rich vs. poor "two cities"); (3) Military weakness (fear of arming poor, stingy funding); (4) Violation of specialization (multi-role citizens; Cross-ref: 434a–b).  
  - Evidence: Unrestricted property sales create "drones" (spendthrifts, beggars, criminals; Citation: 551c–552b; Footnotes 13–16).  
- **Conclusion**: Oligarchy fosters poverty/crime ("drone" blight), illusion of utility, and social decay; greatest evil is economic inequality enabling malefactors (parallels unjust soul; Citation: 552c–553a).  

**Relationships**: Degeneration sequence (<entity>aristocracy</entity> → timocracy → <entity>oligarchy</entity>); city-soul analogy extends (oligarchic man as money-loving drone); foreshadows democracy (Footnote 15 contrasts Sparta/Athens).

### **Section 1: Oligarchic City and Evils (553a–553c)**
**Chunk Summary**: Dialogue establishes the <entity type="regime">oligarchic regime</entity> as flawed, ruled by property qualification, rife with <entity type="concept">criminals</entity> and <entity type="virtue">lack of education</entity>. Transitions to the <entity type="soul-type">oligarchic man</entity>.

**Dialogue Separation**:
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: Yes, that’s obvious. And don’t you find beggars in cities with oligarchic regimes? Can we avoid the conclusion, then, that in these cities there is a large number of <entity type="concept">criminals</entity> with stings, and that the authorities systematically and forcibly keep them under control? And can we not say that the cause of people like this coming into existence there is <entity type="virtue">lack of education</entity>, together with poor upbringing and constitutional arrangements? Well, that’s roughly what the <entity type="regime">oligarchic city</entity> would be like. And those are the evils it would contain—plus some others besides, perhaps. Then that’s another regime we can regard as dealt with—the one known as <entity type="regime">oligarchic regime</entity>, whose rulers are chosen on the basis of a property qualification. Let’s look next at the man who resembles it—how he comes into existence, and what he’s like when he does. Doesn’t the change from the <entity type="regime">timocratic character</entity> to the <entity type="regime">oligarchic</entity> take place more or less like this? He has a son, who starts by emulating his father’s achievements and following in his footsteps. But then one day he sees him suddenly fall foul of the city, like a ship striking a reef. He sees all his father’s possessions, and even his life, spilled out over the waves. He may have been <entity type="historical">general</entity>, or held some other high office, but then been dragged into the lawcourts, and injured by the evidence of informers. He may have been put to death, exiled or disfranchised, and lost everything he possessed...<footnote id="17">Athenian generals were chosen by popular election, and were held to account in the lawcourts, before a popular jury. Cross-ref: Relates to <entity type="concept">justice</entity> in legal proceedings [Republic 1.327–331].</footnote> When the son sees this, my friend, when he lives through it, and loses everything he possesses, he is gripped by fear, I imagine. He promptly tumbles the love of honour and that <entity type="soul-part">spirited element</entity> we were talking about headlong from their throne in his soul. Demeaned by poverty, he turns to making money. Greedily and gradually he saves and works, and so amasses wealth. The next step, don’t you think, for someone like this, is to enthrone the <entity type="soul-part">desiring and avaricious element</entity>, and crown that as the great king within his soul, girding it with chains and ceremonial swords and tiaras?<footnote id="18">Greeks referred to the Persian monarch as the ‘great king’. He was emblematic for them of vast empire and wealth, and of absolute sovereignty over a servile populace. Cross-ref: Metaphysical analogy to soul hierarchy [Republic 4.439–441].</footnote> As for the <entity type="soul-part">rational</entity> and <entity type="soul-part">spirited parts</entity> of the soul, he makes them sit on the ground, one on each side, below the <entity type="soul-part">desiring element</entity>, reducing them to slavery. The <entity type="soul-part">rational part</entity> he bans from all subjects of calculation or inquiry other than ways of turning a little money into a lot, while the only things he allows the <entity type="soul-part">spirited part</entity> to admire and respect are wealth and wealthy people. The only thing it may pride itself on is the acquisition of money, or anything which contributes to this end. There is no swifter or surer way to turn an ambitious young man into an avaricious one. And is this the <entity type="soul-type">oligarchic type</entity>? Let’s see, then, if he will be like the <entity type="regime">oligarchic regime</entity>. And won’t the first point of similarity be his regarding money as of supreme importance? And of course in his being a toiler, counting every penny, who satisfies only the most pressing and necessary of the desires he has, refuses to spend money on anything else, and keeps all his other desires in subjection, since he regards them as idle. A sordid little fellow, looking to turn everything to his advantage. A miser. And this is what most people admire. Won’t this be the man who is like this regime? And the reason, I take it, is that this kind of person never applied himself to his <entity type="concept">education</entity>. Now, the next question. Can we say of him that his <entity type="virtue">lack of education</entity> gives him drone-like desires—some beggarly, some vicious—but that they are forcibly suppressed by his habitual cautiousness? So do you want to know the best place to look for these people’s <entity type="concept">crimes</entity>? When they are guardians of orphans, or in any situation of that kind where they find they have a free hand to behave unjustly. Isn’t this a clear indication that when this kind of person has a good reputation in most of his business dealings, and is generally regarded as a just man, he is using something decent in himself to suppress by force other, evil desires that he possesses? He does not persuade them that what they want is wrong, or use <entity type="concept">reason</entity> as a civilising influence. He uses compulsion and fear, because he is afraid of losing the rest of his fortune. Though god knows, my friend, when it’s a question of spending other people’s money, you will find then that most of them possess drone-like desires. In which case, someone of this sort will not be free from conflict within himself. He is two individuals, not one, though for the most part his better desires have the upper hand over his worse desires. That, I think, is the reason why someone of this sort makes a comparatively good impression. But he’s a far cry from the true excellence of the harmonious and well-tuned soul. And of course, for any prize in public life, or any other highly regarded distinction, the penny-pincher, as an individual, is a poor competitor. He refuses to spend money in the cause of reputation or this kind of success, because he is frightened of awakening his extravagant desires and entering into alliance with them in order to compete. He brings only a small part of himself to the fray, fighting with slender resources, oligarchically.<footnote id="20">The pun on olig-archy is the same as at 551e (note 13 above). Cross-ref: Ethical critique of <entity type="virtue">self-discipline</entity> [Republic 4.430–432].</footnote> So he generally loses—and remains rich. Does that leave us in any doubt, then, if we are asking about similarity, the penny-pinching and money-loving man is in the same class as the <entity type="regime">oligarchic city</entity>? Democracy, then, would seem to be our next object of enquiry—how it arises, and what it is like when it does arise. Then we can recognise the character of the <entity type="soul-type">democratic man</entity> in his turn, and bring him forward for appraisal. Very well. Isn’t the way a city changes from <entity type="regime">oligarchy</entity> to <entity type="regime">democracy</entity> something like this? Isn’t it the result of their greed in pursuing the ideal they have set themselves—the requirement to become as rich as possible? Well, the reason the rulers in it are rulers, I take it, is because of their great wealth. So if any of the young turn out to have no <entity type="virtue">self-restraint</entity>, the rulers, predictably, are not prepared to restrain them by a law prohibiting them from spending what they own, and losing it all. Their aim is to buy up the property of people like this, or lend them money with the property as security, and in this way become even richer and more highly respected. And isn’t it obvious by now that a high regard for wealth in a city is incompatible with the possession of <entity type="virtue">self-discipline</entity> on the part of the citizens? They will inevitably lose interest in one or the other. So through negligence, and the consistent licence they give well-born individuals to behave without restraint, the rulers in oligarchies can sometimes drive them into poverty. And these people, I take it, sit around armed in the city—in debt, or disfranchised, or both. They are <entity type="concept">drones with stings</entity>. Eager for revolution, they hate and plot against those who now possess their property, and the others like them. The money-makers, eyes fixed on the ground, pretend not to see them. And they inject the poison of their money into any of the other citizens who offer no resistance, gaining for themselves in interest many times the original sum lent. In this way they create a large class of <entity type="concept">drones</entity> and beggars in the city. As the flames of discontent begin to take hold, they refuse to put them out either in the first way, by forbidding people to dispose of their possessions as they wish, or again in a different way, using a second law which can stop this kind of thing happening. Well, it’s the next best after the first one I mentioned. And it does compel the citizens to pay some regard to <entity type="virtue">virtue</entity>. If you have a law that voluntary agreements should in general be entered into at each party’s own risk, there would be less shameless money-making in the city, and fewer dangers of the kind we’ve just been talking about would arise there. As it is, for all the reasons we have given, the rulers treat the subjects in the city in the way I have described. As for themselves and their families, don’t they bring their children up to be luxurious, incapable alike of physical and mental exertion, weak when it comes to resisting pleasure or pain, and lazy? Haven’t they themselves lost interest in everything other than making money? Have they paid any more attention to <entity type="virtue">virtue</entity> and excellence than the poor have? With this background, what do you think happens when rulers and ruled come into close contact, on a journey, perhaps, or in some other joint activity—an embassy or military expedition, or sailing in the same ship, or as fellow-soldiers? Or when they watch each other in the actual moment of danger, and the poor find that here at least they are not looked down on by the rich? In fact it often happens that a poor man, lean and sunburnt, is stationed in battle alongside a rich man who has had a comfortable upbringing in the shade, and who is carrying a good deal of superfluous flesh. When he sees him wheezing and struggling, don’t you suppose he blames his own cowardice for the fact that people like this are rich? Don’t they egg one another on when they are alone together? “They’re ours for the plucking,” they say. “There’s nothing to them.” It’s like an unhealthy body. It only takes a trivial external cause to tip the balance towards actual illness. Or the body can sometimes come to be at war with itself without any outside intervention at all. It’s just the same with a city. An unhealthy city needs only the slightest pretext—one side appealing for outside help to an <entity type="regime">oligarchy</entity>, or the other to a <entity type="regime">democracy</entity>—to become ill, and start fighting against itself. Can’t it even sometimes be at war with itself without any outside intervention at all? And presumably it turns into a <entity type="regime">democracy</entity> when the poor are victorious, when they kill some of their opponents and send others into exile, give an equal share in the constitution and public office to those who remain, and when public office in the city is allocated for the most part by lot. Very well, then. How will these people live? What will this regime, in its turn, be like, since it’s obvious that the man who resembles it will prove to be a <entity type="soul-type">democratic man</entity> of some sort?<footnote id="22">The picture of the democratic regime that follows owes many of its touches to the social life of Plato’s Athens. But there was something of Athens in the description of the oligarchic regime also. Cross-ref: Epistemological critique of <entity type="concept">knowledge</entity> in democratic excess [Republic 6.488–489].</footnote> Well, aren’t they free men, for a start? Isn’t it a city full of <entity type="concept">freedom</entity>, and <entity type="concept">freedom of speech</entity>? Isn’t there liberty in it for anyone to do anything he wants? And where there is liberty, then obviously each person can arrange his own life within the city in whatever way pleases him. The most varied of regimes, I would think, as far as human character goes. It’s probably the most attractive of the regimes. Like a coat of many colours, with an infinite variety of floral decoration, this regime will catch the eye with its infinite variety of moral decoration. Lots of people are likely to judge this regime to be the most attractive—like women or children looking at prettily painted objects. And I tell you, it’s a good place to look if you want a particular kind of constitution. Because the liberty it allows its citizens means it has every type of constitution within it. So anyone wanting to found a city, as we have just been doing, will probably find he has to go to a city with a <entity type="regime">democratic regime</entity>, and there choose whatever political arrangements he fancies. Like shopping for constitutions in a bazaar. Then, when he has made his choice, he can found a city along those lines.
