## Section 1: Critique of Democratic Freedom and Tolerance [Republic 8.558a–c]
### Dialogue Separation
- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘There’s no compulsion to hold office in this city,’ I said, ‘even if you’re well qualified to hold office, nor to obey those who do hold office, if you don’t feel like it, nor to go to war when the city is at war, nor to be at peace when everyone else is, unless peace is what you want. Then again, even if there’s a law stopping you holding office or being a member of a jury, there’s nothing to stop you holding office and being a member of a jury anyway, if that’s how the mood takes you. Isn’t this, in the short term, a delightful and heaven-sent way of life?’

- **Speaker**: <person>Adeimantus</person>  
  ‘It probably is, in the short term.’

- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘And what about the relaxed attitude of those sentenced by the courts? Isn’t it civilised? Or have you never seen people who have been condemned to death or exile in a regime of this kind, who nonetheless remain in person, hanging about at the centre of things, and haunting the place like the spirit of a departed hero,<footnote>23 In Greek religion, heroes became minor deities after death and were worshipped in their place of origin.</footnote> without anyone caring or noticing?’

- **Speaker**: <person>Adeimantus</person>  
  ‘I’ve seen plenty,’ he said.

- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘Then there’s the tolerance of this city. No pedantic insistence on detail, but an utter contempt for the things we showed such respect for when we were founding our city — our claim that only someone with an outstanding nature could ever turn out to be a <concept>good man</concept>, and only if from earliest childhood he played in the best company and the right surroundings, and did all the right kinds of things. How magnificently the city tramples all this underfoot, paying no attention to what kind of life someone led before he entered political life! All anyone has to do to win favour is say he is a friend of the people.’

- **Speaker**: <person>Adeimantus</person> (sarcastic)  
  ‘Ah, yes, that’s true nobility!’

- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘These and related qualities will be the ones possessed by <concept>democracy</concept>. You’d expect it to be an enjoyable kind of regime - anarchic, colourful, and granting equality of a sort to equals and unequals alike.’

- **Speaker**: <person>Adeimantus</person>  
  ‘Yes, that’s a pretty familiar story,’ he said.

  - <premise>Condemned individuals (death/exile) remain unpunished, like haunting <entity type="other">heroes</entity> [558b].</entity>
  - <premise>City ignores <concept>virtue</concept>'s foundations (outstanding nature, noble upbringing) in favor of populist claims ("friend of the people") [558c].</premise>

</argument>

## Section 2: Origin of the Democratic Man [Republic 8.558c–559d]
### Dialogue Separation
- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘Look and see, then,’ I said, ‘what the individual resembling this regime is like. Or rather, should we ask first, as we did with the regime, how he comes into being?’

- **Speaker**: <person>Adeimantus</person>  
  ‘Yes.’

- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘Doesn’t it happen like this? He might come into being, I imagine, as a son of the thrifty oligarchic character we were talking about, brought up under his father’s direction and with his father’s habits.’  
  ‘He might well.’  
  ‘So he too will use force to master those desires within him which are extravagant and not money-making - the ones called unnecessary desires.’  
  ‘Obviously,’ he said.  
  ‘Would you like us to start by defining <concept>necessary</concept> and <concept>unnecessary desires</concept>? We don’t want to be completely in the dark about what we’re discussing.’  
  ‘Yes, I would.’  
  ‘Very well. Is it the ones we can’t deny which can properly be called necessary - plus the ones whose satisfaction does us some good? Our nature demands that we try to satisfy both these classes, doesn’t it?’  
  ‘Very much so.’  
  ‘So we shall be justified in using the name “necessary” for these desires.’  
  ‘We shall.’  
  ‘What about the desires you _can_ get rid of, if you work at it from childhood, the ones moreover whose presence does you no good — may even perhaps do you some harm? Wouldn’t we be right in saying that all these are unnecessary?’  
  ‘We would.’  
  ‘Let’s take an example of each class. It’s easier to grasp them if we have a pattern, or model.’  
  ‘That’s a good idea.’  
  ‘Won’t the desire to eat for one’s health and well-being, the desire just for bread and cooked food, be a <concept>necessary desire</concept>?’  
  ‘Yes, I think it will.’  
  ‘The desire for bread is necessary on both counts. It is not only beneficial, but also the difference between life and death.’  
  ‘Yes.’  
  ‘Whereas the desire for cooked food is necessary if it can contribute in some way to our well-being.’  
  ‘Precisely.’  
  ‘What about the desire, over and above this, for other sorts of foods? This desire can be eliminated, in most people, by discipline and education from early childhood. And since it is harmful to the body, and harmful to the soul’s capacity for <concept>thought</concept> and <concept>self-control</concept>, would it be correct to call it unnecessary?’  
  ‘Absolutely correct.’  
  ‘In which case, shall we say that these desires are extravagant, whereas the others are productive, because they contribute to some function?’  
  ‘By all means.’  
  ‘And we’ll say the same about sex, and the rest of our desires.’  
  ‘Yes, we shall.’  
  ‘Well, then. Did we say that this person we were calling a <entity type="other">drone</entity> a few moments ago was the one who was stuffed with pleasures and desires of this sort, and that he was ruled by <concept>unnecessary desires</concept>? Whereas the person ruled by <concept>necessary desires</concept> was thrifty and oligarchical?<footnote>24 555c–556a vs. 554a.</footnote>’  

- **Speaker**: <person>Adeimantus</person>  
  ‘We did indeed.’

### Extracted Arguments
<argument id="desires-definition">
  - <premise><concept>Necessary desires</concept>: Inescapable (e.g., basic food for survival) and beneficial (contribute to well-being) [559a–b].</premise>
  - <premise><concept>Unnecessary desires</concept>: Eliminable by habituation/education, harmful to body/soul (e.g., gourmet foods beyond basics, impairing <concept>self-control</concept> and <concept>thought</concept>) [559b–c].</premise>
  - <conclusion>Democratic man emerges from oligarchic father by indulging <concept>unnecessary desires</concept>, contrasting thrifty <concept>oligarchy</concept> (ruled by <concept>necessary desires</concept>) with drone-like excess [559d].</conclusion>
  - <analogy>Desires as internal factions: Productive (<concept>necessary</concept>) vs. extravagant (<concept>unnecessary</concept>); cf. oligarchic man [555c–556a].</analogy>
</argument>

## Section 3: Transition to Democracy in the Soul [Republic 8.559d–561b]
### Dialogue Separation
- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘Let’s return, then,’ I said, ‘to our account of the way the <concept>democratic man</concept> comes into being from the oligarchic. I think it generally happens like this.’  
  ‘Like what?’  
  ‘Imagine a young man who has been brought up in the uneducated and stingy way we described just now, but who gets to taste the honey the <entity type="other">drones</entity> enjoy, and spend his time with wild, fiery creatures who can offer him pleasures of every kind, hue and variety. That’s probably the point you must regard as the beginning of the change from the <concept>oligarchy</concept> within him to <concept>democracy</concept>.’  
  ‘No question about it,’ he said.  
  ‘Just as the city changed when one party received support from an external ally of a similar persuasion,<footnote>25 556e.</footnote> doesn’t the young man now change in the same way when one group of his desires in its turn receives support from a class of external desires which are related and similar to it?’  
  ‘He certainly does.’  
  ‘And if some countervailing help comes to the oligarchic element within him - from his father, perhaps, or from the lectures and reproaches of the rest of his family — I imagine that’s when faction and counter-faction arise, and internal warfare against himself.’  
  ‘Of course.’  
  ‘Sometimes, I imagine, the democratic element loses ground to the oligarchic element, and some of his desires are either destroyed or banished, as some sense of <concept>shame</concept> is born in the young man’s soul, and order is restored.’  
  ‘Yes, it sometimes happens like that,’ he said.  
  ‘But as one set of desires is banished, I imagine another related set has grown up in succession. The father, who has no idea how to bring up his son, cannot prevent these desires becoming numerous and powerful.’  
  ‘Yes, that’s certainly what tends to happen.’  
  ‘These desires, then, draw the young man to the same company as before, and secret intercourse breeds a mob of further desires.’  
  ‘And then?’  
  ‘Finally, I imagine, they seize the citadel of the young man’s soul, realising that it is empty of <concept>learning</concept>, <concept>good habits</concept> and <concept>true arguments</concept>, which are of course the best defenders and guardians in the minds of men loved by the gods.’  
  ‘Much the best,’ he said.  
  ‘False, seductive arguments and opinions run up and seize this stronghold in the young man’s mind, I expect, replacing the true defenders.’  
  ‘They do indeed.’  
  ‘Doesn’t he then return to that land of the <entity type="other">Lotus-eaters</entity>, and take up residence there quite openly? If any help from his family reaches the thrifty part of his soul, those seductive arguments bar the gates of the royal walls within him.<footnote>26 The citadel or acropolis of a Greek city was typically the seat of its ancestral kings.</footnote> They will neither allow entry to the actual allied force, nor even admit an embassy of wise words, in a private capacity, from the young man’s elders. They join battle, and the seductive arguments win. A sense of <concept>shame</concept> is classed as simple-mindedness, deprived of rights, and driven into exile. <concept>Self-discipline</concept> is called cowardice, heaped with insults, and sent packing. As for <concept>moderation</concept> and economy, don’t the seductive arguments persuade the young man that these are mean and parochial? Don’t they join forces with his many useless desires, and despatch these qualities beyond the borders?’  
  ‘Absolutely.’  
  ‘And when they have somehow emptied and purged the soul of the young man they are taking possession of and initiating with solemn rites, they then promptly bring <concept>insolence</concept>, <concept>anarchy</concept>, <concept>extravagance</concept> and <concept>shamelessness</concept> back from exile, in a blaze of glory, with a great retinue, and crowned with garlands.<footnote>27 The imagery parodies the ritual of the Eleusinian Mysteries. (For mystic cults in general, see note 9 to 363c above.)</footnote> They sing their praises, and find flattering names for them. <concept>Insolence</concept> becomes sophistication, <concept>anarchy</concept> freedom, <concept>extravagance</concept> generosity, and <concept>shamelessness</concept> courage. Isn’t this likely to be the way a young man exchanges an upbringing among <concept>necessary desires</concept> for the liberation and release of <concept>unnecessary</concept> and useless desires?’  
  ‘Yes, it is,’ he said. ‘Quite clearly.’  
  ‘From then on, I imagine, a young man of this sort lives his life spending at least as much money, effort and time on <concept>unnecessary</concept> as on <concept>necessary desires</concept>. If he is lucky, he may not get too carried away by his orgy. As he grows older and the first flush of excitement fades, he may accept back some elements of the party he exiled, and avoid complete surrender to the usurpers. Putting all his pleasures on an equal footing, he grants power over himself to the pleasure of the moment, as if it were a magistrate chosen by lot. And when he has had his fill of it, he surrenders himself in turn to another pleasure. He rejects none of them, but gives sustenance to all alike.’  
  ‘He does indeed.’

<argument id="soul-transition">
  - <premise>Young oligarchic man exposed to external <concept>unnecessary desires</concept> (drones, wild company), sparking internal change [559d–e].</premise>
  - <premise>Internal factions: Oligarchic (<concept>shame</concept>, <concept>self-discipline</concept>) vs. democratic (seductive arguments banish virtues, install vices with new names) [560a–c].</premise>
  - <premise>Soul's citadel undefended without <concept>true arguments</concept> and <concept>knowledge</concept> [560b].</premise>
  - <conclusion>Democratic man equates all pleasures, yielding to momentary whims, equating <concept>necessary</concept> and <concept>unnecessary desires</concept> [560d–561a].</conclusion>
  - <analogy>Soul as besieged city (external allies aid factions; cf. city change [556e]); vices as returning exiles in ritual procession.</analogy>
</argument>

## Section 4: Character and Life of the Democratic Man [Republic 8.561b–562a]
### Dialogue Separation
- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘If someone tells him that some pleasures are the result of fine and <concept>good desires</concept>, others of evil desires, and that he should follow and value the first, and punish and hold in subjection the second, he does not admit this truth, or allow it into the fortress. He shakes his head at any claims of this sort, saying that all desires are equal, and must be valued equally.’  
  ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘that’s exactly how he feels, and exactly how he behaves.’  
  ‘And so he lives out his life from day to day, gratifying the desire of the moment. One day he drinks himself under the table to the sound of the pipes, the next day he is on a diet of plain water. Now he is taking exercise, but at other times he is lazing around and taking no interest in anything. And sometimes he passes the time in what he calls <concept>philosophy</concept>. Much of his time is spent in politics, where he leaps to his feet and says and does whatever comes into his head. Or if he comes to admire the military, then that is the way he goes. Or if it’s businessmen, then that way. There is no controlling order or necessity in his life. As far as he is concerned, it is pleasant, free and blessed, and he sticks to it his whole life through.’  
  ‘You’ve given us an excellent account of the life of the man who puts equality before everything.’  
  ‘Yes. I take it to be a variegated life, full of all sorts of characteristics. This <concept>democratic man</concept> is elegant and colourful, just like the <concept>democratic</concept> city. Many men and women might envy him his life, with all the examples of regimes and characters it contains within it.’  
  ‘Yes, that is what it is like,’ he said.  
  ‘Very well, then. Can a man like this be ranked on a par with <concept>democracy</concept>? Can he properly be called democratic?’  
  ‘Yes, he can.’

## Section 5: Preview of Tyranny from Democracy [Republic 8.562a–563b]
### Dialogue Separation
- **Speaker**: <person>Socrates</person>  
  ‘In that case,’ I said, ‘that leaves us with the task of describing the most delightful of regimes, and the most delightful of individuals. <concept>Tyranny</concept> and the tyrant.’  
  ‘It certainly does,’ he said.  
  ‘Very well, my good friend, how does <concept>tyranny</concept> manifest itself? That it is a change from <concept>democracy</concept> is pretty obvious.’  
  ‘Yes, it is.’  
  ‘In which case, does <concept>tyranny</concept> in its turn arise out of <concept>democracy</concept> in rather the same way as <concept>democracy</concept> arises out of <concept>oligarchy</concept>?’  
  ‘How do you mean?’  
  ‘The thing they held up as an ideal,’ I said, ‘the thing which formed the basis of <concept>oligarchy</concept>, was wealth, wasn’t it?’  
  ‘Yes.’  
  ‘It was the insatiable longing for wealth, and the neglect of everything else in the pursuit of profit, which destroyed <concept>oligarchy</concept>.’  
  ‘True,’ he said.  
  ‘And is it the insatiable longing for what it defines as <concept>good</concept> which destroys <concept>democracy</concept> too, in its turn?’  
  ‘What is it you say it defines as <concept>good</concept>?’  
  ‘<concept>Freedom</concept>,’ I said. ‘This is the thing, I imagine, which in a <concept>democratic</concept> state you will hear described as its finest attribute, and what makes it, for any man of free spirit, the only place worth living in.’  
  ‘Yes, that is certainly something you often hear said.’  
  ‘Well, then, as I was saying just now, is it the insatiable longing for this <concept>good</concept>, and the neglect of everything else, which brings about a change in this regime too, and creates the need for <concept>tyranny</concept>?’  
  ‘How does that happen?’ he asked.  
  ‘I imagine it’s when a <concept>democracy</concept>, in its thirst for the wine of <concept>freedom</concept>, finds the wine being poured by unscrupulous cupbearers, and when it drinks more deeply than it should of pure, unmixed <concept>freedom</concept>.<footnote>28 The Greeks drank their wine diluted with water.</footnote> Then if its magistrates are not totally easy-going and do not offer it that <concept>freedom</concept> in large quantities, it accuses them of being filthy oligarchs, and punishes them.’  
  ‘Yes,’ he said. ‘That is what they do.’  
  ‘Those who obey the rulers are heaped with insults. They are regarded as servile nonentities. Praise and respect, whether in private or public life, go to rulers for behaving like those they rule, and to those they rule for behaving like rulers. Isn’t the desire for <concept>freedom</concept> in a city of this type bound to run to extremes?’  
  ‘Of course it is.’  
  ‘And isn’t the <concept>anarchy</concept> bound to make its way, my friend, into private households? Until finally it starts appearing among dumb animals.’  
  ‘And how do we reckon this happens?’  
  ‘A father, for example, gets used to being like a child, and being afraid of his sons. A son gets used to being like his father. He feels no respect or fear for his parents. All he wants is to be free. Immigrants are put on a par with citizens, and citizens with immigrants. And the same with visiting foreigners.’  
  ‘Yes, that’s what happens.’  
  ‘That, plus a few more trivial examples of the same kind,’ I said. ‘In a society of this sort teachers are afraid of their pupils and curry favour with them. Pupils have an equal contempt for their teachers and their attendants. In general, the young are the image of their elders, and challenge them in everything they say and do. The old descend to the level of the young. They pepper everything with wit and humour, trying to be like the young, because they don’t want to be thought harsh or dictatorial.’

### Section 563c–564a: Freedom in Democracy and Its Excesses
<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Precisely,’ he said. ‘But the high-water mark of mass-<concept>freedom</concept> in a <location>city</location> of this kind comes when those who have been bought as <entity>slaves</entity> - whether male or female - are every bit as <concept>free</concept> as those who bought them. As for the <concept>relationship</concept> of women to men and men to women, I all but forgot to mention the extent of the <concept>legal equality</concept> and <concept>liberty</concept> between them.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Shall we then, borrowing a phrase from <author>Aeschylus</author>, say whatever it was that “came to our lips” just now?’<footnote id="29" ref="563c">The Aeschylean play from which this phrase derives is unknown.</footnote>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘By all means,’ I said. ‘It’s certainly what *I’m* going to do. You wouldn’t believe, without seeing it for yourself, how much more <concept>free</concept> <entity>domestic animals</entity> are here than in other <location>cities</location>. Dogs really *are* like the women who own them, as the <entity>proverb</entity> says. And horses and donkeys are in the habit of wandering the streets with total <concept>freedom</concept>, noses in the air, barging into any passer-by who fails to get out of their way. It’s all like that — all full of <concept>freedom</concept>.’ (563d)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Talk about telling people their own <entity>dreams</entity>,’ he said. ‘I’ve often had that experience myself on my way out of the <location>city</location>.’

In the end, as I imagine you are aware, they take no notice even of the <entity>laws</entity> - written or unwritten<footnote id="30" ref="563e">‘Unwritten law’ was a common phrase for the customary beliefs and social strictures respected in any particular community.</footnote> - in their determination that no one shall be master over them in any way at all.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, I am well aware of that,’ he said. (563e–564a)

### Section 564a–c: Transition from Democracy to Tyranny; The Ailment of Excess
<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘This is the <concept>form of government</concept>, my friend, so attractive and so headstrong, from which I believe <concept>tyranny</concept> is born.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Certainly headstrong,’ he said. ‘But what is the next step?’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘The same <entity>ailment</entity> which arose in <concept>oligarchy</concept>, and destroyed that, arises in this <concept>regime</concept> also - only more widespread and virulent because of the <concept>licence</concept> it is given. Here it enslaves <concept>democracy</concept>. Indeed, <concept>excess</concept> in one direction generally tends to produce a violent <concept>reaction</concept> in the opposite direction. This is true of the <entity>seasons</entity> of the year, of <entity>plants</entity> and <entity>animals</entity>, and particularly true of <concept>political regimes</concept>.’ (564a)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Probably so,’ he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Yes, since the only likely <concept>reaction</concept> to excessive <concept>freedom</concept>, whether for an individual or for a <location>city</location>, is excessive <concept>slavery</concept>.'

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Very likely.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘In which case,’ I said, ‘the chances are that <concept>democracy</concept> is the ideal place to find the origin of <concept>tyranny</concept> - the harshest and most complete <concept>slavery</concept> arising, I guess, from the most extreme <concept>freedom</concept>.’ (564b)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘That makes sense,’ he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘However, that doesn’t by itself answer your question, presumably. What you wanted to know was the nature of this <entity>ailment</entity> which arises not only in <concept>oligarchy</concept> but also in <concept>democracy</concept>, enslaving it.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘True.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Very well,’ I said. ‘What I had in mind was that class of idle and extravagant men, the most <concept>courageous</concept> element leading, the less <concept>courageous</concept> element following. We compared them to <entity>drones</entity> — the leaders to <entity>drones with stings</entity>, the followers to <entity>drones without stings</entity>.’<footnote id="31" ref="564c" cross-ref="552c-e">552c e.</footnote>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Rightly so.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Both these classes,’ I said, ‘disturb the balance of any <concept>regime</concept> in which they arise. Like <entity>phlegm</entity> and <entity>bile</entity> in the <entity>body</entity>.<footnote id="32" ref="564c">These were two of the so-called ‘humours’ — the Greek term simply means ‘juices’ — upon whose balance in the body much of Greek medicine made physical health depend.</footnote> The good <entity>doctor</entity> and <entity>lawgiver</entity> for a <location>city</location> must be far-sighted in his precautions against both of them - just like a good <entity>beekeeper</entity>. His intention, ideally, should be to prevent their occurrence at all. If they do occur, he should make sure they are cut out, cells and all, as swiftly as possible.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Heavens, yes. And as completely as possible.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘All right, then,’ I said. ‘To help us see what we are after in a more clear-cut way, let’s tackle the question like this.’ (564c)

### Section 564d–565b: Division of the Democratic City
<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Like what?’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Let’s make a theoretical division of the <concept>democratic city</concept> into three parts. After all, this is how it is in fact composed. This class of <entity>drones</entity>, I imagine, is one part, and because of the absence of restrictions it grows at least as freely in a <concept>democracy</concept> as in an <concept>oligarchy</concept>.’ (564d)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘That is so.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘But it is much fiercer in a <concept>democracy</concept> than in an <concept>oligarchy</concept>.'

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘In what way?’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘In an <concept>oligarchy</concept> it is treated as of no value, and excluded from <concept>power</concept>. So it gets no exercise, and does not develop its strength. In a <concept>democracy</concept>, by contrast, barring a few individuals, it is the dominant influence in the <entity>state</entity>. The fiercest element in this class does the talking and acting; the remainder sit around the <entity>rostrum</entity> buzzing, and refusing to allow the expression of any other view. The result is that in a <concept>regime</concept> of this kind everything, with very few exceptions, is run by the class of <entity>drones</entity>.’ (564e)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Exactly,’ he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Then there’s a second class which always separates itself off from the majority.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘What class is that?’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘When everyone is engaged in making <entity>money</entity>, presumably it is those with the most <concept>disciplined temperament</concept> who generally become the richest.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Very likely.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘They provide a plentiful supply of <entity>honey</entity> for the <entity>drones</entity>, I imagine, and an easy source from which to extract it.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes,’ he said. ‘After all, they can’t extract much from those who haven’t got much.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘They’re called the <entity>rich</entity>, these people we are talking about, the <entity>drones’</entity> feeding-ground.’ (565a)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘That’s about it,’ he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘The general <entity>populace</entity> would be the third class - <entity>manual labourers</entity> with little interest in <concept>politics</concept>, and very little <entity>property</entity> of their own. This is the most numerous and powerful class in a <concept>democracy</concept>, but only when it is assembled together.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘It is indeed,’ he said. ‘But if it isn’t getting some share of the <entity>honey</entity>, it is reluctant to assemble very often.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘That’s why it always does get a share of it, if its leaders have anything to do with it. They take it away from those who possess <entity>property</entity> and distribute it among the people, keeping only the lion’s share for themselves.’ (565b)

### Section 565b–566a: Class Conflict and the Rise of the Champion
<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, the people do get a limited share of that sort,’ he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Those whose <entity>property</entity> is taken away are presumably compelled to defend themselves by speaking in the <entity>assembly</entity> and taking whatever other action they can.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Of course.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘It is indeed.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Then you get <entity>impeachments</entity>, <entity>litigation</entity> and <entity>lawsuits</entity> between the two classes.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘They do.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘In that case, what prompts the change from <entity>champion</entity> to <concept>tyrant</concept>? <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘What story?’ he asked.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘That there is one piece of human <entity>innards</entity> chopped up among all the pieces of the other <entity>sacrificial offerings</entity>, and that anyone who tastes it will inevitably turn into a <entity>wolf</entity>. Or haven’t you heard that story?’ (565e–566a)

### Section 566a–e: The Champion's Transformation into Tyrant
<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, I have heard it.’

### Section 567a–568e: The Tyrant's Happiness and Methods of Rule
<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Bound to be.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And this <entity>champion</entity> of ours is obviously not going to be the one lying there, “measuring his full length”<footnote id="35" ref="567a" cross-ref="Homer">Homer, *Iliad* 16.776.</footnote> in the <entity>dust</entity>. <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Undoubtedly.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And if there are some independent-minded people whom he suspects of challenging his <concept>rule</concept>, doesn’t he try to find a good excuse for handing them over to the <entity>enemy</entity> and destroying them? For all these reasons, isn’t a <concept>tyrant</concept> always bound to be stirring up <entity>war</entity>?’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, he is.’ (567b)

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Doesn’t this tend to make him increasingly unpopular with the <entity>citizens</entity>?’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Of course it does.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Then the boldest of those who helped to make him <concept>tyrant</concept>, and who are now in positions of <concept>power</concept>, start to speak their minds freely, don’t they, both to him and to one another, criticising what is going on?’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Probably.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘So the <concept>tyrant</concept>, if he wants to go on ruling, must be prepared to remove all these people, until he is left with no one who is any use — whether <entity>friend</entity> or <entity>enemy</entity>.’ (567c)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Obviously he must.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘He will need a sharp pair of <entity>eyes</entity>, then. He needs to pick out the <concept>brave</concept>, the <concept>noble</concept>, the <concept>wise</concept> and the <entity>rich</entity>, since it is his unavoidable good fortune, whether he likes it or not, to be the <entity>enemy</entity> of all of them. He must plot their downfall, until he has got the <location>city</location> clean.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘A fine way to clean a <location>city</location>,’ he said.

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Yes. The exact opposite of what <entity>doctors</entity> do to the <entity>body</entity>. They remove what is worst, and leave what is best. With the <concept>tyrant</concept> it is the other way round.’ (567d)

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘That’s what he *has* to do, apparently, if he is to go on ruling.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘In which case,’ I said, ‘he is firmly and inevitably impaled on the horns of a delightful <entity>dilemma</entity>, which requires him either to spend his life with the worthless <entity>mob</entity> - and be hated by them into the bargain - or not to live at all.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘That’s about the size of it,’ he said. (567e)

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And the more hated by the <entity>citizens</entity> his behaviour makes him, the larger and more reliable a <entity>bodyguard</entity> he will need, won’t he?’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Of course.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Who are these reliable people, then? Where can he send to for them?’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘They’ll come winging their way of their own accord,’ he said. ‘Any number of them, as long as he pays the going rate.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Ye gods!<footnote id="36" ref="568a" cross-ref="399c">See note 50 to 399c above on Socrates’ habit of using this oath.</footnote> <entity>Drones</entity> again! Foreign ones, all kinds of them, I think you’re talking about.’<footnote id="37" ref="568a">Mercenaries were increasingly used in warfare throughout the Greek world in the fourth century, but it was characteristic only of tyrants to use them for a personal bodyguard.</footnote>

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Good. I haven’t given you the wrong impression, then.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And from the <location>city</location> itself? Might he not bring himself...'

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘To do what?’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘To deprive the <entity>citizens</entity> of their <entity>slaves</entity>, set the <entity>slaves</entity> free, and make them part of his <entity>bodyguard</entity>?’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Indeed he might. They are, after all, the most reliable people he can find.’ (568a–b)

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘What a wonderful thing you make a <concept>tyrant</concept> out to be,’ I said, ‘if these are the people he has as his <entity>friends</entity>, the people he can trust, once he has destroyed the <entity>friends</entity> he started with.’

<speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Well, these certainly *are* the kind of <entity>friends</entity> he has.’

<speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘So while he enjoys the admiration of these <entity>friends</entity>, and the company of these new <entity>citizens</entity>, do decent people hate him and avoid him?’ (568c–e)

## Extracted and Structured Philosophical Arguments
Arguments are hierarchically structured for retrieval: Premise → Evidence/Analogy → Conclusion. Linked to dialogue sections and key concepts/themes. All original content preserved in summaries/quotes.

### Argument 1: Excess Freedom Leads to Slavery (563c–564b; Theme: Ethics of Balance)
- **Premise**: In <concept>democracy</concept>, extreme <concept>freedom</concept> extends to <entity>slaves</entity>, <entity>animals</entity>, and <concept>gender equality</concept>, making citizens intolerant of any mastery (563c–e).
- **Evidence/Analogy**: Observations of <concept>free</concept> animals/dream-like liberty; <concept>reaction</concept> principle in nature (<entity>seasons</entity>, <entity>humors</entity>) mirrors political <concept>excess</concept> → opposite extreme (564a–b). Cross-ref: Body-soul-state analogy (Books 4–5).
- **Conclusion**: <concept>Democracy</concept>'s <concept>licence</concept> breeds excessive <concept>slavery</concept>, originating <concept>tyranny</concept> from extreme <concept>freedom</concept> (564b). <concept>Justice</concept> requires balance to avoid degeneration.

### Argument 2: Drones as Disruptive Force in Regimes (564c–565b; Theme: Epistemology via Division)
- **Premise**: <entity>Drones</entity> (idle/extravagant men) arise in all regimes but thrive in <concept>democracy</concept> due to lack of restrictions (564c–d).
- **Evidence/Analogy**: City divided into three: <entity>drones</entity> (fierce dominators), <entity>rich</entity> (honey-providers), <entity>populace</entity> (numerous but passive laborers) (564d–565a). <entity>Beekeeper/doctor</entity> must excise them like <entity>humors</entity> (564c; cross-ref: 552c–e).
- **Conclusion**: <entity>Drones</entity> unbalance the state, leading to <entity>litigation</entity> and <concept>redistribution</concept>; <concept>virtue</concept> (discipline) in <entity>rich</entity> is exploited, forcing <concept>oligarchic</concept> resistance (565b–c).

### Argument 3: Champion to Tyrant via Moral Corruption (565c–568e; Theme: Metaphysics of Degeneration)
- **Premise**: Class conflict accuses <entity>rich</entity> of <concept>oligarchy</concept>, implanting evil via <entity>drone</entity> stings; people elevate a <entity>champion</entity> (565c–d).
- **Evidence/Analogy**: <entity>Champion</entity> tastes "blood" like Arcadian <entity>wolf</entity> myth, sparking <concept>civil war</entity>, <entity>exile</entity>, <entity>assassination</entity> plots (565e–566b). Requests <entity>bodyguard</entity>; <entity>rich</entity> flee (Croesus oracle, 566c). Wars impoverish/oppress; purges <concept>brave/noble/wise</concept> (567a–d). Recruits <entity>foreign drones/mercenaries/slaves</entity> (568a–c; cross-ref: Historical tyrants like Pisistratus/Dionysius).
- **Conclusion**: <concept>Tyrant</concept> trapped in <entity>dilemma</entity>: rule with hated <entity>mob</entity>/slaves or die; "cleans" city oppositely to <entity>doctors</entity>, embodying <concept>slavery</concept> from <concept>freedom</concept> (567e–568e). Ethical irony: <concept>Happiness</concept> feigned, true <concept>justice</concept> absent.

## Structured Text by Section

### Section: 568a–c (Book 8: Tragedy, Poets, and Tyranny)
**Context**: Discussion on poets' praise of <entity>tyranny</entity> and their exclusion from the ideal state. Argument: Poets as apologists for tyranny justify their banishment. Cross-ref: Ties to earlier critique of imitation in poetry (Republic 3, 395a–b).

**Dialogue**:
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘How can they help doing so?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: (Implied agreement, leading to...)
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘It’s no wonder,’ I said, ‘that <entity>tragedy</entity> in general, and <entity>Euripides</entity> in particular, has such a reputation for <entity>wisdom</entity>.'
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Why?’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Because among other insight-filled utterances he produced this one: “A <entity>tyrant</entity>’s <entity>wisdom</entity> comes from wise companions.”<footnote id="38">The play from which this statement comes is lost, and some sources attribute it to <entity>Sophocles</entity> rather than <entity>Euripides</entity>. Poets and intellectuals were frequently to be found at the courts of powerful patrons. Cross-ref: Citation 40 on poets at tyrants' courts.</footnote> Clearly it was these associates of the <entity>tyrant</entity> that he was referring to as the wise.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes,’ he said. ‘And <entity>Euripides</entity> also praises <entity>tyranny</entity> as “godlike”<footnote id="39"><entity>Trojan Women</entity> 1169. Cross-ref: Euripides' works in Plato's *Symposium*.</footnote> — and a whole lot else besides. And not just <entity>Euripides</entity> - other poets as well.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘That’s why writers of <entity>tragedies</entity>, being so wise, will forgive us and those with regimes like ours, if we refuse to accept them into our state on the grounds that they are apologists for <entity>tyranny</entity>.'
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Well, if you want my opinion,’ he said, ‘they will forgive us. Or the more civilised of them will, at any rate.’

**Argument Structure** (Extracted):
- **Premise 1**: Poets like <entity>Euripides</entity> praise <entity>tyranny</entity> (e.g., via wise companions, godlike status).
- **Premise 2**: Such praise seduces states toward <entity>tyranny</entity> and <entity>democracy</entity> (cross-ref: 568c–d).
- **Conclusion**: Justify excluding poets from the ideal state to preserve <entity>justice</entity> and <entity>virtue</entity>.
- **Relationship**: Analogous to soul's corruption; poets as "seducers" mirror internal desires (cross-ref: Book 9, 572e–573b).

### Section: 568c–d (Book 8: Poets' Influence on Regimes)
**Context**: Poets' tours promote vice; respect diminishes in better regimes. Cross-ref: Degeneration sequence (timocracy → oligarchy → democracy → tyranny, Book 8, 543a–569c).

**Dialogue**:
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘They can tour the other cities, presumably, drawing great crowds and hiring actors with fine, loud, persuasive voices, and so seduce those states into <entity>tyranny</entity> and <entity>democracy</entity>.'
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘They certainly can.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘What is more, they get paid for this, and are treated with respect. First and foremost by <entity>tyrants</entity>, as you might expect, but also by a <entity>democracy</entity>.<footnote id="40"><entity>Pindar</entity>, <entity>Simonides</entity> and <entity>Aeschylus</entity> are said to have attended the court of the Sicilian <entity>tyrant</entity> <entity>Hiero</entity>, while <entity>Euripides</entity> and <entity>Agathon</entity> — the tragedian featured in Plato’s <entity>Symposium</entity> — attended the court of the Macedonian <entity>tyrant</entity> <entity>Archelaus</entity>. We also know of non-Athenians who came to Athens to have their dramas performed. Cross-ref: Poets as patrons' associates (fn. 38).</footnote> But the higher they climb in the ascending scale of political regimes, the fainter respect for them becomes, as if it were short of breath, and unable to progress further.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Exactly.’

**Argument Structure** (Extracted):
- **Premise 1**: Poets thrive in degenerate regimes (<entity>tyranny</entity>, <entity>democracy</entity>) via payment and respect.
- **Premise 2**: Respect wanes in virtuous regimes (e.g., aristocracy, <entity>justice</entity>-based).
- **Conclusion**: Poets' influence inversely correlates with regime virtue; banishment protects the state.
- **Relationship**: Mirrors <entity>tyrant</entity>'s army maintenance (cross-ref: 568d–e); poets as external "drone" desires.

### Section: 568d–569c (Book 8: Tyrant's Army Maintenance and Parricide)
**Context**: How a <entity>tyrant</entity> sustains power; shift from democracy to tyranny via force. Cross-ref: Frying pan into fire metaphor (freedom to slavery, 569c).

**Dialogue**:
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘We have strayed from the point, however,’ I said. ‘Let us return to that army the <entity>tyrant</entity> has - that fine, large, varied and ever-changing army and ask how it is going to be maintained.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Well, obviously, if there is money in the city’s temples, then as long as it lasts he will spend that. Plus the money of his victims, allowing him to exact smaller contributions from the people.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘But what happens when these run out?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘He will use his father’s money, obviously - to support himself, his drinking-companions, and his male and female friends.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: (Implied: CI see. The people, who spawned the <entity>tyrant</entity>, will support him and his friends.’)
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘It will have no choice,’ he said.
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘What if the people resent this?’ I asked. ‘“It is not right,” they might say for a start, “for a grown-up son to be supported by his father. Quite the reverse, in fact. A father should be supported by his son. What is more, the reason we fathered you and put you in power was not so that we could ourselves become slaves to our own slaves, as soon as you became powerful, and support you and them and the rest of your collection of human flotsam. No, with you as our champion we wanted our political <entity>freedom</entity> from the rich and the so-called aristocracy. We order you to leave the city now, you and your friends.” Suppose the people spoke to him in this way, like a father driving his son and his unruly drinking-companions from the house? What do you think would happen then?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘My god!’ he said. ‘Then the people really will find out what they are, and what kind of offspring they have fathered, taken to their hearts, and allowed to grow. They’ll realise it’s a case of the weaker trying to drive out the stronger.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘What do you mean?’ I asked. ‘Will the <entity>tyrant</entity> have the effrontery to use force against his parent? Will he beat him if he disobeys?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes - once he has taken away his weapons.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘A parricide, then, this <entity>tyrant</entity> you are describing. A cruel guardian for man’s old age. At this point, it seems, the thing is an acknowledged <entity>tyranny</entity>. The people have jumped out of the proverbial frying pan into the fire, from their enslavement to free men to a despotism of slaves. They have exchanged the ample - too ample - <entity>freedom</entity> they had before for the hair shirt of the most harsh and galling form of <entity>slavery</entity>, the <entity>slavery</entity> imposed by slaves.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, that is precisely how it happens.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Will there be any objection, then,’ I asked, ‘to our saying that we have given an adequate description of the way <entity>tyranny</entity> evolves out of <entity>democracy</entity>, and of what it is like when it has done so?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘No,’ he said, ‘our description is perfectly adequate.’

**Argument Structure** (Extracted):
- **Premise 1**: <entity>Tyrant</entity> exhausts public/private funds, then exploits "father" (people).
- **Premise 2**: People (as parent) demand <entity>freedom</entity>; <entity>tyrant</entity> responds with force (disarms, parricide).
- **Conclusion**: Tyranny = extreme <entity>slavery</entity> from excess <entity>democracy</entity>; people trade liberty for despotism.
- **Relationship**: Familial metaphor for regime (people as father, tyrant as son); cross-ref: Soul's tyranny (Book 9, 571a–c).

### Section: 571a–572e (Book 9: Transition to Tyrannical Man and Desires)
**Context**: Shift to individual soul; analysis of <entity>desires</entity> (necessary vs. unnecessary). Cross-ref: Tripartite soul (Republic 4, 435a–441c); earlier desires (fn. 1: 558d–559d).

**Dialogue**:
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘That still leaves the <entity>tyrannical man</entity> himself,’ I said. ‘We must ask how he develops out of the <entity>democratic man</entity>, what sort of person he is, and what manner of life he leads. Is he wretched or blissful?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, we are still left with him.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And there’s something else I need before I can deal with him. Shall I tell you what it is?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘What?’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘I’m not very satisfied with our analysis of the nature and extent of our <entity>desires</entity>.<footnote id="1">558d-559d. Cross-ref: Oligarchic/democratic types.</footnote> Until we remedy that, we shall be pretty much in the dark in our present enquiry.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘And is it too late now?’ he asked.
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Not at all. I want to make the following distinction between <entity>desires</entity>. Think about it. Among the unnecessary pleasures and <entity>desires</entity> there are some which seem to me to be violent or lawless. Everyone is born with them, in all probability, but in some people, under the control of the laws and the better <entity>desires</entity>, allied with <entity>reason</entity>, they are either eliminated completely, or remain few and weak. In other people, however, they become stronger and more numerous.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Which <entity>desires</entity> do you mean?’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Those which are aroused in sleep,’ I said, ‘when the rest of the soul — the rational, gentle and ruling element in it — slumbers, and the bestial, savage part, filled with food or drink, suddenly comes alive, casts off sleep, and tries to go out and satisfy its own nature. In this state, as you know, since it is released and set free from all shame or rational judgment, it can bring itself to do absolutely anything. In its imaginings it has no hesitation in attempting sexual intercourse with a mother - nor with anyone or anything else, man or god or animal. There is no murder it will not commit, no meat it will not eat. In short, it will go to any length of folly and shamelessness.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘How right you are,’ he said.
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘I imagine someone with a healthy and self-disciplined disposition will awaken the rational part of himself before going to sleep, feast it on fine arguments and enquiries, and so bring himself into a state of harmony with himself. As for his desiring part, he will expose it neither to want nor to excess. He wants it to go to sleep, and not disturb what is best in the soul with its pleasure or pain, but allow it all by itself, solitary and pure, to follow its enquiries and reach out for a vision of something - be it past, present or future - that it does not know. The same goes for the spirited part of the soul. He will calm it down, and avoid getting into a rage with anyone and going to sleep with his spirit in a state of turmoil. Before retiring to rest he needs to pacify two elements in the soul and awaken the third, which is the birthplace of <entity>reason</entity>. Under these conditions, as you know, he can most easily grasp <entity>truth</entity>, and the visions which appear in his dreams are least lawless.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘I entirely agree.’

**Argument Structure** (Extracted):
- **Premise 1**: <entity>Desires</entity> divide: necessary (controlled by <entity>reason</entity>/laws) vs. unnecessary/lawless (e.g., sleep fantasies of incest, murder).
- **Premise 2**: Virtuous person harmonizes soul (rational awake, desires/spirit pacified) for <entity>truth</entity>-seeking dreams.
- **Conclusion**: Lawless <entity>desires</entity> reveal in sleep; basis for <entity>tyrannical man</entity>'s wretchedness (cross-ref: 572e–573b).
- **Relationship**: Soul-regime analogy; uncontrolled desires = internal tyranny (metaphysics of soul).

### Section: 572e–573d (Book 9: Democratic to Tyrannical Man)
**Context**: Evolution via "drone" lust (<entity>Eros</entity>). Cross-ref: Democratic man (fn. 2: 558d).

**Dialogue**:
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Well, we’ve been carried along slightly further than we needed. What we need to know is that there is in everyone a terrible, untamed and lawless class of <entity>desires</entity> — even in those of us who appear to be completely normal. This becomes quite clear in our sleep. Am I talking sense? Do you agree?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, I do.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Take the <entity>democratic man</entity>, then, the man of the people. Remember what we said he was like.<footnote id="2">558d. Cross-ref: Thrifty father to excess.</footnote> He was the result, I think I’m right in saying, of an upbringing from earliest childhood under a thrifty father, who valued only the money-making <entity>desires</entity>, and felt contempt for the unnecessary <entity>desires</entity> whose aim is entertainment or display. Is that right?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘When he met more sophisticated men, who were full of the <entity>desires</entity> we have just described, hatred of his father’s stinginess made him plunge into excess of every kind, and into these people’s kind of behaviour. However, because he had a better nature than those who were corrupting him, he was drawn in both directions, and finished up midway between the two positions. He enjoyed the benefits of each in moderation — or so he thought - and led a life that was neither mean nor lawless. In this way he developed from the oligarchic type into the <entity>democratic</entity>.'
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes,’ he said. ‘That was — and still is — our opinion about this kind of person.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Imagine, in that case, that someone like this has now grown old in his turn, and that again a young son has been brought up in his father’s way of life.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘All right, I’m imagining that.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Now imagine further that the same happens to him as happened to his father before him. He is led into all kinds of lawlessness — or “liberty,” as those who are leading him call it. His father and the rest of his household come to the support of the intermediate <entity>desires</entity>, while his seducers support his other <entity>desires</entity>. When these cunning magicians and <entity>tyrant</entity>-makers despair of keeping control of him any other way, they contrive to implant in him a kind of <entity>lust</entity> or <entity>passion</entity>,<footnote id="3">‘Lust or passion’ translates <entity>erōs</entity>, which in Greek normally means the kind of love we fall in rather than the love we bear to family or friends; hence it also refers to sexual passion, and, by extension, any vehement desire. It is in addition the name for <entity>Love</entity> personified, who was depicted on vase-paintings of the time as a winged boy-god. Plato exploits this semantic range, particularly its darker reaches, in describing the <entity>tyrannical</entity> character. The word is variously translated ‘passion’, ‘lust’ (or ‘Lust’) or ‘<entity>Eros</entity>’, according to context. Cross-ref: Mythic Eros (fn. 4).</footnote> a champion of those idle <entity>desires</entity> which want to consume whatever is available, a kind of giant winged drone. Isn’t that the only description for the <entity>lust</entity> found in people of this kind?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘The only possible description, if you ask me.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Very well. When the other <entity>desires</entity> come buzzing round, full of incense, perfumes, garlands, wine and the dissolute pleasures typical of such gatherings, they feed this drone, help it grow to an enormous size, and so plant the sting of yearning in it. Then this champion of the soul takes <entity>madness</entity> for its bodyguard, and goes berserk. If it detects in the man any <entity>desires</entity> or opinions which can be regarded as decent and which still feel some sense of shame, it kills them off or banishes them from its presence, until it has purged the soul of restraint and filled it with foreign <entity>madness</entity>.'
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, that’s a perfect description of the way a <entity>tyrannical man</entity> comes into being.’

**Argument Structure** (Extracted):
- **Premise 1**: <entity>Democratic man</entity>: Balanced from oligarchic thrift to excess (moderation illusion).
- **Premise 2**: Son corrupted by "seducers" implanting <entity>Eros</entity> (drone lust), purging shame via <entity>madness</entity>.
- **Conclusion**: <entity>Tyrannical man</entity> emerges from democratic via unchecked <entity>desires</entity>; soul enslaved.
- **Relationship**: Generational cycle mirrors regime degeneration (cross-ref: 568d–569c); <entity>Eros</entity> as internal tyrant.

### Section: 573d–574c (Book 9: Nature of Eros and Tyrannical Life)
**Context**: <entity>Eros</entity> as tyrant; life of excess leading to crime. Cross-ref: Cosmic/mythic <entity>Love</entity> (fn. 4).

**Dialogue**:
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Is that the kind of reason, then,’ I asked, ‘why <entity>Eros</entity> has traditionally been called a <entity>tyrant</entity>?’<footnote id="4">In myth and in poetry the irresistible power of <entity>love</entity> over men and gods is frequently acknowledged. <entity>Love</entity> also figures as a primeval and mighty power in some traditions and speculations concerning the origins of the cosmos. Cross-ref: Plato's *Symposium* on Eros.</footnote>
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Probably,’ he said.
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And does a man who is drunk also have something of the <entity>tyrant</entity> in him, my friend?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘He does.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And of course someone who is mad or deranged attempts to rule over gods as well as men, and imagines himself capable of doing so.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Absolutely.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Strictly speaking, then, a man becomes <entity>tyrannical</entity> when either his nature or his habits, or both, lead him to drink, <entity>lust</entity> and <entity>madness</entity>.'
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Precisely.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘That is the origin of the <entity>tyrannical man</entity> in his turn, apparently. But what is his life like?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘This is like one of those question-and-answer jokes. All right, then, I don’t know. What _is_ the <entity>tyrannical man</entity>’s life like?’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘I’ll tell you. The next step, I think, for those in whom <entity>Lust</entity> dwells as an internal <entity>tyrant</entity>, directing the entire course of their soul, is for there to be feasting and parties, celebrations and call-girls, and everything of that sort.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, there’s bound to be.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And each day and night countless unspeakable <entity>desires</entity>, with countless needs, spring up in addition, don’t they?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Yes, countless.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Any source of income there may be is speedily exhausted.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Of course.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘After that comes borrowing, and drawing on his capital.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Naturally.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And when it’s all gone, isn’t there bound to be an outcry from the dense mass of fledgling <entity>desires</entity>? When people are driven both by the stings of the other <entity>desires</entity> and in particular by <entity>Lust</entity> itself, which stands at the head of them all like a <entity>tyrant</entity> at the head of his bodyguard, aren’t they bound to run amok, and start looking for anyone with anything which can be taken from them by deception or force?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘They certainly are,’ he said.
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘They have no choice, then, but to help themselves to anything they can lay their hands on, or else find themselves labouring in the grip of pain and agony.’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘No, they have no choice at all.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘The behaviour of the <entity>tyrannical man</entity> himself is just like that of the pleasures within him, isn’t it? They came along after the older pleasures, took over from them and usurped their enjoyment. Won’t he, young as he is, make up his mind in the same way to take over from his father and mother and usurp what is theirs, awarding himself a share in his father’s property now that he has spent what is his own?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Of course he will,’ he said.
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘If they refuse, won’t his first resort be theft and fraud against his parents?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘Absolutely.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘And whenever he can’t get away with that, won’t his next step be to seize what he wants by force?’
- <speaker>Adeimantus</speaker>: ‘I imagine so.’
- <speaker>Socrates</speaker>: ‘Really? And if the old man and the old woman resist him, and put up a fight, how careful will he be to steer clear of anything <entity>tyrannical</entity>?’

## Text Type Identification
This excerpt is a **dialogue** in the form of a Socratic treatise on political philosophy and ethics. It features conversational exchanges but builds a structured argument via analogy (soul-city) and inductive reasoning. The dialogue advances Plato's theory of <entity>justice</entity> by contrasting the <entity>tyrannical soul</entity> with ideal forms, emphasizing internal harmony over external power.

### Section 1: 574e–575a (Socrates and Adeimantus: Origins of Tyrannical Impiety)
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic*, Book 9, 574e–575a.  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Adeimantus.  
**Context**: Socrates questions the impious acts of a man dominated by <entity>Lust</entity>, contrasting essential (<entity>kin</entity>) vs. inessential attachments.

- **Socrates**: ‘For god’s sake, Adeimantus, are you saying that for something inessential, like his latest mistress, someone like this would come to blows with his mother, dear to him all his life, his essential kin? And for an inessential such as his latest pretty boy, would he come to blows with his father, who is aged, past his prime, essential to him, and the oldest of those dear to him? And if he brought these people under the same roof, would he enslave his parents to them?’
- **Adeimantus**: ‘Heavens, yes.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Blessed are those, apparently, who produce a tyrannical son.’
- **Adeimantus**: ‘Blessed indeed,’ he said.

**Extracted Argument Structure**:
1. **Premise**: The <entity>tyrannical man</entity> prioritizes <entity>Lust</entity>-driven attachments (mistress, pretty boy) over <entity>essential kin</entity> (parents).
2. **Evidence**: Hypothetical scenario of violence and <entity>enslavement</entity> toward parents.
3. **Conclusion**: Parents of such a son are ironically "blessed" (sarcastic; implies curse).  
**Philosophical Entities Marked**: <entity>tyrannical son</entity>, <entity>Lust</entity> (implied as driver), <entity>essential kin</entity>, <entity>enslavement</entity>.

### Section 2: 575a–e (Socrates and Adeimantus: Escalation to Crime and Tyranny of the Soul)
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic*, Book 9, 575a–e.  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Adeimantus.  
**Context**: Describes the <entity>tyrannical man</entity>'s progression from minor crimes to total lawlessness, ruled by <entity>Lust</entity> as a <entity>tyrant</entity>.

- **Socrates**: ‘How about when his father’s and mother’s possessions start to run out, and the swarm of pleasures now accumulated within him has grown large? Won’t someone like this turn his hand, initially, to a little gentle house­breaking, or to the cloak of some late traveller - and follow that up with a clean sweep of some temple? In all these exploits, his original childhood opinions about good and bad, opinions which are generally regarded as right, will be overwhelmed by those new opinions just released from slavery, which are the bodyguard of <entity>Lust</entity>, and act in company with it. Previously, while he was still under the control of the laws and of his father, and his mind was a <entity>democracy</entity>, they were set free only in sleep, as dreams, but now that he is tyrannised by <entity>Lust</entity>, and has become per­manently, in his waking life, that which he used to be only occasionally, in his dreams, there will be no foul murder, no food, no deed, from which he will abstain. <entity>Lust</entity> will dwell within him as a <entity>tyrant</entity>, in total anarchy and lawlessness. As you’d expect of a sole ruler, it will lead its possessor, like a <entity>tyrant</entity> leading a <entity>city</entity>, into every kind of outrage, as it attempts to provide upkeep for itself and the mob surrounding it - some of them brought in from outside, the result of the bad company the man keeps, others native to him, released and liberated by the same bad habits in himself. Isn’t that an accurate picture of the life of the <entity>tyrannical man</entity>?’
- **Adeimantus**: ‘It is,’ he said.

**Extracted Argument Structure**:
1. **Premise**: Resource depletion forces initial crimes (housebreaking, theft, temple robbery).
2. **Mechanism**: Childhood <entity>virtue</entity> (opinions of good/bad) is overthrown by <entity>Lust</entity>'s "bodyguard" (new, enslaved opinions now freed).
3. **Analogy**: <entity>Soul as democracy</entity> → <entity>tyranny</entity>; dreams become waking reality.
4. **Conclusion**: The <entity>tyrannical man</entity> lives in internal <entity>anarchy</entity>, driven by <entity>Lust</entity> like a <entity>city</entity> by a <entity>tyrant</entity>, surrounded by imported/native vices.  
**Philosophical Entities Marked**: <entity>Lust</entity>, <entity>democracy</entity> (soul-state), <entity>tyrant</entity>, <entity>city</entity>, <entity>anarchy</entity>, <entity>lawlessness</entity>, <entity>tyrannical man</entity>.

### Section 3: 575b–c (Socrates: Minor Crimes and Rise to Tyranny in the City)
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic*, Book 9, 575b–c (minor emendation from text: "cIt is" likely "It is").  
**Speakers**: Socrates (implied continuation; Adeimantus responds earlier).  
**Context**: Shifts to societal impact; <entity>tyrannical men</entity> as precursors to <entity>tyranny</entity> in the <entity>city</entity>.

- **Socrates**: ‘If there are not many of them in a <entity>city</entity>, if most of the population is sensible, people like this emigrate. They become bodyguards to some foreign <entity>tyrant</entity>, or serve as mercenaries, if they can find a war somewhere. But if they arise at a time of peace and quiet, then they stay where they are, and commit all sorts of minor crimes in the <entity>city</entity>.’
- **Adeimantus**: ‘What sort of crimes?’
- **Socrates**: ‘Theft, housebreaking, picking pockets, stealing clothes, robbing temples, kidnapping. Malicious prosecution, perhaps, if they are per­suasive speakers, perjury, accepting bribes.’
- **Adeimantus**: ‘Minor crimes? Only if the people committing them are few in number.’
- **Socrates**: ‘No, they _are_ minor,’ I said. ‘Minor crimes are defined with reference to major crimes. And when it comes to the wretchedness and misery of the <entity>city</entity>, none of these can hold a candle, as the saying goes, to the <entity>tyrant</entity>.[^5] When you get a large number of these people in a <entity>city</entity>, and others following them, when they become aware of their own numbers, then it is they, aided and abetted by the folly of the common people, who give birth to the <entity>tyrant</entity> - that one who stands out among them as possessing the greatest and most bloated <entity>tyrant</entity> in the <entity>soul</entity> within him.’
- **Adeimantus**: ‘Very probably,’ he said. ‘After all, he would be the most <entity>tyrannical</entity>.’
- **Socrates**: ‘That’s assuming they submit to him willingly. If the <entity>city</entity> does not prove compliant, then he will punish his country in its turn, if he can, in the same way as he punished his mother and father earlier. He will bring in new, foreign friends, and he will keep in <entity>slavery</entity> to them the fatherland — or motherland, as the Cretans call it - he once loved. That is how he will cherish it. And this would be the ultimate goal at which the <entity>tyrannical man</entity>’s desire is directed.’
- **Adeimantus**: ‘It certainly is.’

**Extracted Argument Structure**:
1. **Premise**: Isolated <entity>tyrannical men</entity> emigrate or commit minor crimes (theft, perjury, etc.).

### Section 4: 576a–c (Socrates and Glaucon: Private Life of the Tyrannical Man)
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic*, Book 9, 576a–c.  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon (Glaucon now primary).  
**Context**: Examines pre-power <entity>tyrannical man</entity>'s relationships; lack of true <entity>friendship</entity> or <entity>freedom</entity>.

- **Socrates**: ‘And what are they like as private individuals before they come to power? Shall I tell you? The company they keep, for a start. They either associate with people who flatter them, who are prepared to do anything for them. Or if they want something from someone, they get down on their knees themselves, and have no hesitation in putting on a full show of being close friends. Once they’ve got what they want, then they are strangers.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Complete strangers.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Throughout their life, then, they are never friends with anybody. They are always one man’s master and another man’s slave. The <entity>tyrannical</entity> nature never gets a taste of <entity>freedom</entity> or true <entity>friendship</entity>.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Exactly.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Wouldn’t we be right in calling people like this distrustful?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Of course we would.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Not to mention <entity>unjust</entity> - outstandingly <entity>unjust</entity>, if we were correct in our earlier conclusions about the kind of thing <entity>justice</entity> is.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Which we undoubtedly were,’ he said.
- **Socrates**: ‘Let us sum up this worst of all men. He is, I take it, the waking em­bodiment of the kind of man we described as existing in dreams.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Precisely.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Anyone with a highly <entity>tyrannical</entity> nature who becomes sole ruler ends up like this. And the longer he spends in his <entity>tyranny</entity>, the more like this he becomes.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Inevitably,’ said Glaucon, taking up the argument.
- **Socrates**: ‘Well, then, will whoever proves to be the most wicked prove also to be the most unhappy? And will be the one who is <entity>tyrant</entity> for the longest time, who is <entity>tyrant</entity> to the fullest extent, prove, if truth be told, the most unhappy, and for the longest time? Though mind you, for the general run of people, it’s a question of everyone having their own opinion.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘That _has_ to be true, of course.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Isn’t it the case that the <entity>tyrannical man</entity> corresponds to and resem­bles the <entity>city</entity> ruled by a <entity>tyrant</entity>? And that the <entity>democratic man</entity> corresponds to the <entity>city</entity> ruled democratically? And the others like­wise?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Yes, of course.’
- **Socrates**: ‘And is the comparison between man and man, when it comes to goodness and happiness, the same as the comparison between <entity>city</entity> and <entity>city</entity>?’

### Section 5: 576d–577c (Socrates and Glaucon: Comparative Happiness of Souls and Cities)
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic*, Book 9, 576d–577c.  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon.  
**Context**: Compares <entity>tyrannical city/soul</entity> to ideal <entity>monarchy</entity>; true judgment requires internal insight.

- **Glaucon**: ‘Naturally.’
- **Socrates**: ‘In terms of goodness, then, what is the relation between a <entity>city</entity> ruled by a <entity>tyrant</entity> and a <entity>monarchy</entity> of the kind we described as the first of our regimes?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘They are exact opposites,’ he said. ‘One is the best, the other is the worst.’
- **Socrates**: ‘I won’t ask which is which, because it’s obvious. But when it comes to happiness and unhappiness, is your verdict still the same, or different? And let’s not dazzle ourselves by looking at one individual - the <entity>tyrant</entity> or at some few who surround him. No, since the entire <entity>city</entity> is the proper object of our journey and enquiry, let us not present our opinion to the world until we have burrowed our way right into the heart of the <entity>city</entity>, and viewed the whole thing.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘That’s a fair requirement,’ he said. ‘Anyone can see that there is no unhappier <entity>city</entity> than the one ruled by a <entity>tyrant</entity>, and no happier <entity>city</entity> than the one ruled by a <entity>king</entity>.’
- **Socrates**: ‘And would it be fair to impose the same requirement when it comes to the men as well, if I think that the best judge of these matters is the person who can mentally worm his way into a man’s character, and take a long, hard look at it? He must not see it from the outside, like a child, and be dazzled by the display of grandeur which <entity>tyrants</entity> put on for outward show, but must look at it fairly and squarely. And if I were to think that we should all listen to the man who is qualified to form a judgment, who has lived under the same roof as a <entity>tyrant</entity>, who has been in a <entity>tyrant</entity>’s company and seen his behaviour - both in his private life, the way he deals with each member of his household, where he can best be seen stripped of his theatrical costume and props, and then again in public, when he is in danger - should we tell the person who has seen all this to give us his report on how the <entity>tyrant</entity> compares, in terms of happiness and unhappiness, with other people?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Yes, it would be absolutely correct to impose this requirement as well.’
- **Socrates**: ‘In which case,’ I said, ‘do you want us to pretend that _we_ are among those who would be qualified to form a judgment, and who have met <entity>tyrants</entity> in the past? That would at least give us someone to answer our questions.[^6]’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Yes, please.’

**Extracted Argument Structure**:
1. **Premise**: <entity>Tyrannical city</entity> opposites <entity>monarchy</entity> in goodness (worst vs. best).
2. **Method**: Judge happiness by internal view, not external pomp; eyewitness testimony preferred.
3. **Application**: Extend to souls; Plato/Socrates as qualified judges.[^6]  
**Philosophical Entities Marked**: <entity>city</entity>, <entity>tyrant</entity>, <entity>monarchy</entity>, <entity>happiness</entity>, <entity>unhappiness</entity>, <entity>tyrants</entity>, <entity>king</entity>.  
**Cross-Reference**: Ideal <entity>monarchy</entity> from Books 5–7 (philosopher-kings); <entity>happiness</entity> as <entity>virtue</entity>-aligned life (Book 1).

### Section 6: 577c–578e (Socrates and Glaucon: Enslavement and Misery in Tyrannical City/Soul)
**Citation**: Plato, *The Republic*, Book 9, 577c–578e.  
**Speakers**: Socrates, Glaucon.  
**Context**: Point-by-point analogy: <entity>tyrannical city/soul</entity> as enslaved, poor, fearful.

- **Socrates**: ‘Can I ask you to go about it like this, then? Remembering the similar­ity between the <entity>city</entity> and the man, examine each of them in turn, point by point, and tell us how things are for each of them.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘What sort of things?’ he asked.
- **Socrates**: ‘Start with the <entity>city</entity>. Are you going to describe a <entity>city</entity> ruled by a <entity>tyrant</entity> as free or enslaved?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Enslaved. As enslaved as it is possible to be.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Though of course you can see masters and free men in it.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘I can see a small element of that,’ he said. ‘Not much. But more or less the whole thing - and certainly the most decent element in it - is shame­fully and miserably enslaved.’
- **Socrates**: ‘In which case,’ I said, ‘if the man is like the <entity>city</entity>, won’t we inevitably find the same arrangement of elements in him as well? Won’t we find his <entity>soul</entity> crammed with all sorts of <entity>slavery</entity> and servility, with those parts of his <entity>soul</entity> enslaved which used to be the most decent, and a small element, the most evil and insane, possessing the mastery?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Yes. Inevitably.’
- **Socrates**: ‘All right, then. What are you going to call a <entity>soul</entity> of this kind? Slave or free?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Slave, I guess. Well, that’s my opinion, anyway.’
- **Socrates**: ‘And the slave <entity>city</entity>, the <entity>city</entity> ruled by a <entity>tyrant</entity>, is the one least able to do what it wants.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘By far the least.’
- **Socrates**: ‘In which case, the <entity>soul</entity> which is ruled by a <entity>tyrant</entity> will also be least able to do what it wants - at any rate if we are talking about the entire <entity>soul</entity>. Despite itself, it will be forever driven onward by the gadfly of desire, and filled with confusion and dissatisfaction.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Of course it will.’
- **Socrates**: ‘And is it certain to be rich or certain to be poor, this <entity>city</entity> ruled by a <entity>tyrant</entity>?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Certain to be poor.’
- **Socrates**: ‘So the <entity>tyrannical soul</entity> too is certain always to be impoverished and insatiable.’
- **Glaucon**: ‘True,’ he said.
- **Socrates**: ‘What about fear? Aren’t the <entity>tyrannical city</entity> and the <entity>tyrannical man</entity> bound to be full of it?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘Yes. Bound to be. Inevitably.’
- **Socrates**: ‘Do you think there is any other <entity>city</entity> in which you will find more wailing, groaning, lamentation and grief?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘No.’
- **Socrates**: ‘And in a man - do you think anyone possesses these qualities more abundantly than this <entity>tyrannical individual</entity>, maddened as he is by desires and lusts?’
- **Glaucon**: ‘No, that’s impossible,’ he said.

**Extracted Argument Structure**:
1. **Point 1 (Enslavement)**: <entity>Tyrannical city/soul</entity>: Mostly enslaved; best parts subjugated by worst.
2. **Point 2 (Freedom/Action)**: Least able to act on true wants; driven by insatiable desires.
3. **Point 3 (Wealth)**: Impoverished and insatiable.
4. **Point 4 (Fear/Grief)**: Filled with fear, lamentation; <entity>tyrannical man</entity> most afflicted.  
**Conclusion**: <entity>Tyrannical city</entity> unhappiest (agreed).
